text:
🚨 A new ADB presentation strips the rare-earth debate down to cold, hard numbers, and exposes where the supply chain is really vulnerable. 🧲🌍

⛏️🧪⚗️🔥🔬🧲

⛏️The rare-earth problem is not simply a shortage of mines. As we all know by now! 

🧪It is the extreme concentration of processing, ⚗️Separation and 🔥Metallisation and 🔬manufacturing capabilities that convert an unusual deposit into a qualified 🧲permanent magnet.

According to the Asian Development Bank’s June 2026 Rare Earth Elements Overview:

⛏️🧪 China supplies approximately 60% of magnet rare-earth feedstock

⚗️🔥 China controls approximately 91% of refining

🔬🧲 China produces approximately 94% of permanent magnets

🌏 Yet China represents only around 50% of magnet demandasiacleanenergyforum.

📍The supply chain becomes more concentrated, not less, as material moves downstream.

📍Not all deposits are equal

⚠️The ADB divides the Nd-based magnet feedstock universe into several broad geological sources. Its percentages are explicitly indicative, but they highlight why tonnes of “rare-earth resource” cannot be compared without understanding mineralogy, grade, recoveries and element distribution.

🪨 Carbonatites: the LREE workhorses

Carbonatites are unusual carbonate-rich igneous rocks and have supplied most of the world’s light rare earths since the 1960s. They commonly contain bastnäsite and monazite and are generally weighted toward lanthanum, cerium, praseodymium and neodymium.

Examples include:

🔹 Mountain Pass in the US
🔹 Mount Weld in Western Australia, where weathering enriched the carbonatite
🔹 Bayan Obo and Maoniuping in China

These deposits can offer large tonnage and comparatively high grades, but they usually produce far more low-value La/Ce than scarce heavy magnet elements such as Dy and Tb.

🏖️ Heavy-mineral sands, HMS 

Heavy-mineral sands, or HMS, form when water and gravity concentrate dense minerals in coastal, river and ancient placer environments.

⛏️They are generally mined for minerals such as ilmenite, rutile and zircon, with rare-earth-bearing monazite or xenotime recovered as potential by-products. Monazite is normally LREE-rich, while xenotime can carry more yttrium and heavy rare earths.

Examples include:

🔹 Eneabba, Western Australia, a historic mineral-sands district where monazite and xenotime occur with ilmenite, rutile and zircon; Iluka is now recovering a rare-earth-rich stockpile.

🔹 Donald, Victoria, a development-stage WIM-style deposit containing monazite and xenotime alongside zircon and titanium minerals.

🔹 WIM150/Wimmera, Victoria, another large fine-grained mineral-sands deposit containing substantial monazite and xenotime resources.

🔹 Indian and Brazilian coastal placers, long-established mineral-sands districts where monazite has historically been recovered alongside titanium minerals and zircon.

The challenge is that these minerals may also contain thorium or uranium, making radioactive-residue management, permitting and downstream processing central to project economics.

🌋 Alkaline intrusives
Alkaline and peralkaline igneous systems can contain broader and sometimes more HREE-enriched baskets than typical carbonatites.

Examples include:

🔹 Strange Lake, Canada, a peralkaline-granite deposit enriched in zirconium, yttrium and heavy rare earths.

🔹 Nechalacho at Thor Lake, Canada, a layered alkaline-intrusion deposit containing both light and heavy rare-earth mineralisation.

🔹 Norra Kärr, Sweden, a peralkaline intrusion noted for its unusually high proportion of heavy rare earths.

🔹 Bokan Mountain, Alaska, a peralkaline system containing complex REE-yttrium mineralisation distributed across numerous minerals.

🔹 Kvanefjeld and Kringlerne, Greenland, large deposits hosted by the Ilímaussaq alkaline complex.

🔹 Dubbo, New South Wales, an advanced Australian polymetallic project hosted by an alkaline volcanic complex.

These systems can contain attractive quantities of Dy, Tb, Y and other heavy rare earths without producing the same overwhelming La/Ce volumes as many carbonatites.

But their rare earths may be distributed across complex silicate minerals that are difficult to beneficiate, crack and separate. A valuable basket does not automatically produce a simple or economic flowsheet.

🟤 Ionic-adsorption clays

Ionic clays are completely different from conventional hard-rock ores.

Weathering releases rare-earth ions from the underlying rock, and those ions become weakly adsorbed onto clay particles. Grades can be low, but the material may avoid the energy-intensive crushing and mineral cracking required for hard rock because the rare earths can be desorbed through leaching.

Examples include:

🔹 Southern China’s Jiangxi, Guangdong and neighbouring districts, the historic foundation of China’s heavy rare-earth industry.

🔹 Myanmar’s ionic-clay districts, an important upstream source feeding China’s separation industry.

🔹 Pela Ema/Serra Verde, Brazil, in commercial production since 2024 and producing Nd, Pr, Dy and Tb from weathered ionic-clay saprolite.

🔹 Makuutu, Uganda, a development-stage ionic-adsorption clay project with approximately 45% of its product basket comprising heavy rare earths, including strategically important Dy and Tb.

🔹 Caldeira, Brazil, a large development-stage clay-hosted project with completed feasibility work and substantial NdPr potential.

🔹 Colossus, Brazil, a development-stage weathered-clay project in the Poços de Caldas alkaline complex, targeting production of magnet rare earths.x

These deposits can have much lower grades than hard-rock mines, but they may avoid conventional crushing, grinding and high-temperature mineral cracking where the rare earths are genuinely ionically adsorbed.

Some ionic-adsorption clays contain disproportionately valuable dysprosium, terbium and yttrium, which is why southern China’s clays became the world’s primary historical source of heavy rare earths.

⚠️ But “ionic clay” does not automatically mean HREE-rich. Each project must be judged by its individual Nd, Pr, Dy and Tb distribution, recoveries, leach chemistry, reagent consumption and environmental performance.

The hidden pinch point

The ADB values the Nd-based permanent-magnet chain at approximately US$6–7 billion:

🔹 Upstream feedstock: US$3–4 billion
🔹 Midstream processing: approximately US$1 billion
🔹 Downstream magnets and end use: approximately US$2 billion

⚗️🔥One of my favourite subjects, the smallest segment by headline value, separation and metallisation, is arguably the most strategically important.

A mine typically produces a mixed concentrate, carbonate or oxide. That material must then be:

1️⃣ Cracked or leached
2️⃣ Separated into individual rare-earth oxides
3️⃣ Converted into metals
4️⃣ Blended into magnet alloys
5️⃣ Manufactured into qualified NdFeB magnets

Mining more ore does not solve the strategic problem if the concentrate still has to pass through China for separation, metalmaking or magnet production. ⚗️➡️🧲

Four elements dominate

The ADB identifies four magnet rare earths that drive much of the sector’s value:

🔹 Neodymium and praseodymium provide the magnetic strength

🔹 Dysprosium and terbium help high-performance NdFeB magnets retain coercivity under demanding thermal conditions

La and Ce may dominate physical production from many deposits, but Nd, Pr, Dy and Tb largely determine the strategic and economic value of the magnet basket.

Demand is global

Permanent-magnet demand in 2024 was distributed across:

📱 Consumer electronics: 30%
🚗 Automotive, including EVs: 29%
🌬️ Wind turbines: 19%
🤖 Industrial robotics: 4%
🛡️ Defence: 4%
⚙️ Other applications: 14%

🇨🇳China may control the production chain, but the magnets power factories, vehicles, turbines, electronics and defence systems around the world.

That is why this is not simply a mining story. It is an industrial-capability story.

♻️🧲Recycling matters

The ADB diagram shows recycling entering at multiple stages, from processing residues and metal production to manufacturing scrap and end-of-life magnets.

🔗https://t.co/TXQ4WJB8Kq

But recycling is not one universal loop:

♻️ Clean production scrap can sometimes return directly to alloy or magnet manufacturing

♻️ Mixed or contaminated magnets may require liberation, leaching and full separation

♻️ End-of-life supply remains constrained by collection, dismantling and the long service life of EV motors and wind turbines

Recycling will become increasingly important, but it complements primary supply rather than eliminating the need for mines, separation plants and metalmaking capacity.

The real message

The world is diversifying rare-earth mining faster than it is diversifying separation, metallisation and magnet manufacturing.

China’s advantage is not just geology. It is the integrated system connecting feedstock, chemical separation, metals, alloys, magnet IP, equipment, skilled workers and qualified customers.

⛏️ A resource is not a separated oxide.
⚗️ An oxide is not a metal or alloy.
🧲 An alloy is not a qualified magnet.
⚙️ And a magnet is not yet a finished motor or component.

The countries that master every conversion step, not merely the mine, will control the next generation of EVs, robotics, wind power, electronics and defence manufacturing. 🌍🧲

text:
🚨⚗️ Magnet recycling has an uncomfortable truth: the scrap can run short for now, Very early stages of EOL products, We all know this 

BUT!

⛏️⚒️🧲The winners will hold separation IP that Process ANY rare earth feed, and scales BOTH ways: small enough for today's scrap, big enough for the MREC wave coming late this decade. Same plant, every market, every year. 🧵

🔀 Same Universe, New Lens

📍Regular followers have seen my feedstock universe ranked by value density, swarf wins that one (~36% of magnet RE value, nearly free). 

📍This is the SAME six streams ranked by a different question: how close is each feed to a separation circuit?

1️⃣ MREC, mixed carbonate dissolves straight into separation. Zero liberation.

2️⃣ MREO & SEG+ concentrates, already concentrated, enters mid-circuit

3️⃣ Manufacturing swarf, demag and leach, but no dismantling

4️⃣ EOL magnets, the full collection-and-liberation chain runs first

5️⃣ Phosphors, niche chemistry, dispersed collection

6️⃣ E-waste, logistically unviable at scale

📍Two rankings, zero contradiction: value tells you what feed is worth chasing. Distance tells you whose plant never sits idle.

🧪 Why Feed-Agnostic Chemistry Is THE Moat

♻️A recycler locked to clean magnet feed runs at whatever the scrap supply allows, and the US import data I posted shows how thin and slow that supply arrives. A feed-agnostic platform swings:

📉 Scrap tight? Buy carbonate and fill the plant.

📈 Scrap wave lands? Swing the same circuit to magnets.

🏭 Utilisation is the entire game in processing economics, idle separation capacity burns cash no matter how elegant the chemistry.

And no, taking mined feed isn't a bolt-on: carbonates bring gangue and radionuclides, permits, thorium handling. That's exactly why chemistry that separates ANY feed is a moat and not a feature.

⚗️ The Chemistry, Six Routes, Different Appetites

I ran a full series on the separation technologies. Read them by what they can Process, not by their purity claims:

🔬 Counter-current SX, P204/P507 in kerosene, 100–1,000 mixer-settler stages. Eats ore concentrates, MREC, mixed REO at 98–99.9%+. The proven workhorse, and the reason China owns midstream. Cost: colossal footprint, ammonia wastewater, reagent dependency on China.

🔬 Intensified column SX, same chemistry, mixer-settlers replaced by packed columns. 3× faster mass transfer, ~⅓ the footprint, >50% lower capex, and reconfigurable for any feedstock.

🔬 LAD chromatography, EDTA/DTPA isotachic trains on titania sorbent. No VOCs, no organophosphorus extractants. Eats magnet leachate, ore concentrates AND battery black mass at 99.5–99.999%.

🔬 MAIL extraction, task-specific ionic liquids exploiting a 2.6Å vs 2.9Å coordination difference to grab Dy and Tb while La and Ce stay in the aqueous phase. ~15 stages instead of 150+. Eats EOL magnets AND ionic-clay MREC AND ore concentrate. ~61% lower CO₂ than primary mining.

🔬 Membrane SX, TODGA immobilised in hollow polypropylene fibres; extraction and back-extraction across one wall. No emulsions, no flooding, zero Fe/Cu/Ni co-extraction. Eats magnet scrap and PCB/e-waste leachates.

🔬 Solvometallurgy, separation in non-aqueous media, which fundamentally alters solvation thermodynamics and amplifies LREE/HREE separation factors. Direct Dy/Tb enrichment, no process wastewater. Advanced pilot.

🧩 Here's the pattern that matters: every new route scales by REPLICATION, more columns, more modules, more container trains. Traditional SX scales by vessel size and stage count. 

That's why the new chemistries fit today's thin scrap feeds so neatly, and it's exactly where their scale-up question lives: replication de-risks each unit, but reaching 10,000 tpa means multiplying units AND the sorbent, solvent and reagent supply chains that feed them. Modularity is a genuine advantage, as long as the module count and its consumables can actually be manufactured.

⏳ The Two Clocks, Scale Is A Filter

Feed-agnostic only wins if plant size matches the feed curve, and there are two curves on different clocks:

🧲 Magnet scrap: thin today, building through the 2030s as EVs and turbines retire. Recyclers must START SMALL, demo scale now, hundreds of tonnes next, thousands only when the wave arrives. 

🏭Oversized plants starve. Modular plants follow the feed.

⛏️ Western MREC & concentrates: carbonate from new Western sources, ionic clays in Uganda and Brazil, new hard-rock projects, doesn't land in volume until late this decade into the early 2030s. When it does, separators need trains that MULTIPLY.

🧪⚗️And here's the filter almost nobody prices in. The new separation chemistries , MAIL, LAD chromatography, membrane SX, intensified columns, solvometallurgy, are real advances on 60-year-old solvent extraction. 

But traditional SX holds the one credential none of them have yet: proven at 10,000+ tpa. China runs it at that scale every single day.
https://t.co/Bl2j7c4d0a

The new IPs scale DOWN brilliantly — that's their whole design win, and it fits today's scrap reality. The unanswered question is UP. Some will stall between demo and commercial train: solvent lifetime, sorbent cycles, hydraulics at diameter, reagent logistics. The ones that prove the scale-up inherit the feed, and acquire the ones that don't.

That's why a demo plant running 24/7 for 30+ months matters more than any flowsheet: scale-up risk retires one proven step at a time.

🌍 The Field, And How To Read It

The Landscape graphic below shows the ten Western players. Read it through the two-clock lens: feed breadth on paper is table stakes, converting it into certified purity at commercial scale is the whole game.

The separation platforms, I covered all six chemistries in my separation series, on paper their feedstock lines span magnets, carbonate and concentrates: MAIL in Belfast, dual-feed SX at Lacq, the La Rochelle heritage circuit, chromatography and membrane systems in the US, accelerated column SX in Canada.

📍The public signals that separate paper from plant:

✅ Continuous demo hours, thousands, run 24/7, not campaign weeks

✅ Third-party purity validation, a customer's certificate beats your own assay

✅ Binding offtakes with quality clauses, someone betting money on your spec

✅ A funded commercial train, not a rendering of one

The complementary layers (feeders, not competitors):

🏗️ Cyclic, mechanical liberation at scale; its MREO feeds the separators

🧲 HyProMag & Noveon, short-loop magnet-to-magnet, no separation needed while the magnet spec allows it

Ten players, one pattern: everyone durable either separates any feed and proves it at scale, or feeds those who do.

👀 The Bottom Line

Separation Chemistry that only  process clean magnets starves when scrap tightens. Chemistry that process any Rare Earth Products into high Purity Separated REOs owns the consolidation. Two clocks, one filter: start small enough to survive today's scrap, and prove the scale-up before tomorrow's carbonate lands. Watch who signs MREC offtakes AND magnet supply deals, those are the plants that never sit idle, and the acquirers when single-feed recyclers stall.

DYOR

cemindia projects nse cempro bse 509496. this is not a new company. it started in india in 1931 as a branch of the cementation company uk doing grouting piling and dam repair. in 1978 the india business became a local subsidiary under the cemindia name. over the decades it passed through trafalgar house uk, kvaerner norway and skanska sweden. in 2005 italian-thai development of bangkok bought control and the listed entity ran as itd cementation india. that is the lineage. there is no single indian founder-promoter from day one. it is an old specialist contractor that changed owners several times.

in may 2025 control moved again. renew exim dmcc, an adani group entity linked to vinod adani, bought the 46.64 percent stake from italian-thai and then picked up more in the open offer. promoter holding sits around 67.5 percent. name changed to cemindia projects in august 2025. so the stock you see as cempro is the old itd cem franchise under adani ownership.

current management. chairman is malay mahadevia, non executive, from the adani side. managing director is jayanta basu. civil engineer from iiest shibpur, about 61, nearly four decades inside this company, md since 2019. he is the execution face, not a new hire after the takeover. cfo is nitesh sharma, joined june 2025. company secretary rahul neogi. board independents include manoj kohli, sangeeta bhatia, abizer diwanji. k s rao sits as non executive. operating layer has evps for projects, commercial, tech and business development. culture is still contractor-first. promoter is new. operating bench is old.

what the company actually does. heavy civil epc. maritime structures jetties berths docks. urban infra metro airports. industrial plants and buildings. data centres. water and wastewater. highways bridges flyovers. foundation and specialist geotech piling diaphragm walls. some hydro dams tunnels. not a pure road epc. not a building-only name like psp. closest listed cousins are afcons, parts of l&t, man infra, j kumar, patel on the tunnel hydro side.

order book. this is the core of the story right now. as of 30 june 2026 backlog was about 31307 crore. end fy26 it was 24545 crore. a year earlier around 18000-18800 crore. q1 fy27 alone they booked 8519 crore of new work. july added about 1247 crore. l1 pipeline another ~1000 crore. management target for full fy27 inflows is around 25000 crore. they already have a large chunk in q1.

book mix as of june 2026 roughly: maritime 23 percent, urban infra mrts airports 21 percent, industrial buildings 17 percent, data centre 13 percent, water wastewater 11 percent, highways bridges 8 percent, foundation specialist 4 percent, hydro dams tunnels 2 percent. india is about 98 percent of the book. client mix has swung private-heavy. government plus psu used to dominate. after adani orders, private is now the bigger slice. adani group is about 50 to 53 percent of current backlog. that is the single biggest debate on the stock. captive work gives visibility and bidding edge. it also concentrates counterparty and related-party risk.

q1 fy27 numbers. revenue 2721 crore, up about 6 percent. ebitda 285 crore, margin 10.5 percent versus 10.1 percent last year. pat 141 crore, up about 3 percent. growth in the p and l is lagging the order book on purpose. large new jobs in rajasthan reservoir, data centres, sail plant, delhi underground metro take time to mobilise. fy26 full year revenue was about 10061 crore, pat 598 crore, strong jump in profit versus fy25. net worth around 2400 crore. net debt around 430 to 700 crore depending on the date, net debt to equity near 0.2x. balance sheet is not stretched for an epc of this book size. roce and roe have been high-20s to low-30s on recent prints. that is better than a typical mid-cap contractor.

micro. positives: specialist skills in marine metro underground and foundations that not every ncc-type bidder has. equipment and tbm/piling kit. long bid history with government and now group capex. data centre and water adding new pools. low leverage. working capital needs watching as the book scales. labour shortage is an industry issue they flagged. bangladesh residual work is winding down. vadhavan and a few large sites have had start delays, which is why quarterly revenue can look dull versus the 25000 crore inflow target. related party orders from adani need clean execution and arm-length optics or the multiple compresses.

macro. india is still in a multi-year capex cycle. union capex, state irrigation, metro packages, port capacity, airport city-side, steel plant civil, and private data centres are all live bid pools. management cited a tender pipeline near 90000 crore with a historical hit rate they talk about in the mid teens. if even part of that converts, book can stay 3x sales. risks on the macro side: election and state-level payment cycles, steel and cement inflation eating fixed-price jobs, interest rates if working capital spikes, any freeze or scrutiny on adani group capex, and a general mid-cap derating if fii flows stay weak. cempro beta is high. it moves more than nifty.

technical as of late september 2026. last regular close around 1256 on 21 sep, 52-week range 503 to 1649. market cap near 21700 crore. pe around 36 on ttm earnings, pb around 9. stock ran hard after the adani deal and fy26 profit jump, then gave back a chunk from the july high. 200 dma is near 1040. 50 dma near 1270-1275. price has been wrestling just under the 50 day after the slide from 1649. daily support zone 1235-1250. resistance 1275 then 1340 then the 1490-1650 supply from the top. rsi near mid-40s, macd still soft on daily after the correction. volume on down days has not been panic-level recently. structure from the 500 area is still a large higher-low base, but near term it is a digestion phase not a fresh breakout. a hold above 1200-1230 keeps the intermediate uptrend intact. a close back over 1340-1350 would reopen the high. below 1040-1100 the 200 dma break would change the tape.

valuation frame. you are paying a premium to many road epcs because of marine metro specialist work, clean-ish balance sheet and the adani order engine. you are not paying a bargain versus history after a 50 percent plus one-year move. the bull case is book conversion to 20-25 percent revenue growth with 10-11 percent ebitda held, and the multiple stays because group plus external mix remains. the bear case is q1-style slow billing continues, adani concentration worries rise, and pe mean-reverts toward mid-20s while earnings stall.

text:
Everyone has access to the exact same AI models.

The edge isn’t the prompt. The edge is your pipeline graph, your context brain, and your verification gates.

Here is the exact AI marketing engine we use to turn one half-formed thought into a multi-channel campaign:

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

PHASE 1: PLANNING

1. Raw Voice Ingest
I dictate everything out loud—unfiltered stream-of-consciousness. An ingest skill cleans the mess and compiles a standardized starting brief. (The Karpathy principle: get it out of your head first, structure second).

2. Angle Expansion
The brief auto-generates 10 distinct campaign angles. We cut 80% immediately and keep the 2 sharpest hooks.

3. Context Injection (gBrain + Live Market)
• Internal: Past conversion data, ICP parameters, brand voice rules, and active offer economics.
• External: Live competitor ad formats, trending search volume, and active platform hooks.

4. Synthesis & Model Routing
Opus handles the architectural trade-offs, positioning strategy, and campaign plan. Narrow, low-context sub-tasks get routed to cheap, high-speed models. Never pay flagship token prices for commodity parsing.

5. Verification Gate (Human Sign-Off)
Nothing touches production without manual review. The draft is audited against our brand protocols and SOPs.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

PHASE 2: EXECUTION

6. Graph vs. Loop Execution
• Narrow tasks run in autonomous loops (Draft → Critique → Self-Correct → Verify).
• Multi-asset campaigns run on predefined graphs, routing data between agents automatically.

7. Production Fan-Out
That single idea splits across every commercial asset:
• Single-product landing pages
• Video scripts & short-form hooks
• Automated email nurture flows
• Organic distribution carousels

8. Human-in-the-Loop Taste

text:
The fastest way to kill a good idea? Judge it while you're still having it. ✋

At Stanford, Professor Jonathan Levav named a mistake I've made in almost every brainstorm I've run.

Creativity has two phases, and they must never happen at the same time:

Generation — quantity, variety, wild, no judgment allowed.
Selection — now you evaluate, cut and choose.

The enemy of the first is the little voice (yours or your colleague's) that evaluates each idea the moment it appears. 

"That's too expensive." 
"We tried that." 
"Legal will hate it." 

Every one of those is probably true — and every one shuts the tap off.

It's why most brainstorms quietly fail. Someone offers a half-formed idea, someone else raises their own status by poking a hole in it, and within ten minutes the room has learned to only say safe things.

The fix is almost embarrassingly simple: split the two into separate sessions, and say out loud which one you're in.

"Right now we're only generating — no buts, no budgets. We'll judge on Thursday." 

It feels artificial for about five minutes. Then the ideas get braver.

What's your rule for keeping judgment out of the room while ideas are still forming? 👇

📚 Stay tuned! For the next few weeks I'll continue sharing my key takeaways from Stanford's Senior Executive Programme. Let’s gooooo!

→ Claims SOL outperformed Nasdaq-100 by 54% this quarter

Elon's X launches trade-from-timeline
→ Cashtag Partner Program now connects to Coinbase, Gemini, Kraken, Interactive Brokers & Moomoo
→ Tap a ticker → see chart → hit "Trade" → redirected to the exchange (X doesn't execute trades itself)
→ US-only for now; also rolled out Big Charts + Grok 4.7

Trueo migrates from Base to #Ethereum
→ Prediction market protocol says Ethereum offers deeper liquidity & better long-term fit
→ Vitalik Buterin publicly welcomed the move, calling it "ethical and not corposlop"
→ TRUE token spiked ~940% on the announcement

ECB goes live with Pontes
→ New platform lets banks settle tokenized asset trades in central bank money, an alternative to stablecoins
→ Separate from the retail digital euro, which starts its 12-month pilot in H2 2027
→ Part of ECB's broader push to keep central bank money at the core of tokenized markets

#Ondo lets institutions convert stocks directly
→ New in-kind system: institutions can mint/redeem tokenized stocks using actual shares instead of cash
→ Live on Ethereum & BNB Chain, via Alpaca-approved accounts
→ Ondo now has ~$3.63B in tokenized assets across 441 products

$SEC: first tokenized stock venues could launch next quarter
→ Officials expect firms to start filing operating notices under last week's 5-year exemption order
→ Venues need a named operator, SEC calls it "more onchain finance than DeFi"
→ Issuers get a 30-day veto window before their stock can be tokenized on a venue

Kraken's parent eyes US route for Hyperliquid perps
→ Payward (Kraken) exploring using its regulated Bitnomial exchange/clearing infra for HIP-3 markets
→ Hyperliquid averaged ~$9B in open interest in Q2 2026
→ Still needs regulatory approval,separate from BitGo's existing wallet-based access

Absa launches digital asset custody with Ripple
→ African institutional clients get custody built on Ripple's tech, live now
→ Follows a partnership first announced Oct 2025
→ Details on supported assets/pricing not yet disclosed

Whitehats recover 52 bitcoin:native  from the Coldcard hack
→ Ethical hackers swept 52.37 BTC into a recovery trust address (https://t.co/SYjtSCd3RL)
→ Part of the July Coldcard exploit that caused $100M+ in losses via weak seed generation
→ ~40% of "Wave 2" exploit funds now identified as whitehat-recovered

Circle launches cirBTC + Agora gets preliminary OCC nod
→ Circle Wrapped Bitcoin (cirBTC) now live on Arc,1:1 BTC-backed, usable as collateral to borrow USDC
→ Agora gets preliminary OCC approval for a national trust bank to house stablecoin/custody ops under federal supervision (final approval still pending)

Bottom line: treasuries keep stacking, tokenized stocks are inching toward a real regulatory timeline, and TradFi infrastructure (ECB, OCC, Kraken) is quietly building the rails for all of it.

text:
How I Built a Car Hire Business From Nothing in Murang'a

I started car hire with 2 cars. No office. No team. Just me, my phone, and a dream.

I would wake up at 5 AM, wash the cars myself, post on WhatsApp status, and wait for calls. Some days, no calls. Some days, 3 bookings. But I never gave up.

The first challenge? Clients who would hire the car and disappear. Or return it late. Or return it with damage. I learned quickly: this business is not for the soft-hearted.

So I put rules in place. Every client must sign an agreement. Every car must have a tracker. Every payment must be recorded. No exceptions.

Then something strange happened. Clients started respecting the business more. They saw structure. They saw seriousness. They saw a professional operation — not a hustle. The bookings increased. The reputation grew.

Car hire is not just about cars. It is about trust. Reliability. Clean vehicles. On-time service. Professional communication.

Today, we offer self-drive hire, airport transfers, chauffeur services, corporate logistics, and weddings and events. From 5 seaters to 7 seaters. All clean. All tracked. All ready.

From 2 cars to 7. Not because I was lucky. Because I showed up every day. Because I treated every client like a king. Because I never compromised on structure.

If you need a car in Murang'a  for a day, a week, or a month  we are here. Self-drive. Chauffeur. Airport transfer. Corporate. Wedding. We have you covered.

AI Overview
These three names share a deep linguistic and historical connection, primarily originating in Ancient Mesopotamia, the Middle East, and the Caucasus.
Sargon
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Greek and biblical translation of the Akkadian regnal name Šarru-kīn. It combines šarru (Akkadian for "king") and kīnu (meaning "true," "established," or "legitimate").
Historical Significance: It is most famously associated with Sargon of Akkad (24th century BCE), the legendary founder of the Akkadian Empire. Later, the Neo-Assyrian ruler Sargon II (8th century BCE) adopted the throne name to establish the legitimacy of his rule.
Sargis
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Classical Syriac and Armenian form of the Latin name Sergius. It originates from the ancient Roman gens (clan) Sergia, which etymologists suspect may connect to the Latin verb servare ("to guard" or "to preserve").
Sako
Origin & Etymology: Sako operates on a few different historical tracks depending on the region:
In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.
In the Balkans: In Albania, it functions as a standalone occupational surname for a "church servant" or as a nickname for the Muslim name Isak (Isaac).
In Asia: It is also an unrelated Japanese surname (written as 佐古) meaning "HELP" and "ancient".

LOUIS Raphaël I Sako (Arabic: لويس روفائيل ساكو;[2] born 4 July 1948) is a Chaldean Catholic prelate who served as Patriarch of Baghdad from 2013 to 2026. Pope Francis made him a cardinal in 2018.

Biography
Early life
Sako was born in the city of Zakho, Iraq, on 4 July 1948.[3] He comes from an ethnic Assyrian family of the Chaldean Catholic Church that has roots in a religious community that has had a presence in the city of his birth since the 5th century AD.[4]

He completed his early studies in Mosul and then attended the Dominican-run Saint Jean’s Seminary there. He was ordained a priest on 1 June 1974 and filled his first pastoral assignment at the Cathedral of Mosul until 1979. He then earned a doctorate in Eastern patrology at the Pontifical Oriental Institute. When denied a license to teach because he was only qualified for religious instruction, he earned a second doctorate in history from the Sorbonne in Paris.[5] With this he secured his teaching license and was able to provide religious instruction. From 1997 to 2002 he was rector of the Patriarchal Seminary in Baghdad. He then returned to Mosul and guided the parish of Perpetual HELP for a year.[6][7]

Sako speaks Neo-Aramaic, German, French, English, Italian, Kurdish and Arabic.[3]

AI Overview
These three names share a deep linguistic and historical connection, primarily originating in Ancient Mesopotamia, the Middle East, and the Caucasus.
Sargon
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Greek and biblical translation of the Akkadian regnal name Šarru-kīn. It combines šarru (Akkadian for "king") and kīnu (meaning "true," "established," or "legitimate").
Historical Significance: It is most famously associated with Sargon of Akkad (24th century BCE), the legendary founder of the Akkadian Empire. Later, the Neo-Assyrian ruler Sargon II (8th century BCE) adopted the throne name to establish the legitimacy of his rule.
Sargis
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Classical Syriac and Armenian form of the Latin name Sergius. It originates from the ancient Roman gens (clan) Sergia, which etymologists suspect may connect to the Latin verb servare ("to guard" or "to preserve").
Sako
Origin & Etymology: Sako operates on a few different historical tracks depending on the region:
In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.
In the Balkans: In Albania, it functions as a standalone occupational surname for a "church servant" or as a nickname for the Muslim name Isak (Isaac).
In Asia: It is also an unrelated Japanese surname (written as 佐古) meaning "HELP" and "ancient".

The Lion at the Head of Nubia – Apedemak, heard danger before the watchmen saw dust on the horizon.

In the southern heartland of Kush, between Meroe, Naqa, and Musawwarat es-Sufra, Apedemak belonged to the land itself: lion-headed, strong of arm, and named in stone as the god at the head of Nubia.

The oldest singers said he first appeared when failed rain emptied the reservoirs and drove cattle toward the last wells. Officials ordered the remaining water guarded for the capital.

Apedemak did not debate beneath a shaded roof.

He crossed the burning plain, broke the royal seal upon a reservoir, and opened it to the thirsty. When raiders descended upon the crowd, he met them before the waterline with bow drawn and mane black against the sun. By nightfall, their weapons lay in the dust and their captives walked free.

The court called his act disobedience. The people called it protection.

The king offered him a place beside the throne if power came before need. Apedemak refused: a kingdom was not its gold, but the lives able to reach its walls alive.

That choice cost him the ease of royal favor. He became the god of exposed roads, distant garrisons, iron workers, hunters, and rulers who understood that command must move faster than fear. At Musawwarat, worshippers praised the Lion of the South. At Naqa, artisans carved him in forms no neighboring kingdom could mistake for its own. Meroe still honored Egyptian gods, but Apedemak carried the unmistakable authority of Kush.

He was never a patron of violence for its own sake. His arrows belonged to the instant before cruelty became irreversible. He favored leaders who entered danger first and accepted consequences without ceremony.

Once, legend says, he spared a defeated commander who had surrendered water rather than poison it. The decision angered allies hungry for revenge, but the spared man rebuilt the ruined wells. Years later, those wells kept both armies alive during another drought.

Time buried palaces and dimmed the meanings of the Meroitic script, but the lion remained on temple walls: alert, sovereign, and facing outward.

Apedemak is the courage that protects before permission arrives.

text: The Queen of the Burning Spring – Sulis, ruled the water before Rome knew the road to Britain. Beneath a valley, the earth released water hot enough to steam in winter. Britons lowered coins, bracelets, and whispered names into it, believing its warmth could draw sickness from the body and falsehood from the heart. Sulis listened most closely to those who arrived with nothing. Then the legions crossed the hills. Engineers bound the spring with lead and stone, and Aquae Sulis rose around it. The newcomers called the goddess Minerva. Sulis accepted the name as a bridge, demanding that conqueror and conquered kneel before the same water. That choice made her sanctuary rich, but never peaceful. Veterans sought relief from wounds. Enslaved people prayed beside citizens who claimed ownership of them. Families offered thanks, while thieves disappeared with rings, gloves, and the last coins of the poor. The injured scratched petitions onto lead, naming stolen things, suspected enemies, and punishments fierce enough to make judges tremble. More than a hundred pleas descended into the spring. Sulis could have answered every wound with ruin. Instead, legend says she weighed the desperation beneath each curse. The proud heard only bubbling water; the forgotten heard their accusations roll through the temple like thunder. Some thieves returned what they had taken. Others dreamed of burning eyes until confession became sweeter than sleep. Her mercy was never softness. Sulis healed the wounded, yet refused to let cruelty escape consequence. Justice, she taught, must restore the person harmed, not satisfy a crowd's anger. The burden changed her. Every prayer entered her memory: each betrayal, fever, unpaid debt, and private grief. She could comfort a city because she allowed the city to wound her first. Centuries broke the temple roof. Statues fell, and the empire withdrew, but the spring did not cool. It still rises through the old stones, carrying iron, heat, and thousands of offerings from those who trusted Sulis to remember what human courts forgot. She is the queen who makes strangers one people—and asks what they will do with the warmth they receive.

text: The Eight-Banner War God – Hachiman, entered legend not with a cry of conquest, but with the measured silence before an arrow leaves the string. The people remembered him as the divine spirit of Emperor Ōjin, a ruler linked with new crafts and state-building. His presence later revealed itself at Usa beneath red shrine beams. There he became guardian of the nation, patron of archery and protector of warriors—not because battle was sacred, but because power required a hand steady enough to restrain it. As Buddhist teachings spread, Hachiman was honored as a great bodhisattva, joining shrine, temple, duty and compassion. The Minamoto carried his name into war, and his banners rose above armies. That devotion became dangerous when Lord Koretada claimed every victory as Hachiman’s command. He seized farmers’ rice for his cavalry, burned a village that resisted conscription, and hung eight white banners above the road, claiming heaven favored him. The priests begged for thunder. Hachiman arrived as a quiet bowyer. He inspected the lord’s weapons and corrected a warped bow limb. Then floodwater broke the eastern gate. While the court argued over duty, the stranger cut cords from Koretada’s banners, bound the gate beams, and diverted the river with an abandoned shield. Only one young retainer set down his bow to help. Hachiman gave him one arrow and ordered him to strike the bell above the granary. The retainer refused; frightened families sheltered beneath it. Koretada called him a coward. Hachiman called him worthy. The god revealed himself, but offered no glorious battle. He broke Koretada’s finest bow across his knee and withdrew his name from the army. Without divine prestige, allied houses abandoned the lord. The rebellion ended before harvest, though Hachiman accepted the cost of seeing his banners cut down and his shrines questioned by those who had mistaken obedience for faith. The salvaged cords were carried to Usa and woven into one plain bow case. Warriors still invoke Hachiman before danger, yet the oldest lesson beneath his banners is quieter: skill proves what the hand can do; honor decides when it should stop.

A woman walks into a quiet temple one day and kneels at a low table. The monk enters without hurry. He sets down the kettle, the bowl, the small tea caddy, the bamboo scoop, the whisk. He wipes the bowl in slow circles. He warms it with hot water, empties it, dries it. He lifts a measure of green powder, tips it in, ladles the water, then whisks until a fine foam rises. No one rushes. The steam hangs. The room becomes smaller and kinder.

He does not ask, “What is wrong with you?”
He says, almost like part of the pouring,“What has the long night been asking of you?” She tells him. The years. The reaching that never quite arrived. The body that kept bleeding its own story. exhuation sitting in the bones like unpaid weather. He listens while the tea settles. After the silence has done its work, he speaks the passage she already carried but had not yet heard in this room: It was never the cloak. It was the faith that reached for it. The current that rose from her, touched the hem, and returned glorified. “Your faith has made you well.” And in that same breath the Lord is heard saying, almost in wonder,

“Today you have blessed Me with your faith.”Hope and trust are born from that upward reach. Faith does not keep the healing as a trophy. It recognizes the Source and lifts Him higher still.

The ritual does not cure by name. It cures by action: wipe, warm, empty, measure, pour, whisk, offer, receive. A mind is given something precise and gentle to rest inside. The person is treated as worthy of that gentle slowness.

text:
PAYPAL $PYPL TURNED DOWN $60.50 A SHARE IN CASH. THE MARKET NOW SAYS $52.62:

Six Len5es, six different ways of reading a market, and this morning they keep landing on the same uncomfortable shape: almost nothing is both obviously good and obviously cheap. Where a real discount exists, there is a question attached to it - and on every name below, that question already has a date.

PayPal PYPL at $52.62 (premarket), $0.00 / 0.00% on the day; Monday itself was +$0.21 / +0.40%. The San Jose company runs the PayPal checkout button, Venmo and Braintree, moving money between shoppers and shops and keeping a slice of it.

On July 15, Stripe and the private-equity firm Advent International offered $60.50 a share in cash, more than $53B. PayPal's directors said that was too low, and they had an argument: the shares climbed straight past the offer, closing at $62.30 on August 20, which the board read as its own turnaround being noticed rather than deal chatter. On August 27 the buyers walked. Next session the stock fell $7.81 / -12.71% to $53.66 on 36.3M shares against an 11.4M average, and it has leaked lower since.

Which leaves this morning's price 13.0% below the number PayPal's own board called insufficient.

The quarter underneath, reported July 28 for the three months to June 30:

- Total payment volume, the money moving through its systems: $486.4B, +10%
- Transactions 6.8B, +8%; active accounts 439M, +0.3%; revenue $8.68B, +5%
- Transaction margin dollars - what PayPal keeps from each payment after the cost of moving it - $3.9B, +1%
- Adjusted profit $1.38 a share, -1%; free cash flow, the cash left after running the business and buying equipment, $1.78B, +157%

Read the first line against the third and you have the whole fight. Ten percent more money went through the pipe. The profit on that money grew one percent. That gap is what a buyer was trying to buy cheaply and what the board insists is temporary.

Meanwhile the company is buying itself: 33M shares for $1.5B in the quarter, 111M shares for $6.0B over twelve months - more than a tenth of a business the market now values at $45.0B. In June it also paid the first dividend in its history, $0.14 a share, with the next due September 25.

VERDICT: a payments network at about 10 times the $5.38 of full-year profit it has guided to, whose directors publicly valued it north of $60.50 seven weeks ago, and one line in its own accounts arguing the other way. WHEN: third-quarter results Tuesday, October 27 before the open, a date PayPal has confirmed, with about $1.32 a share expected against $1.34 a year earlier.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:

PayPal, 28th of 59 names. This Len5 wants a business almost nobody could rebuild, bought for less than it is worth, and both halves have to be present. The rebuild half is real - 439 million accounts and a checkout button already wired into millions of merchant sites is not stood up from scratch. The price half is 10 times guided profit with the share count shrinking underneath it. What would knock it off the Quality-Value Len5: transaction margin dollars going flat or negative rather than merely growing slowly, which would make 10 times earnings the right price instead of a cheap one.

MOMENTUM LEN5:

NIQ Global Intelligence (NIQ) at $18.39, $0.00 / 0.00% - nothing has traded since Monday's close, which was +$0.20 / +1.10%. Thirteenth of 30. The Chicago company counts what shoppers actually buy, in shops and online, and sells that count back to the brands and retailers who need to know. This Len5 wants a price near its own one-year high with the recent climb and the longer one agreeing: NIQ sits 6.6% under the $19.69 high of August 28, up from $7.93 on June 3. August 10 after the close did it - revenue $1.12B, +8%; adjusted profit $0.27 a share against $0.20 expected; cash left after paying interest turning positive at $74.1M; and the year raised to 7.1%-7.4% revenue growth. The shares jumped about 15.6% that evening from $11.68. The caveat worth knowing: this was a July 2025 listing priced at $21, so even after doubling since June, the people who bought at the offer are still down. What would knock it off the Momentum Len5: a close back under $17.65, its weakest finish of the past fortnight. Third-quarter results are penciled for November 12, not company-confirmed.

DEEP-VALUE AND SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:

The New York Times Company (NYT) at $70.53, $0.00 / 0.00% since Monday's close, which was +$0.32 / +0.46%. Fifteenth of 90. It sells subscriptions to its journalism plus Games, Cooking, The Athletic and Wirecutter. This Len5 wants a sound business knocked down by a fixable problem, or settled earnings bought cheaply, and the honest reading is that NYT is here for the first only: it carries no debt at all, holds $1.22B of cash and investments, and sits 19.0% under the $87.10 it reached April 7. At about 29 times profit it is not the cheap half. August 5 is the knock-down - 280,000 net digital subscribers added, to 13.35M; digital subscription revenue $407.9M, +16.4%; digital advertising $114.0M, +20.7%; total revenue $762.5M, +11.2%; adjusted profit $0.69 a share against $0.66 expected. Then the guide: digital-only subscription revenue to grow 12%-15% this quarter, down from 16.4%. The shares fell about 9% before the open that morning. What would knock it off the Deep-Value Len5: that growth landing under the 12% floor, which turns one slower quarter into a direction. Third-quarter results are not company-confirmed; last year's landed November 5.

GROWTH LEN5:

EPAM Systems (EPAM) at $112.64 (overnight), -$0.49 / -0.43%. Seventeenth of 30. The Newtown, Pennsylvania company employs 62,850 engineers who design and run software for other companies. This Len5 wants profit growth the price has not charged for, and the price has stopped charging: 49% under the $222.53 of January 15, at about 15 times the past year's profit. August 6 carried both halves at once. Revenue $1.415B, +4.5%, but adjusted profit $3.38 a share against $3.00 expected and $2.77 a year earlier - up 22%, five times the pace of sales. AI-native work passed $160M in the quarter, more than 11% of the business. In the same release the company cut its full-year revenue growth outlook to 3.2%-4.2%, because North American clients are pulling money out of routine project work faster than the AI replacement work arrives, and put the larger AI contracts in the first half of 2027. What would knock it off the Growth Len5: revenue growth landing under that 3.2% floor, which would say the old work is leaving faster than the new work turns up. Third quarter is penciled for November 5, against the company's own guide of $1.410B-$1.425B and $3.38-$3.46 a share.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:

Liquidia (LQDA) at $67.00 (after hours), +$0.57 / +0.86%. Ninth of 30. The Morrisville, North Carolina company sells YUTREPIA, a dry-powder inhaler for pulmonary arterial hypertension - dangerously high blood pressure in the arteries feeding the lungs. This Len5 wants very fast growth on a base big enough that the rate describes a real business, and August 12 delivered exactly that: YUTREPIA sales $170.4M, up 31% from the March quarter alone, produced by 216 employees; net income $74.7M, or $0.74 a share, a fourth straight profitable quarter; more than 5,000 patients started; cash $284.2M, up $61.4M in three months. Management put the drug near 30% of its market and guided above $1B of revenue in 2027. The honest mark against it: $0.74 landed under the $0.81 modeled, and one drug carries everything. What would knock it off the Hypergrowth Len5: a September quarter that fails to build meaningfully on $170.4M. That report is penciled for November 2, about $0.94 a share expected against a 4-cent loss a year ago.

INCOME LEN5:

Macy's (M) at $22.19 (premarket), $0.00 / 0.00% on the day; Monday was +$0.25 / +1.14%. Sixteenth of 30. It owns Macy's, Bloomingdale's and Bluemercury. This Len5 wants cash reaching owners that the business itself pays for, and the arithmetic is easy: $0.1915 a quarter, about $0.77 a year, near 3.5% of the price, taking roughly a third of the $2.15-$2.35 of adjusted profit now guided to. September 10 was a good quarter - comparable sales +2.7%, a fifth straight quarter of growth, with Bloomingdale's +11.3%; net sales $4.87B, +1.1%; adjusted profit $0.40 a share, which excludes a 23-cent benefit from tariff refunds. The company raised its year. The stock fell $1.01 / -4.70% to $20.50 anyway, because roughly $96M of those refunds is being spent on the turnaround rather than kept. What would knock it off the Income Len5: the payout ceasing to look comfortable, which is not an idle worry - analysts model a loss of about $0.17 a share for the quarter ending in October, against 9 cents of profit a year earlier. That report is penciled for December 2.

Six boards, six industries, one shape: a price that looks generous, and a question the company has already put a date on. One of those dates is confirmed and the rest are penciled, running from October 27 to December 2. None of these arguments gets settled by a chart. They get settled by a number nobody has printed yet. PayPal's directors said in August that the company was worth more than $60.50 a share. On October 27 they start showing their work.

Not investment advice.

7. Costco Travel — vacation packages that beat Expedia with member-only extras.

Costco Travel is the most underused member benefit in the entire Costco ecosystem — and the one that delivers the largest per-transaction savings.

What Costco Travel offers:

Vacation packages: bundled flights + hotels + rental cars — often at prices 10-25% below Expedia, https://t.co/BbCE1S2VVi, and Kayak for comparable itineraries.

Member-only extras: many Costco Travel packages include perks the OTAs don't — resort credits ($100-$300 in spending money at the resort), room upgrades, free breakfast, spa credits, or excursion vouchers — included in the package price.

Cruises: Costco negotiates group rates with major cruise lines — often including onboard credits ($50-$200) that other booking channels don't offer.

Rental cars: member-exclusive pricing on Avis, Budget, and Enterprise — often 10-20% below what you'd find on the rental car company's own website.

Theme parks: discounted tickets to Disneyland, Disney World, Universal Studios, and other parks — with bundled hotel packages.

Executive members earn 2% back on Costco Travel purchases — applied to their annual reward. A $5,000 Hawaii package earns $100 in Executive Reward.

She booked a family vacation through Expedia: flights + 5-night resort in Cancun = $4,200. Her neighbor booked the same resort, same dates, through Costco Travel: $3,580 — with a $200 resort credit included. $620 less + $200 in resort spending money. $820 in total value difference — on one vacation.

"Costco Travel doesn't look flashy. The website is basic. There's no app. The interface feels like 2010. And the prices — consistently — beat Expedia, Booking, and the cruise lines' own websites. Most members book travel without checking Costco first. The members who check Costco first save $300-$800 per trip."

efficient executioners, despatching twelve heads per guillotine every thirteen minutes.
Executioners from other parts of France were sent to Paris to learn their technique.79
Many of the acts committed during the Terror defy belief. Typical was the fate of the Princess de
Lamballe, a pleasant, middle-aged aristocrat who had escaped from the city. Driven by loyalty to
her mistress Marie Antoinette, Princess Lamballe returned to Paris to minister to her. The
Princess was promptly seized by the mob, publicly disemboweled, and her private parts paraded
through the city as trophies of the triumph of the Revolution! After the storming of the
Guilerriers, a young apprentice fell victim to the mob. A great plan was fetched, and a fire built

242
In western France Keltic peasants and farmers, called calves and dogs by the revolutionists,
"were herded into churches and burned to death. Other Kelts were piled into cargo ships, the
holds nailed down and the ships sunk. Grand Orient forces went through towns killing everyone
in sight, even pulling portable guillotines which worked around the clock."80
Between 1789 and 1795, 3.5 million Kelts met their death at the hands of benevolent Grand
Orient Freemasonry. To this day, Grand Orient Lodges throughout France re-enact the genocide
of Kelts by ritually guillotining calves and dogs during an annual celebration.
The most grandiose celebration in all French Grand Orient Lodges today is the mimed murder of
King Louis XVI and his wife, Marie Antoinette. Attending this annual event are the
Establishment notables dressed up in elaborate regalia. At the banquet "special stewards herd a
number of calves to waiting guillotines. The terrified animals are then beheaded to the cries of
'Death to Louis; death to the king; death to the lilies (the French royal emblem).' The calf heads
are then thrown into boiling water and are subsequently consumed by the revelers."81
The significance of the ritual is that Louis XVI, a kind and gentle man, was called "the Calf' by
the Grand Orient before they beheaded him.
When Louis XVI was executed in 1793, an elderly Mason dipped his hands in the royal blood,
and said, "I baptise [sic] thee in the name of Liberty and Jacques." Templar revenge was
complete. Albert Pike gloated that "The secret movers of the French Revolution had sworn to
overturn the Throne and the Altar upon the Tomb of Jacques de Molay. When Louis XVI was
executed, half the work was done; and thence forward the Army of the Temple was to direct all
its efforts against the Pope. "82
Meanwhile, Sionist Weishaupt, author of the French Revolution was in exile far from the
dangers he had set in motion. During the Reign of Terror, when the Templars gained control
through the Jacobin Clubs, the Grand Orient Lodges founded by the duke of Orleans and
illuminated by Weishaupt, ceased activity. In 1793 the Jacobins seized the Merovingian traitor,
Philippe, duke of Orleans, and beheaded him. With the Duke dead, Weishaupt had no chance for
further contact with the Revolution.
By 1794 there were 6,800 Jacobin Clubs, totaling half a million members.83 All were former
Grand Orient Masons, first taught revolution by Sion's Illuminati, then indoctrinated by the
Knights Templar to avenge the death of their medieval Grand Master, Jacques de Molay. In so
doing they avenged themselves of the injustices brought by their adversaries, the Merovingian

Even with as dominant and organized a force as the Jacobins propelling it, the revolution began

architects of the Reign of Terror, Marat, Danton, and Robespierre, were themselves assassinated
243
or beheaded, and Paris slowly began to return to normal.
The anti-religious fervor of the Revolution was truly demonic. Orthodox Rabbi Antelman notes
that "During the Reign of Terror, all houses of worship were closed in accordance with Jacobin
anti-religious policy. The churches and synagogues were reopened after Robespierre was
guillotined on July 28, 1794, signifying the end of terror and the Jacobin power base."~ To
protect its bloodthirsty terrorists from further legal action, the Constituent Assembly quickly
passed a resolution that France would harbor political terrorists. The law remains on the books to
this day.
Albert Pike mourned what he saw as the failure of the Revolution: Jacques de Molay and his
companions were perhaps martyrs, but their avengers dishonored their memory. Royalty was
regenerated on the scaffold of Louis XVI., the Church triumphed in the captivity of Pius VI.,
carried a prisoner to Valence, and dying of fatigue and sorrow, but the successors of the Ancient
Knights of the Temple perished, overwhelmed in their fatal victory. "85
Pike is referring to Napoleon Bonaparte's failure to conquer Europe for the Templars. The
Masonic Templars had selected Napoleon for that purpose after he shored up their Revolution
following the Reign of Terror disaster. Msgr. Dillon writes that in 1804 when the Jacobin

In 1799, when Napoleon seized power, Grand Orient Lodges were opened in every place and

There is no record that Napoleon was ever an Illuminatus. There is ample record, however, that

Napoleon, however, failed the Templars. His military adventures became too extended

He said Apple Maps in CarPlay just got dramatically smarter at understanding what you actually mean.

"The old way: 'Navigate to 1245 Oak Street, Austin, Texas.' Precise. Robotic. Required you to know the exact address."

"The new way: 'Take me to the Target near my office.' 'Find a gas station on the way that has diesel.' 'Route me home but avoid the highway.' 'Take me to where I met Sarah for coffee last month.'"

"Apple Maps in iOS 27 extended natural language search to navigation in CarPlay. You can describe your destination conversationally — and Siri AI interprets the intent, searches for the location, and starts navigation."

"'Find a restaurant with good reviews near my 3 o'clock meeting.' — Siri AI checks your calendar for your 3 PM meeting location, searches for restaurants near it, and presents options ranked by reviews."

"'Is there a cheaper gas station on my route?' — Siri AI checks gas prices along your current navigation route and offers alternatives."

"'Navigate to the airport but stop for coffee on the way.' — Siri AI adds a coffee stop to your existing route without replacing the final destination."

"This is the difference between a GPS and a co-pilot. A GPS follows addresses. A co-pilot understands intent. Siri AI in CarPlay is becoming a co-pilot."

AI Overview
These three names share a deep linguistic and historical connection, primarily originating in Ancient Mesopotamia, the Middle East, and the Caucasus.
Sargon
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Greek and biblical translation of the Akkadian regnal name Šarru-kīn. It combines šarru (Akkadian for "king") and kīnu (meaning "true," "established," or "legitimate").
Historical Significance: It is most famously associated with Sargon of Akkad (24th century BCE), the legendary founder of the Akkadian Empire. Later, the Neo-Assyrian ruler Sargon II (8th century BCE) adopted the throne name to establish the legitimacy of his rule.
Sargis
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Classical Syriac and Armenian form of the Latin name Sergius. It originates from the ancient Roman gens (clan) Sergia, which etymologists suspect may connect to the Latin verb servare ("to guard" or "to preserve").
Sako
Origin & Etymology: Sako operates on a few different historical tracks depending on the region:
In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.
In the Balkans: In Albania, it functions as a standalone occupational surname for a "church servant" or as a nickname for the Muslim name Isak (Isaac).
In Asia: It is also an unrelated Japanese surname (written as 佐古) meaning "HELP" and "ancient".

LOUIS Raphaël I Sako (Arabic: لويس روفائيل ساكو;[2] born 4 July 1948) is a Chaldean Catholic prelate who served as Patriarch of Baghdad from 2013 to 2026. Pope Francis made him a cardinal in 2018.

Biography
Early life
Sako was born in the city of Zakho, Iraq, on 4 July 1948.[3] He comes from an ethnic Assyrian family of the Chaldean Catholic Church that has roots in a religious community that has had a presence in the city of his birth since the 5th century AD.[4]

He completed his early studies in Mosul and then attended the Dominican-run Saint Jean’s Seminary there. He was ordained a priest on 1 June 1974 and filled his first pastoral assignment at the Cathedral of Mosul until 1979. He then earned a doctorate in Eastern patrology at the Pontifical Oriental Institute. When denied a license to teach because he was only qualified for religious instruction, he earned a second doctorate in history from the Sorbonne in Paris.[5] With this he secured his teaching license and was able to provide religious instruction. From 1997 to 2002 he was rector of the Patriarchal Seminary in Baghdad. He then returned to Mosul and guided the parish of Perpetual HELP for a year.[6][7]

Sako speaks Neo-Aramaic, German, French, English, Italian, Kurdish and Arabic.[3]

text:
There are several problems with the oil market dropping on this anonymously sourced story.    

1. "Open" is an interesting term. Iran has consistently said it will "open" Hormuz, but not under any pre-war interpretation of the term. They have said since the MoU this means opening under Iranian arrangements developed with Oman, where Iran will establish control over (at least in bound) traffic. The market is repeatedly misreading Iran-Oman arrangements as somehow favourable. They wouldn't be, particularly if allied to an agreement from the US to end Oman shuttles.    

2. On that, also from the same Kyodo story:   "Iran is seeking signs from Washington that it is prepared to return to negotiations and take steps toward an end to the U.S. military blockade of Iranian ports and a halt to military operations related to the Strait of Hormuz"  

The second part of this is the "tell" on Hormuz. Ending military operations in Hormuz refers to US escorts of tankers via the Oman corridor. Ending those would reduce flows immediately - bad for oil markets. Of course, lifting the blockade would mean Iran could sell Oil - the best of both worlds for them.  This is consistent with Iranian objectives for sometime - open Hormuz on their terms (see 1.), which gives them considerable control, whilst immediately ending the dark transit route. Meanwhile they get access to market for their oil.  Of course they would want this. Not sure the US, its allies or the markets do.  

3. In any event, will the US buy this? Unlikely even if the conditions mentioned in the Kyodo story were the only conditions.  On that, also from the same story:       "Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei said on Saturday that Tehran had presented Washington with seven conditions, including an end to the blockade of Iranian ports and the unfreezing of Iranian assets.  The Iranian official who spoke to Kyodo News did not say whether the latest proposal amounted to a partial relaxation of any of those conditions."      

Did not say, means did not contradict, which means it is most likely Iran are wrapping any offer on the same conditions that Razaei communicted explicitly on the weekend, and which he said had already been relayed to mediators. Why would Iran put out conditions from a powerful "veto player" on the one hand, then some anonymous official signal they are prepared to abandon most of them just to get to negotiations? It makes no sense, certainly when viewed through the history of Iranian negotiations, and regime decision making.

text:
In 1873, the first hospital in Nigeria opened in Lagos with a handful of beds and doctors shipped in from England. This month, a Nigerian surgeon in Ogun State removed a cancerous kidney from a patient in Abuja without being in the same city. That is the whole distance in one country's medicine, and it took exactly 153 years to cover.

It was not a straight road.

University College Hospital, Ibadan, opened in 1957 as the country's first teaching hospital, three years before independence. In 1974, a team at the University of Nigeria Teaching Hospital in Enugu opened a human chest and performed the first open-heart surgery in the country. In 1989, Nigeria's first test-tube baby was born at LUTH. In 2000, the first kidney transplant was done at St Nicholas Hospital in Lagos. Every one of those firsts was done with borrowed equipment, thin budgets and surgeons who had every reason to leave.

Many did. Today there are more than 10,000 Nigerian-trained doctors practising in the UK alone, and Nigeria is left with around four doctors for every 10,000 people at home. Nigerians spend well over a billion dollars a year travelling abroad for treatment, most of it to India, the UK and the US, for procedures the country could not offer.

Then, on a Thursday in September 2026, Professor Ekwenna Davis sat at a Toumai surgical console at Redeemer's Health Village in Mowe. Five hundred kilometres away, a patient at Nisa Premier Hospital in Abuja was under anaesthesia with a tumour on his right kidney. For about three hours Davis moved his hands in Ogun and a robot moved in Abuja, carried over a Starlink satellite link with MTN as backup. The kidney came out. It was the first tele-robotic surgery ever performed in Nigeria, and in West Africa.

The first time anyone on earth did this was 2001, when a surgeon in New York operated on a woman in Strasbourg over a private fibre line that cost about a million dollars to lay. Twenty five years later, Nigeria did it over a dish on a roof.

The part that matters comes next. Davis said this was a pilot, and that a Nigerian surgeon in London, Houston or Toronto can now sit at a console and operate on a patient in Kano. The doctors who left did not have to come back for their hands to.

The hospital of 1873 needed to import its doctors.

The hospital of 2026 can import their skill without importing them. https://t.co/8XxU2K99EV

text:
Full ownership of Neville Fernando Teaching Hospital to the government - administrative and operational activities to the Air Force 

Steps have been taken to acquire full ownership of Dr. Neville Fernando Teaching Hospital by the government under a new operational framework approved by the Cabinet, and to entrust its daily administrative and operational activities to the Sri Lanka Air Force. Cabinet approval for this new mechanism has been granted based on a joint proposal submitted by His Excellency President Anura Kumara Dissanayake as the Minister of Defence and the Minister of Health and Mass Media.

Under this new program, the hospital and all its assets will be transferred to a company with full ownership by the General Treasury, and the responsibility for the hospital's administrative as well as day-to-day operational activities will be entrusted to the Air Force. The entire share ownership of this company, established as a state enterprise under the Companies Act, will remain with the General Treasury, and it will be governed by an 11-member Board of Directors appointed by the Secretary to the Treasury based on the recommendations of the Secretary to the Ministry of Defence.

Regarding financial provisions, the General Treasury is expected to provide funds for the salaries and operational expenses of the hospital staff during the period from 2026 to 2028. After this period, the hospital is planned to be maintained as a self-financing institution that generates its own required funds.

In addition to the free medical services provided to the public, this hospital also offers inpatient and outpatient medical services on a payment basis. To support the provision of free healthcare services, approximately 125 million rupees worth of medicines, medical supplies, and other essential items are expected to be provided annually through budget allocations from the Ministry of Health and Mass Media.

In accordance with a Cabinet decision taken on June 27, 2017, the administrative functions of this hospital were transferred to the Ministry of Health, effective from August 01, 2017.

If you want to live in a really good locality in India, I think your options are actually quite limited.

1. College campuses, either as a student or faculty member.

2. Government-controlled areas, like Army cantonments, ministry areas and embassy zones. These places have great roads, greenery, cleanliness and overall maintenance.

3. Private townships. Places like Bhartiya City in Bangalore, some of the larger townships coming up in Pune, and the new ones being developed around Gurgaon.

Only these areas offer a quality of life that extends beyond just your apartment complex. You can actually step outside and have good roads, greenery, walkability, cleanliness, and facilities (schools, hospitals, parks, etc.).

What other options are there in India where you can get that kind of experience?

text: The Obsidian Lynx – Seryava, was born during the Eclipse of Ash, when the lamps in the Nightglass Court died and mountain cats cried from roofs. Priests named her an omen. Her mother named her “the eye that opens when kingdoms sleep.” At twelve, Seryava was taken from the lynx clans as the living seal of an unwanted peace. The nobles expected a savage in silk. Instead, she learned their dances, rivalries, and the breath before a lie. Soon she could cross a feast and know who carried poison, grief, or a dagger for the king. The court adored her beauty and feared how she made strangers feel seen. Each banquet became a hunting ground; she gathered secrets through laughter while lords mistook joy for foolishness. Her mother’s final lesson remained sacred: gold has no worth unless it seals a promise. Then winter starved the mountain passes. The royal granaries were full, yet caravans vanished and children died beneath black banners. Seryava followed lamp oil through forbidden corridors and found the truth beneath the throne: the chancellor had sold the grain to finance a private army. The ledgers also bore her father’s claw-mark. He had helped create the famine, believing it would drive the clans back to war. On coronation night, Seryava had one hour to choose between blood and truth. She entered the hall in obsidian and gold, danced before the assembled houses, stole the treasury key from the chancellor’s chain, and opened the ledgers before the realm. By dawn, the chancellor hung from the western gate. Her father died cursing the daughter who had saved his people from him. The king offered Seryava a crown for her loyalty. She refused it. A throne, she had learned, was only a beautiful cage built high enough to resemble freedom. Now she rules no country, yet no treaty survives without her shadow. To her friends, she is reckless warmth, sudden laughter, and loyalty sharpened into a weapon. To her enemies, she is the last sound heard before the lamps go dark. Seryava wears obsidian for the truths that wounded her and gold for the promises she still chooses to keep. She does not ask what destiny prepared for her. She chooses what destiny must become.

text:
The next few days could determine whether the Iran war moves toward another major escalation or a negotiated settlement.

Washington has strong reasons to avoid another prolonged confrontation. Oil prices remain elevated, U.S. interceptor and munitions inventories are under pressure, the midterms are approaching, and another major campaign risks triggering further Iranian retaliation against Gulf infrastructure, shipping and U.S. regional interests.

Tehran also needs an exit. Its economy is under severe pressure, oil revenues have been constrained, and China remains Iran’s most important external economic lifeline. Iran can continue resisting Washington, but the economic cost of doing so is increasing.

That makes the sequence of meetings particularly important.

The GCC is unlikely to welcome another open-ended escalation without a clearly defined endgame. Gulf states have already absorbed substantial economic and security costs from the conflict, giving them strong incentives to push Washington toward negotiations, stronger security guarantees and a sustainable settlement.

Then comes Trump-Xi on September 24.

China enters that meeting with significant bargaining leverage. Beijing has considerable economic influence over Tehran, but Xi is unlikely to use that leverage for Washington without seeking something in return.

And that bargaining could extend far beyond Iran.

Taiwan, U.S. arms sales, AI and semiconductor restrictions, tariffs, technology controls, trade and critical minerals could all become part of the wider U.S.-China negotiation. Washington may have to compromise on issues important to Beijing in return for meaningful Chinese pressure on Tehran.

For Tehran, sustained Chinese pressure would be extremely difficult to ignore. Iran can resist Beijing, but doing so becomes increasingly costly when its economy is deteriorating and its most important external economic relationship is with China.

Washington would also have to compromise. Beijing cannot produce a settlement if the terms offered to Tehran remain unacceptable. Both Washington and Tehran would ultimately need to give something for Chinese pressure to translate into an agreement.

That creates a possible pathway:

GCC pressure for diplomacy → Trump-Xi bargaining → U.S.-China compromise → Chinese pressure on Tehran → compromises from Washington and Iran → negotiated settlement.

But there is another factor that could give Xi even greater leverage.

If Washington and Beijing cannot find an acceptable bargain, Beijing may simply choose to wait. Washington has far less room to do so.

China bears economic costs from higher oil prices and disrupted trade, but it is not directly fighting the war. Washington, meanwhile, faces elevated energy prices, mounting military costs, pressure on munitions inventories and approaching midterms.

Iran is also under increasing economic pressure.

That asymmetry in time could therefore become one of Beijing’s strongest bargaining advantages.

The key question on September 24 may not simply be whether China is willing to pressure Iran.

It may be what Xi demands in return—and whether Washington considers that price lower than the economic, political and military cost of allowing the Iran conflict to continue.

IRAN OFFERS TO REOPEN STRAIT OF HORMUZ WITHIN 7 DAYS IF U.S. EASES BLOCKADE: Kyodo

Iran has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if Washington takes initial steps toward ending the blockade of Iranian ports and halting military operations around the strait, Kyodo reports, citing a senior Iranian official.

The proposal has reportedly been conveyed to Washington through mediators, with Tehran planning further talks around the U.N. General Assembly.

No agreement has been reached yet. Iran has previously tied reopening Hormuz to an end to the U.S. blockade.

Source: Kyodo
