- Testers (Sep 11 TeslaZoa): Robotaxi tracking site — fleet at 994 after +14 vehicles; 6 short of 1,000.
- Testers (Sep 11 AIScottAdams): sleep-through long-haul thesis — lie-flat Robotaxi rides could cannibalize short- and long-haul flights (tester/AI channel, not Official).

- Testers (Sep 12 Alexs_jame): “BREAKING” clip framed as Elon Musk and Tesla AI celebrating a Robotaxi service launch day — tester/media claim, not Official robotaxi.
- Testers (Sep 13 gailalfaratx): Austin UT campus — Robotaxis ferrying football fans fully unsupervised (no safety supervisor); emotional “how far Tesla has come” note.
- Testers (Sep 13 niccruzpatane): Austin ride comparison — 21 Robotaxi vs 2 human Uber rides; claims Robotaxi comfort next-level (smooth turning, less heavy braking).
- Testers (Sep 13 TeslaZoa): Nashville spot — 26 Cybercabs + 7 Robotaxi validation Model Ys (33 AVs total) on public roads (signal, not a new Official city launch).
- Testers (Sep 13 herbertong / TeslaLarry): peak-demand surge capacity may matter more for profits than steady-state fleet count; Tesla need not own that surge capacity.
- Testers (Sep 13 herbertong / TeslaLarry): network efficiency (charging, cleaning, maintenance, depots, coverage) may beat raw Robotaxi count as the competitive edge.
- Testers (Sep 13 SERobinsonJr): MSM late to a 720-unit figure — tester says more are coming / already on site (fleet/Cybercab count chatter, not Official).
- Testers (Sep 14 MelvinInvests): stack thesis — Tesla owns vehicles/software/charging/customer vs Uber marketplace (tester/investor take, not Official).
- Testers (Sep 14 TeslaNewswire): Slovenia Ministry of Transport tested FSD Supervised; working toward Robotaxi approval (tester/news signal, not Official launch).
- Testers (Sep 14 RobotaxiRadar): fleet officially past 1,000 — 1,001 in service; unsupervised 305; all latest adds unsupervised (tester tracking site).

- Testers (Sep 15 RobotaxiRadar): Tesla hiring for collection/tracking/management of driving data in 27 cities across 15 states (NY, TX, FL, NV, CA, GA, UT, CO, MN, NC, D.C., PA, LA, AZ listed) — hiring signal, not a new Official city launch.

- Testers (Sep 18 RobotaxiRadar): NHTSA building first-ever AV performance standards with SAE ASCEND — outcomes-based safety vs rigid design; 3-year / $5M (tester read, not Official NHTSA summary).
- Testers (Sep 18 rajuvamsi007): future of transport is not private ownership of driverless cars; future Tesla cars designed for 24×7 use (tester/fleet thesis, not Official).
- Testers (Sep 18 nishkidoonoo): “huge! $TSLA” Robotaxi-related media post (tester signal).

OWNING / FLEET (from Owning Robotaxi Fleet dump)
- Elon (Feb 2026, also in Robotaxi folder): Tesla owners will be able to add their cars to the Robotaxi network; Tesla collects 25% of revenue.
- Fleet testers frame the network like Airbnb for cars: owner adds vehicle; Tesla handles software, routing, payments, rider experience; platform fee often modeled ~25–35%; owner keeps the rest after operating costs (tester).
- Fleet / Teslaconomics (Mar 2026): ~$30k/yr net profit per Robotaxi to owner is a base-case assumption from analyst models + Tesla long-term vision — after platform fee, charging, tires, maintenance, insurance, cleaning. No official real-world owner earnings in this dump. Profit/mile chatter ~$0.25–$0.50 after costs at 50k–100k+ miles/yr in high-demand areas.

- Fleet / BrianRoemmele: “all in” on buying into the owning-fleet thesis now; separate Optimus ownership program mentioned but not published in this dump.

This is a new base run. The object is Tawfik’s 21 September 2026 synthesis of a July 2026 Nature Communications paper: thymus-derived thymulin falls with involution; its loss unmasks myeloid NF-κB; the cytokine field accelerates tumors and blunts anti-PD-L1 in aged mice. The thread is substantially faithful. Institution, uniqueness, human translation, and peptide identity are the places it over-smooths.  1. What the post claims
Aging loop: thymus shrinks → inflammatory myeloid cells (IL-1α/β, IL-6, TNF-α) persist → tumors grow faster → checkpoint blockade fails. Heterochronic parabiosis suppresses the aged myeloid program. Bone-marrow chimeras show the suppressor is circulating and not hematopoietic. The candidate is thymulin. Thymulin blocks NF-κB in myeloid cells. In aged tumor-bearing mice it slows growth, lifts CD8 activity, and restores anti-PD-L1. Young mice barely move. Peptide PK is flagged. Extension beyond breast/melanoma is offered as hypothesis.  That is the paper’s own causal sketch. The attached figure is a real panel cluster: young-versus-aged CD11b⁺ cytokine frequencies and AT-3 / E0771 growth–survival curves.  2. Source lock  Item
Fact
Title
Thymulin restrains age-associated myeloid inflammation and enhances cancer immunotherapy
Site
Keck School of Medicine, USC — not Stanford
Date
21 July 2026; open access; NIH/NCI funded
Animals
C57BL/6 and BALB/c, ~65–75 weeks vs 8–12 weeks; AT-3, E0771, B16-F10, EMT6
Humans
PBMCs 21–33 vs 60–87 yr; public breast-tumor scRNA-seq. No treated human trial
Mechanism
Lower NF-κB p65 DNA binding; lower IκBα phosphorylation; IL6-promoter reporter loses the thymulin effect when the NF-κB site is mutated
Lead
Fumito Ito

The Stanford attribution in the post is wrong. The mechanism paragraph tracks the published figures. 

https://t.co/AAHQ4MKHBn +1

  3. Anatomy
The thymus sits in the anterior mediastinum, behind the sternum. After puberty it involutes into fat. Classical teaching stopped at “fewer naïve T cells.” This paper’s claim is that thymic epithelial secretion also holds a brake on innate myeloid transcription. That brake is thymulin (FTS): a zinc-dependent nonapeptide. Activity historically required peptide plus Zn²⁺. A thread reply correctly notes zinc and T3 as cofactors and treats thymulin as a downstream sign rather than the root of aging. The paper does not refute that; it shows one thymus-secreted peptide is sufficient to move myeloid NF-κB and aged-tumor endpoints. 

@dantawfik

  https://t.co/RWeQlQqP6U

Thymus behind the sternum. Involution is the demographic fact the peptide story rides on.  4. Minimal restraint model
Let (M) be the frequency of cytokine-producing myeloid cells, Θ\Theta\Theta
 circulating thymulin activity, and (N) nuclear NF-κB occupancy:  dMdt=α(1−Θ) N−δM,N∝p65 DNA-binding\frac{dM}{dt} = \alpha(1-\Theta)\,N - \delta M, \qquad N \propto \text{p65 DNA-binding}\frac{dM}{dt} = \alpha(1-\Theta)\,N - \delta M, \qquad N \propto \text{p65 DNA-binding}
  Θ(age)\Theta(age)\Theta(age)
 falls as epithelial mass collapses. When Θ→0\Theta \to 0\Theta \to 0
, (M) saturates at the aged set-point. Secondary summaries of the mouse blood data put IL-1β⁺ myeloid cells on the order of ~1% young to ~11% aged; IL-6 and TNF-α rise several-fold in the same direction. Tumor growth then sees an inflammatory source term; checkpoint blockade sees a myeloid sink on T-cell function. Restoring Θ\Theta\Theta
 collapses (N) and (M) in aged hosts and leaves young hosts nearly unchanged — which is what an already-high Θ\Theta\Theta
 predicts. 

https://t.co/w2yq7cWhYV

  This is a restraint model, not a claim that thymulin is the unique cause of aging.  5. What the post gets right  Inflammaging as persistent myeloid cytokine output, not only T-cell exhaustion.  
Parabiosis plus chimera logic: youth factor is circulating and non-marrow.  
Age-dependence of the drug-like effect. Anti-PD-L1 alone failed in their aged models; the combination moved.  
Peptide PK problem: short half-life, repeated injection in mice.  
Scope caution on tumor types: breast and melanoma models, myeloid inflammation common enough to suggest generalization, not prove it.

6. What the post over-smooths  Institution: USC, not Stanford.  
“The missing signal” was isolated by pathway filters plus prior thymulin literature, then validated. Other thymic peptides were in the candidate set.  
Human evidence is associative (blood, tumor atlases) plus ex-vivo PBMC suppression. No aged human received thymulin in this study.  
Survival gains in mice are real and modest in monotherapy summaries (one secondary write-up: E0771 median 27 → 34 days). Combination with anti-PD-L1 is the striking arm, still preclinical. 

https://t.co/w2yq7cWhYV

“Immunotherapy stops working” is too absolute. Age degrades average checkpoint benefit; it does not set efficacy to zero in every older patient.  
CVD, neurodegeneration, kidney, metabolism: hypothesis the authors allow, not a result in this paper.  
Thymulin is not the Russian polypeptide complex sold as thymalin/thymalin. Different molecule, different evidence base.

Thymulin reduces p65 DNA binding and IκBα phosphorylation in aged LPS-activated macrophages. Mutating the NF-κB site on an IL6 reporter removes the peptide effect. That is the molecular lock.  https://t.co/NViOjgoqJT

NF-κB as a hub for myeloid cytokine, survival, and recruitment programs. The paper’s claim is that thymulin turns this hub down in aged myeloid cells, not that it rewrites T-cell development.  Philosophical & Ethical Core

The data do not license self-administration of research peptides, conflation with thymalin, or the claim that checkpoint failure in older adults is a single-molecule problem.  Call to Action

text:
The US Federal Register’s document search briefly offered a Chinese AI model as a search option.

A commodity portfolio manager posted a screenshot of the official journal’s interface. Under “search mode,” the default was semantic search. Two other choices pointed to Qwen3:0.6B, a model from Alibaba Cloud. One listing described a hybrid setup. The other pointed to a lightweight half-billion-parameter model.

About a day after the screenshot spread, both Qwen options disappeared from the live page. An archive snapshot from September 16 still shows them.

The site holds public records. Using Qwen there does not mean a model was siphoning secrets back to Beijing. It does mean the team running search picked a capable, low-cost open-source Chinese model instead of a bulkier US system.

That choice landed in the middle of a louder political story. Washington frames AI as a race with China. US labs charge more per token. Chinese open-source models cost less to run and now sit close enough on capability that cost-conscious operators are using them. The Federal Register listing made that trade-off visible, then staff pulled it.

text:
On 22nd September, US oil for November fell below $91. A tanker allowed through Hormuz could still lose its hull insurance for paying the passage toll, if its policy contains the Lloyd's Market Association's transit fee clause.

Reuters' 11.51 GMT snapshot put November WTI at $90.01 and Brent at $98.23. The reopening story remains conditional and disputed.

Kyodo and Reuters cited unnamed Iranian officials offering to reopen the strait within 7 days if Washington eased military pressure and lifted its port blockade. MarketWatch reported that Iran's Fars agency denied those accounts. Neither report establishes an accepted agreement or a deadline starting today.

The insurance problem is specific. The optional hull clause, published on 23rd July, ends the insurer's obligations for the affected vessel when a transit payment within its scope is made. It includes an exception for particular maritime or navigational services permitted by both maritime law and the policy's sanctions terms. It does not apply automatically to every ship.

Separately, America's sanctions agency warned on 24th August that accepting services from designated Iranian passage and insurance providers can create sanctions exposure even without payment. Iranian permission does not supply American legal authorization.

Insurance terms can change quickly. Skuld offered a way to buy back affected war cover on 9th March, four days after it ended. Government sanctions and the safety of the route are separate constraints.

There is also a supply development beyond the Iranian offer. Reuters reports Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline has restarted at a low rate. Returning to its previous flow of roughly 4 million barrels a day could take weeks.

The International Energy Agency's 11th September report estimated global oil stocks had fallen 507 million barrels since February. Returning supply could rebuild inventories. Whether a glut develops depends on how quickly supply returns relative to consumption and how much stock buyers want to rebuild. Diesel relief also depends on refining and delivery of finished fuel.

Selective passage could keep oil prices swinging if a vessel clears one government's requirements but cannot meet another's sanctions rules or its insurer's terms. That outcome is possible, not inevitable. A workable agreement could remove several constraints together.

For durable reopening, watch repeated cargo movements under published transit terms, applicable legal permissions and valid insurance. A seven-day promise alone cannot establish any of those.

📍NEW YORK | September 22, 2026 | HewadPress:— The United States and Iran have signaled a possible diplomatic opening at the United Nations, even as their months-long conflict continues to threaten regional security and global energy supplies.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that Washington is willing to speak with Iranian representatives during the UN General Assembly in New York. However, he stressed that no meeting has been scheduled.

Rubio told NBC News that the United States would consider talks if they could produce a positive outcome. He said Washington’s central objective remains ensuring that Iran never obtains a nuclear weapon. 

Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is intended for peaceful purposes and denies seeking to build a nuclear bomb.

Iran offers conditional reopening of Hormuz

A senior Iranian official separately told Reuters that Tehran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the United States reduces military pressure and lifts its blockade of Iranian ports.

The official said Iran’s delegation in New York has full authority to revive diplomacy and discuss an agreement to end hostilities through mediators. Tehran reportedly delivered its proposal to Washington on September 16.

Iran is demanding an official U.S. commitment to diplomacy and a clear timetable for negotiations. However, the Iranian official said President Masoud Pezeshkian is not expected to meet President Donald Trump directly during the UN gathering. 

The diplomatic signals come days after Iran warned that any renewed U.S. military operation would trigger retaliation without restrictions.

War remains a dangerous stalemate

The United States and Israel launched major strikes against Iran on February 28, targeting Iranian military, missile and nuclear facilities. Although the attacks severely damaged Iran’s defenses and enrichment infrastructure, Tehran has retained significant missile and drone capabilities.

The war has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway that normally carries roughly one-fifth of the world’s energy supplies.

A Reuters assessment published in August described the conflict as a costly stalemate. Iran has not surrendered, commercial traffic through Hormuz remains severely restricted and the true condition of Tehran’s nuclear program is unclear because UN inspectors have not returned to key sites.

The International Atomic Energy Agency has also been unable to verify the location of approximately 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent following earlier attacks on Iranian facilities. 

Shipping attacks deepen the crisis

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard recently claimed responsibility for striking a Togo-flagged oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, alleging that the vessel attempted to pass without authorization. The incident raised new concerns over the safety of commercial shipping and the possibility of further military escalation. 

The conflict has also expanded beyond Iran. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis have intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping, creating another threat to global trade around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.

Saudi Arabia restarted its East-West oil pipeline Tuesday after drone attacks forced it to shut down on September 13. The pipeline has become increasingly important because it allows Saudi crude to bypass the Strait of Hormuz and reach the Red Sea port of Yanbu. 

Diplomacy faces major obstacles

Despite the public expressions of openness, Washington and Tehran remain far apart.

The United States is demanding firm restrictions on Iran’s nuclear program and an end to threats against shipping and American allies. Iran is seeking an end to military operations, relief from sanctions and the lifting of the U.S. blockade.

🇨🇳 🇺🇲 Xi called out American "unilateral hegemony" and warned Trump directly of "clashes and even conflicts" over Taiwan just weeks ago. Trump's public description of the relationship, repeated warmth, calling Xi "a good man," treating this as a friendship, has no matching statement from the other side. Nowhere in the record does Xi call this a bromance.

The concessions attached to that one-sided framing are concrete and stacking up. Washington reversed its own ban on Nvidia's H20 chips to China, chips Trump himself downplayed as merely the "fourth-best" in Nvidia's lineup, in what multiple Senate Democrats called a trade to keep rare-earth exports flowing rather than a negotiated breakthrough. 

The $14 billion Taiwan arms package has now been paused twice, first in May explicitly to preserve munitions for the Iran war, and again this month ahead of Xi's Washington visit, with Trump himself calling the sale a "negotiating chip" in front of Beijing, discarding the decades-long practice of never discussing Taiwan arms sales with China directly. Taiwan's president had a planned New York stopover blocked after China objected. 

None of this reads as leverage being built. It reads as leverage being spent, one concession at a time, for a relationship only one side is calling personal.

The satellite intelligence-sharing detail is where this stops being about trade optics and becomes a live security question. We've already covered CNN's reporting that Russian satellites tracked a US base in Saudi Arabia before Iran's precision strike there. WaPo's framing adds China explicitly alongside Russia in that same pattern, and Trump's own response, essentially shrugging it off, "they do it, and we do it," is the same posture that's now defined his approach to Xi generally: acknowledging the behavior, declining to treat it as disqualifying.

The Kim Jong Un comparison is the sharpest part of this framing, because it's not rhetorical, it's structural. Trump has now built a diplomatic pattern of describing adversarial leaders in personal, reciprocal terms that those leaders never actually offer back, and using that imagined mutuality to justify real, material concessions, chip access, delayed arms sales, softened responses to intelligence-sharing with a country actively striking US forces. The friendship is the cover story. The concessions are the actual transaction.

text:
Russia’s latest parliamentary election offers a useful lens through which to examine a political model that Zimbabwe could increasingly debate: the dominance of one political organisation as the organising force of the state.

The September 18–20 Russian election, held while the country remains at war with Ukraine and under extensive Western sanctions, returned Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party with 355 of the State Duma’s 450 seats. 

The Kremlin presented the vote as a demonstration of national unity and support for its war effort. Critics, however, point to the restricted political environment and exclusion of significant anti-war opposition.

Still, Russia’s significance lies beyond the election itself. 

Moscow has demonstrated that a state can maintain political cohesion and pursue an independent foreign-policy agenda despite sustained pressure from the United States and European Union. That does not mean sanctions have had no economic costs, nor that Russia’s political system is without controversy. 

However, it does show the resilience that concentrated political authority can provide when the state’s institutions, security apparatus and governing party operate toward a common strategic objective.

China offers an even longer-running example. 

The Chinese Communist Party has retained a monopoly on national political power while building China into an economic, technological and military power.

Ironically these are not new ideas in local politics.

Following the 1987 Unity Accord between ZANU-PF and PF-ZAPU, the two parties formally committed themselves to uniting under ZANU-PF. The agreement explicitly stated that the party would seek to establish a One-Party State in Zimbabwe.

The merger also produced a powerful executive presidency. Constitutional changes that year effectively moved Zimbabwe towards a de facto one-party system, although opposition politics was not formally abolished.

The project ultimately encountered political resistance.

Today, for Zimbabwe, also in light of CAA3, the debate over a dominant-party model need not be framed around the abolition of elections, but around whether greater political continuity, stability and policy coherence can better serve long-term national development under a governing party with a strong and enduring mandate.

The question is whether Zimbabwe can build the institutional discipline and economic capacity that have characterised China’s rise and, in a very different context, Russia’s resistance to external pressure.

A one-party or dominant-party state is not automatically a development model. 

China and Russia have distinct histories, institutions and economies, and neither can simply be transplanted to Zimbabwe. 

However, the current Russian election, conducted in wartime and under intense Western pressure, has reopened a fundamental question: can political cohesion become an instrument of national power, rather than merely an instrument of political control?

For Zimbabwe, that is perhaps the more consequential question.

text:
No matter how well-constructed a lie is, it can only be defeated by the truth...
"Many of the local Muslims of the Morea, who knew no other language besides Greek, would come out of the walls at night begging for their lives. They shouted to the Greek soldiers in their mother tongue, reminding them of old friendships, commercial relations and common origin. They even held makeshift crosses and asked to be baptized immediately. However, the rage of the revolutionaries was such that it considered these manifestations as last-minute hypocrisy for the salvation of their lives, since the same people a few months earlier had taken the lead in the looting of Christian villages..."
These are among the things Maxime Raybaud tells us, a French military man and eyewitness to the siege of Tripolitsa. In his memoirs (Mémoires sur la Grèce), he describes in a shocking way how the common Greek language was used as a lifeline, but also why it failed.
"So," someone asked me at some point, "did we slaughter our own blood?"
If I want to say that I serve the truth, the answer is "yes"! Every action of the Revolution of 1821, however, hides within it shocking and "silenced" chapters, both from historiography and, of course, from the systematic propaganda of the neighbors.
We will start from the fairy tale of the population distribution and the 30 and 40 thousand dead that we read. Let me also add the "Turks" dead which of course constitutes yet another fictional construct.
When we say Muslims in Tripolitsa of 1821, we must know that it was not a homogeneous ethnic group from Anatolia.
Its population, on the days of the fall (September 23, 1821), had more than doubled artificially. The city under normal conditions had about 15.000–20.000 inhabitants, but due to the advance of the revolutionaries, Muslims and Jews from all over the Morea (from Kalavryta, Karytaina, Leontari, etc.) had taken refuge there. On the day of the fall, the population within the walls is documented as estimated between 30.000 and 35.000 people. Of these, the armed ones (that is, let’s call it the army) were about 10.000 to 12.000...
The largest percentage of the city’s Muslims (but also of the Morea), ~55%–60%, were locals, Islamized populations of Greek origin (Moreote Muslims). These people spoke Greek as their mother tongue (many didn’t even know Turkish!). They had common cultural elements, even common surnames or kinship ties with the Christians of the countryside. They were mainly farmers, landowners, townspeople and administrative employees who had changed their faith in the previous centuries for reasons of tax and social privileges.
Another population segment consisted of the so-called Turco-Albanians, ~10%. They were, we would say, the military "backbone" of the city’s defense. They had come as reinforcements (about 2.500–3.500 men) under the leadership of Elmas Bey, sent by Hurshid Pasha. They were experienced warriors, Muslims by religion.
And we also had the Ottoman Officials, ~15%–20%, that is the ruling class of the city (commanders, judges/kadis, senior military officers). These came from Constantinople or Anatolia. They were the minority of the population, but they held all the political power and the wealth of the city. With them were also their families (harems, servants).
To these we must now add about 1.000–2.000 Jews who were mainly Sephardic merchants and some Christians, ~5%, very few (most were driven out due to famine) who spoke Greek.
1821 did not start as a typical war between two modern states with international rules. As we have said many times, in the Ottoman Empire the millet system applied. There was no distinction based on DNA or language, but based on faith. The Muslim was a "Turk" (that’s how the revolutionaries called him) and the Christian was a "Romios/Greek".
When the Revolution broke out in the spring of 1821, the Muslims of the countryside took refuge in the castles. During their retreat, but also through the sorties they made from Tripolitsa (as in the first battle of Tripolitsa), they burned Christian villages, looted properties and proceeded to massacres of civilians in order to terrorize the revolutionaries.
Although the base, I repeat, were Greek-speaking farmers, their leadership (that is the aghas and beys of the Morea) were the ones who ordered and actively participated in the oppression and the executions of Christians. In the eyes of the insurgents, the distinction between "simple believer" and "oppressor" had been lost in the blood of the first months.
And here you will reasonably ask me… why was "besa" given to the garrison of Elmas Bey (that is the Turco-Albanians) and the opportunity to return to "our blood" was not given?
Kolokotronis’ agreement with the armed Turco-Albanians was not made out of humanitarianism, but out of pure military strategy. He wanted to split the defense. This "group" was the toughest and best-trained military force inside the castle. Kolokotronis knew that if they fought "to the death," the Greek losses would be enormous and the fall would be delayed.
By removing them, therefore, from the equation, the city’s defense collapsed from within. Moreover, these men had no emotional or proprietary bond with the Morea. They were mercenaries and all they wanted was to return alive to their place with their weapons.
Now why we did not ask our own blood to change faith, we must seek it in the psychology of 1821 itself.
The Greeks remembered well that half a century earlier, during the Orlov Revolt, many local Muslims had taken the lead in the savage massacres of Christians. Suspicion was absolute.
The fall of Tripolitsa was not an organized surrender of a state, but a disorderly invasion of thousands of enraged and starving revolutionaries who sought revenge for 400 years of slavery. When the gate broke, there was no central authority whatsoever to do "sorting" or to offer religious conversion.
In other words, for the revolutionary of 1821, "blood" (if you like, biological origin) meant nothing if the other wore a turban and worshipped Allah. Identity was religious: "For the Holy Faith of Christ." The Greek-speaking Muslim was considered a "Turk" and, therefore, an enemy!
The truth, however, is that before the final assault, hundreds of Muslim civilians would secretly come out of the walls at night and go to the Greek camps. They sought specific Greek chieftains or notables with whom they had commercial relations or best-man ties before the war. In fluent Greek (the only language they knew) they shouted to the revolutionaries: "We are your brothers, we are Moreotes, we are not Turks from the East."
In some early phases, certain chieftains (such as Giatrakos or Petrobey) accepted them and held them as prisoners for ransom. However, in the last days, the volume of the starving who came out was so large that the Greek soldiers, fearing that they themselves would run out of food, began to execute them outside the walls.
The French philhellene Maxime Raybaud (whose excerpt I gave you at the beginning) and the historian Ioannis Philimon report that entire Muslim families fell to their knees before the Greeks, holding makeshift wooden crosses, and begged to be baptized Christians at that very moment.
In the majority of cases, in the frenzy of battle, the revolutionaries considered these conversions "hypocritical," in order to save their lives, and did not accept them.
There were, however, exceptions for women and children. Many Muslim women who spoke Greek were eventually integrated into Greek families, baptized and married Greek fighters after the end of the war.
It should be noted, however, that although biologically indigenous, the Moreote Muslims had adopted the psychology of the ruling class. When in 1770 or 1821 they needed to defend their privileges, they behaved with the same cruelty as the Ottomans of Constantinople.
Kolokotronis’ aide reports that the local aghas of Tripolitsa were the harshest persecutors of the Christians of Arcadia. The Greeks remembered who had stolen their land, who had imprisoned their children and who had burned their villages a few months earlier...
So when the Muslims remembered their "Greekness" because of the impending massacre, for the revolutionaries it was now too late. Religious hatred and the thirst for revenge had blinded any logic of common origin!
"The majority of the Ottomans residing in Tripoli were autochthonous Peloponnesians, whose ancestors had been Islamized. These spoke the Greek language as their mother tongue and knew very little Turkish. Nevertheless, their participation in the oppressions and the recent outrages against the Christians rendered their Greekness powerless before religious hatred" (Ioannis Philimon, in his work Historical Essay on the Greek Revolution).
-----------------------
Modern historical studies estimate that the dead during the fall of Tripolitsa range between 10.000 and 15.000 people, including those who lost their lives from famine and disease during the last months of the siege. The number of 30.000 or 32,000 dead mentioned in some sources of the time (such as in Kolokotronis’ memoirs) is considered by modern historians to be statistically inflated. This inflation served the psychology of war. The revolutionaries wanted to overemphasize the size of their success against the strongest fortress of the Morea, while the Ottoman side wanted to magnify the size of their own destruction!

Και στα αγγλικά που πάλι το ξέχασα :
"The slaves became the judges and executioners of their torturers" François Pouqueville, French historian and diplomat who lived through the events of the era.
The Greek Revolution of 1821 is often approached as a sudden, isolated historical milestone, but in reality it constitutes the culmination of a long and bloody historical process. The outbreak of the Struggle was not born in a vacuum, nor was the fury of the rebels an unprovoked manifestation of barbarity. It was the accumulated result of four hundred years of institutionalized oppression, violent enslavements, child-levy and successive bloody suppressions.
Today, this specific historical milestone is systematically exploited by the neighboring country, which deliberately isolates the violence of 1821 in order to build a convenient narrative of a supposed "ethnic cleansing." They present the events as if there was never a before, as if everything started one morning in 1821 out of nowhere, erasing four centuries of slavery from the map of memory. In this way, however, history is wronged, because the explosion of the enslaved is presented as an unconnected, primitive act of violence, equating it with the structural and daily violence of a state mechanism that lasted 400 years.
Every war event of 1821, even its darkest and most violent moments, carries within it the deep collective trauma of more than a hundred previous failed uprisings, such as the still-fresh-in-memory Orlov Revolt. To understand the dynamics of the Revolution, one must turn one’s gaze to the darkness of the subjugation that preceded it, where revenge and the desire for freedom smoldered for generations, turning the once powerless slaves into the relentless judges of their oppressors.
The basic tool of the Ottomans to restore "order" was always the mass slaughter of civilians.Let us bring back to our memory:
- The destruction of Thessaloniki (1430), where during the capture of the city by Murad II, thousands of inhabitants were slaughtered, while over 7.000 men, women and children were sold as slaves in the slave markets.
- The massacre of Lefkada and Kefalonia (1479). When Grand Admiral Gedik Ahmed Pasha captured the islands, slaughtering the greater part of the population and sending the survivors to Constantinople as slaves.
- What followed after the Battle of Lepanto (1571). After the defeat of the Ottoman fleet, spontaneous uprisings broke out throughout Greece. The Ottoman response was the "tool": massacres of civilians in Achaia, Mani, Thessaly and Macedonia. In Cyprus, Mustafa Pasha ordered the slaughter of thousands of inhabitants of Nicosia and flayed alive the Venetian commander Marcantonio Bragadin.
- The Movement of Dionysios the Philosopher (1611). After the failure of the uprising in Ioannina, Dionysios was flayed alive. His skin was stuffed with straw and sent to the Sultan, while a mass slaughter of the Christians of the area followed and the abolition of their privileges (the infidel and ungrateful rayahs!).
But for me, the clearest answer to why the Peloponnese reacted that way in 1821 lies in the Orlov Revolt, just 50 years before the great Revolution.
After the failure of the (Russian-instigated) uprising, the Ottomans unleashed thousands of irregular Turco-Albanians on the Peloponnese to punish the Greeks. For nine whole years, the Peloponnese experienced one of the greatest humanitarian disasters in its history. Entire villages were burned, thousands of civilians were slaughtered, and thousands of women and children were sold in the slave markets of North Africa.
Think that the demographic and economic destruction of the Peloponnese was so deep that the Sultan himself was finally forced to send a regular army to exterminate the Turco-Albanians, as the area had been deserted and no longer yielded taxes!
In other words… we all owe it to make it clear from the outset that violence does not have the same character when it comes from different starting points.
The violence of the oppressor (in this case the Ottomans) was institutionalized, daily and continuous for 4 centuries (child-levy, lack of basic rights, beheadings for example, leveling of areas after uprisings, etc.).T
The violence of the revolutionary (here the Greeks) was the violent shaking off of this yoke.
That is why when we point out that Tripolitsa was the seat of the Mora Valisi (the Ottoman governor of the Peloponnese), that it was the administrative, military and economic center of the entire southern Greece (that is why Theodoros Kolokotronis insisted obsessively on its siege. He knew that if Tripoli fell, the entire Ottoman domination in the Morea would collapse), the "tree of slavery" in the central square of Tripolitsa (a large plane tree) on whose branches the Ottoman authorities hanged Greeks for decades (klephts, armatoloi but also civilians) as an example and spectacle for the locals, the prison of the notables whom they held as hostages to prevent the uprising, who were locked in miserable, dark basements under horrific conditions (until the day of the capture, most of them — more than half — died from hunger, hardships and torture inside the prison. Those who survived were in a skeletal state), and also the fact that the tombs were opened for the hidden valuables and not from some "ritual hatred" as the neighbors trumpet (it was an open secret that the rich Ottoman officials, seeing the noose of the siege tightening, buried their valuables, gold coins and jewelry in cemeteries or inside the tombs of their relatives so as not to fall into the hands of the Greeks. The besiegers, as soon as they entered the city, opened the tombs looking for hidden treasures, in other words loot), we give the real extent and not a sense of "symmetry" or, if you will, of "the same fury."
History is not a sum of isolated moments, nor a field for selective readings. Whoever detaches 1821 from the four centuries that gave birth to it is not seeking the truth, but constructing propaganda. The justice of historical memory requires us to look at the past as a whole: with the sacrifices, the traumas, but also the inevitable explosions. Because the freedom of a people is not judged by the day they revolted, but by the depth of the night they endured before seeing the light!
P.S. In Tripolitsa yes we "went completely overboard." It is also the point of reference of the West (especially the romantics of the era) which was shocked by its violence, because it expected to see the "descendants of Plato" fighting like philosophers, ignoring that 400 years of slavery had completely changed the social reality… A nice topic that I would like to analyze at some point.
Good morning to everyone!

The offer depends on the United States easing pressure on Iran. Traffic through the strait has dropped sharply.

The strait is a key route for energy supplies. The offer does not mean the strait has reopened.

It also does not mean the United States has accepted Iran's terms. CNBC reported that the offer raised hopes for new US-Iran talks.

Reports say Iran sent the proposal to Washington through a mediator. This aimed to restart stalled talks to end hostilities.

Reports also say Iran planned to discuss the offer with other countries. This would happen during the United Nations General Assembly week.

Iran had earlier set seven conditions for reopening the strait. These included ending war on all fronts.

Iran also wanted the United States to stop all pressure including sanctions. The Guardian said Iran seems to have eased those earlier conditions.

US stock futures were mixed today. Oil prices were lower, CNBC reported.

text:
he most famous sentence in American history was not new when King said it in Washington. He had already preached it two months earlier, on June 23, 1963, to roughly 125,000 people marching down Woodward Avenue in Detroit.

The Dream Before Washington: Detroit, June 23, 1963

Every January, the country recites one sentence back to itself. That children would one day be judged not by the color of their skin but by the content of their character.

America files that line under a single date, August 28, 1963, and a single place, the marble steps of the Lincoln Memorial.

The filing is wrong. Martin Luther King had already preached that exact sentence two months earlier, to a larger crowd, in Detroit.

He said it inside Cobo Hall on June 23, 1963. I have a dream this afternoon, he told them, and then came the line about his four little children and the content of their character, word for word, while the March on Washington was still only an idea on paper.

A Detroit record label pressed his voice onto vinyl that same summer. Then the country managed to forget the city, the crowd, and the record all at once.

This is the speech before the speech, and the day America lost on purpose.

To feel the weight of what Detroit did, you have to stand inside the week it happened.

Eleven days before the march, a man named Medgar Evers had been shot down in his own driveway in Jackson, Mississippi. He was the NAACP's first field secretary in the state, a decorated veteran of the Second World War, and he was killed carrying a stack of t-shirts that read Jim Crow Must Go.

His wife and three children had been waiting up for him when it happened. They had just watched President Kennedy give a televised address on civil rights, and an hour later their father was gone.

The country was raw with it. Evers had been laid to rest at Arlington only days before Detroit marched.

The date itself was chosen, not convenient. June 23 fell twenty years after the 1943 riot that had torn the same city open, a few days of violence that left thirty-four people dead, the majority of them Black.

Detroit was marching on the anniversary of its own worst wound. More than a few people in that crowd carried a real and reasonable fear that 1943 could come back.

The man who built the day was Reverend C. L. Franklin, pastor of New Bethel Baptist Church and the father of a young singer named Aretha. He chaired the Detroit Council for Human Rights, and with Reverend Albert Cleage he turned an ordinary Sunday into the largest civil rights demonstration the nation had ever seen.

They stepped off down Woodward Avenue in the afternoon heat.

By the time the line filled the avenue, an estimated 125,000 people were moving through downtown Detroit, packed curb to curb in aerial photographs that still survive. It was the biggest civil rights march in the country's history to that day, and it was happening in the North.

The marchers had come out of churches and union halls and schoolrooms. Detroit was about thirty percent Black in 1963, yet only one of the seven people on its governing body was, and Black officers made up barely three percent of the police force.

The people walking down Woodward knew those numbers in their bodies. They walked anyway, and they walked in a discipline that startled the city watching them.

At the very front, the leaders moved with their arms locked together. King was there with Franklin and Cleage, with Walter Reuther of the auto workers, with Mayor Jerome Cavanagh of Detroit at his side.

Hand-painted signs rose over the marchers. Voices broke open into We Shall Overcome and the Battle Hymn of the Republic, and more than five hundred police officers lined a march that gave them nothing to do.

Somewhere in that river of people was a young man named Elliott Hall. He had just finished his second year at Wayne State law school, and he walked with his wife, the two of them holding signs for the Congress of Racial Equality.

Hall had started so far back on Woodward that he could already tell he would never make it inside the hall. He was right about that.

Cobo Hall filled to its walls, and tens of thousands more spilled out onto the lawns and the streets around it.

The ones who could not get in simply stood in the open and listened to King through loudspeakers. Hall was one of them, taking in the most important speech of the year from a Detroit sidewalk.

Inside, King reached the microphone and named the thing in front of him. He called it the largest and greatest demonstration for freedom ever held in the United States, and the building roared it back at him.

Then he went looking for the dream. I have a dream this afternoon, he said, and said it again, and the crowd carried every line of it forward.

He made the dream local before he ever made it national. One day, right here in Detroit, he said, a Black family would buy a house or rent a house anywhere their money could carry them, and a man would be able to hold a job.

Then he spoke the sentence the whole country would later take for its own. His four little children, judged one day on the content of their character and not the color of their skin.

He refused to let the room stay comfortable in its joy. He named Medgar Evers out loud, eleven days into the grief, with the body barely in the ground.

Before the victory is won, he told them, some, like Medgar Evers, may have to face physical death. And if that death freed their children and their white brothers from a deeper kind of death, he said, then nothing could be more redemptive.

He named Emmett Till too, the fourteen-year-old murdered in Mississippi eight years before. He said he dreamed of a day when no child would have to face what Till had faced, or what Evers had faced, and when every man could live with dignity.

He warned them, before he was done, that Black supremacy was as dangerous as white supremacy, and that God was not interested only in the freedom of Black men but in the freedom of the whole human race. Then he left them on the old words, free at last, free at last, thank God almighty, free at last, a full two months before the nation would hear them.

King would later call the day one of the most wonderful things that had happened in America. Days afterward he wrote the city's police commissioner to thank a force that had guarded the march instead of breaking it, a letter he could not have written about most of the South.

Sitting quietly inside that afternoon was a record company that was busy changing American music.

Berry Gordy had built Motown a few miles away, in a house on West Grand Boulevard he had named Hitsville. He decided that what King said in Detroit belonged in every home in America, and so he did something his label had never done, and put a speech on a record.

It was the first time the most successful Black-owned company in the country had openly tied itself to the movement. King had come to see Gordy at the height of it, and told him that what Gordy was doing with music, he was trying to do with politics.

King would not take a cent for the record. Motown had offered him forty cents on every copy sold, and he turned the money down and asked that all of it go to the movement instead.

Gordy added a donation of his own and pressed the album anyway. He titled it The Great March to Freedom, the first spoken word record Motown ever released, from a company that until then had only sold the sound of young America dancing.

He thought so much of it that he carried a copy to King in person. He presented the album at a benefit in Atlanta that August, with Lena Horne standing nearby, and told the room it belonged in the home of every American child, white or Black.

The record went on sale on August 27, 1963.

The very next day, King stood at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington and gave the dream to the entire country, with the cameras running this time.

Washington swallowed Detroit inside of a day. The lenses and the headlines fixed on the capital, and the march that had come first quietly slid out of the national story.

Even the record went under. Motown's own distributors, men who could sell a love song in their sleep, had no idea what to do with a preacher's vision.

The company's sales chief admitted years later exactly what had happened. It just did not sell.

The first dream slid to the back of the record bins. The 125,000 became a footnote, and then they became nothing at all.

So here is the piece worth picking up and carrying out of all this.

The dream did not begin in Washington. It was already alive and on its feet on Woodward Avenue, in a city marching on the anniversary of its own dead, eleven days after they put Medgar Evers in the ground.

Detroit dreamed it first, in front of more people, and pressed it into a record almost no one bought. The smallest thing owed back is to hand the city its own sentence every time we repeat it.

I have a dream this afternoon, he told them in Detroit, that one day right here a man could buy a house and hold a job anywhere his money could carry him. Right here, in Detroit, that part of the dream is still waiting.

text:
Brent crude has fallen below the psychologically important $100 level after Iran signaled that it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if Washington eases military pressure and lifts its blockade on Iranian ports. Reuters reports that Tehran has already conveyed its proposal through mediators and is seeking a path back to negotiations.
The market reaction is immediate because Hormuz represents one of the most important energy chokepoints in the global economy.
But there is an important distinction.
Iran has offered a conditional reopening. The Strait has not yet been reopened.

That difference is precisely what traders must understand.

Brent initially fell below $100, while WTI moved sharply lower as investors began pricing the possibility of a diplomatic resolution and improving physical supply. At the same time, Saudi Arabia has restarted its East West pipeline and is preparing to resume exports through Yanbu, creating another potential source of additional supply outside the Hormuz route.
This creates a powerful combination for the oil market.
Potential diplomatic normalization through Hormuz.
Recovery of Saudi export capacity through the Red Sea.
Lower geopolitical risk premium.
Greater confidence in future physical supply.
That is why crude can lose several dollars in a matter of hours.
The market is not necessarily saying that the energy crisis is over.
It is saying that the probability of a less severe supply disruption has increased.
And probability is what financial markets price.
The next critical variable is therefore not another headline.

It is implementation.
Does Washington actually ease the blockade?
Does Tehran reopen the waterway?
Do tanker movements normalize?
Does Saudi Arabia restore its alternative export infrastructure toward normal capacity?

If the answer to those questions becomes yes, the geopolitical premium embedded in crude could continue to unwind.
Reuters reported that Brent had fallen as much as 3% toward $97.60 on Tuesday as improving supply prospects emerged.

For WTI traders, this is a critical transition point.

Oil is moving from a market dominated by scarcity expectations toward one increasingly dominated by supply normalization expectations.
That does not eliminate geopolitical risk.
It changes the direction of the risk premium.
The oil market is now watching diplomacy almost as closely as production data.
And if barrels begin moving normally again, the repricing could be considerably larger than the initial move below $100.

🚨 IRAN OFFERS SEVEN-DAY HORMUZ REOPENING DEAL AS DIPLOMATIC CHANNEL RE-EMERGES

TEHRAN, IRAN - Oil markets reacted quickly because the proposal introduces something they have lacked for months: a timetable. A seven-day reopening window gives negotiators a concrete benchmark against which diplomatic progress can be measured rather than another open-ended statement of intent.

Tehran appears to be linking commercial navigation, port access and broader negotiations into a single package. That bundles economic relief and security concerns together, making it harder for either side to take partial gains while avoiding larger questions.

The absence of a planned presidential meeting suggests the focus has shifted to intermediaries and technical bargaining rather than headline diplomacy. That often means both sides are testing whether limited confidence-building steps are possible before committing political capital at the highest level.

For Washington, the next practical choice is whether to signal diplomatic intent without surrendering leverage. For Tehran, the value of the proposal lies in converting control over a strategic chokepoint into negotiating room at a moment when pressure on exports remains a constraint. The resource that has changed is negotiating leverage tied directly to maritime access.

🇮🇷|Iran Showcases Maritime Single Window in Georgia: A Sanctioned and Bombed Nation Teaches Regional Neighbors How to Manage Maritime Operations

September 2026, Batumi, Georgia. An International Maritime Organization (IMO) regional technical conference. Participants included Iran, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Georgia, and Romania.

Iran showcased two key systems:

First, the Maritime Single Window (MSW). This is a digital platform that consolidates all procedures for ship entry and exit customs, immigration, quarantine, and port services into a single online system. Shipowners no longer need to visit five different agencies or fill out ten separate forms; a single submission handles everything.

Second, the Integrated Maritime Management System (IMAS). This is a digital monitoring and management system covering Iran's entire coastline. It integrates radar, AIS, satellite data, cameras, and communication systems to monitor vessel movements, port operations, and maritime security in real-time.

IMO experts and representatives from regional nations took a keen interest in Iran's experience.

🎯 Why does this matter?

Because Iran built these systems while facing sanctions, aerial bombardment, and blockades.

· Sanctions prevented Iran from importing Western software. Iranian engineers developed the MSW and IMAS themselves.
· Sanctions blocked Iran from using SWIFT. Iran integrated local currency settlement and alternative payment mechanisms into the MSW.
· War damaged Iran's infrastructure through bombing. Yet, Iran continued to operate and maintain these systems.
· The US targeted 85% of Iran's oil tankers. Iran uses IMAS to monitor every vessel entering its waters—including those attempting "illegal crossings."

This was not merely a "technology showcase"; it was a demonstration of sovereignty. Iran was telling its neighbors: We do not need Western software, Western platforms, or Western permission. We can build it ourselves and we can build it better than you.

🌊 Why did Caspian and Black Sea nations attend?

Because these nations face the same dilemmas:

◾They rely on maritime trade but lack autonomous maritime management systems.
◾They use Western software but fear being cut off.  · They need to monitor their own waters but lack the radar and AIS networks that Iran possesses.
◾They want to participate in the digitalization of global shipping but do not wish to rely on Western platforms.

Iran’s MSW (Maritime Single Window) and IMAS (Integrated Maritime Management System) offer an alternative. They do not rely on the West. They do not rely on the US dollar. They do not rely on SWIFT. They can operate under sanctions. They can operate during wartime.

That is why experts from the IMO are listening. That is why representatives from Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Georgia, and Romania are listening.

It is not because "Iran is the good guy." It is because Iran has what they need.

text:
Anyone still citing the "Katie Johnson" bullshit at this point is either a liar or a moron

- Her story was shopped around as a paid tabloid exclusive (including a recorded interview with a promised cut of proceeds), not independently investigated and then filed

- It was pushed for months by Norm Lubow (aka "Al Taylor"), a literal former Jerry Springer producer with a long history of pitching dubious celebrity sex/crime stories, with help from anti-Trump activist Steve Baer (cash to intermediaries, a "Justice for Katie" site/fund, posting the video against counsel's wishes etc)

- Lubow later told journalist Dylan Howard that he had "details about the Clintons' involvement in the whole Katie Johnson affair," but refused to elaborate out of "fear of retribution from those involved in what he characterized as a fictitious scheme"

- Origin stories conflicted... "Johnson" told Revelist that a mutual friend introduced her to Lubow so he could use his resources to bring the accusations public, but Baer said Taylor told him they met at a holiday party about two years earlier, that Taylor asked about celebrity gossip, and that she then told him the assault story

- Experienced Epstein/victims' lawyers (i.e. Bradley Edwards and Gloria Allred) declined the case... A patent lawyer in NJ (i.e. Tom Meagher) with no relevant experience eventually took it up

- A letter from "Johnson" to NYPD commissioner Bratton contained metadata showing it was created by Baer's wife

- The CA complaint used a dead man's abandoned house, a dead phone number, and pauper status... Court mail was returned... It cited statutes that did not support the claimed civil case... Photos of "Johnson" were shopped for sale... The judge dismissed it for failure to state a claim

- Later NY filings dropped certain flashy details from the first complaint (e.g. abortion cash, Trump calling Epstein a "Jew bastard," a $100 million demand)... Defendants were never served, a press conference was canceled (supposedly due to ambiguous threats, according to the notoriously slimy Lisa Bloom), and the NY lawsuit was then voluntarily dropped days before the 2016 election prior to any discovery or testimony

- There is no physical evidence, document, or independent witness that has been verified in court

- Mike Fisten (a former Miami-Dade homicide detective who worked as a PI for Bradley Edwards) said Lubow and Meagher refused his offer to verify "Tiffany Doe's" contact book free of charge, and that Trump's name was just "thrown in" to the lawsuit

- Emily Shugerman, one of the few journalists who did speak with "Johnson," left the phone conversation with her "more confused than ever' and unsure "if [Johnson] even exists"

- In 2019 journalist Raheem Hosseini hired a PI and traced "Johnson's" phone number to a Riverside County, CA esthetician who would've been only ~4 years old in 1994 (when the alleged Trump assaults took place), not 13 as she claimed

- An insider source told the Daily Mail, "[N]ew information emerged that suggested [Johnson] had not been telling the truth. Ultimately it was discovered that Donald Trump's name had been inserted into this, he was not involved whatsoever. After that she had no credibility."

"There are more files coming to the museum through donations, but you might already be aware; I am sure you can get access. The FBI supposedly has files never fully released above the impact zones." The NIST 9/11 Video & Photo Archive: How to Access the WTC Visual Database 🧵👇

NIST assembled one of the largest collections of 9/11 video and still photography as part of its World Trade Center investigation. The material is publicly available, but it isn't a polished streaming library—it’s a massive technical archive released mainly through FOIA.

Here is how it works, what it contains, and how to explore it:

📂 The Official Starting Point NIST hosts the files on its Disaster and Failure Studies Repository. The site points to NIST-controlled Google Drive folders containing: • Organized photos and video clips (the most usable starting set) • Original raw video from tapes • NIST-generated simulations, fire-test footage, and steel photographs
Link: https://t.co/skuMK0vQAb
🔓 How It Reached the Public The bulk of the raw tapes became public through FOIA request #09-42 filed by the International Center for 9/11 Studies around 2009. NIST released dozens of DVDs containing MPEG/VOB files with original tape labels (e.g., CNN NIST Dubs, news-station field tapes, and amateur footage). The original torrent site that hosted these is defunct, but the files live on through community preservation.
🔍 Practical Ways to Explore the Archive Depending on what you are looking for, here are the best ways to access the media:
1. NIST Official Drive Folders: Closest to the original files. Best for verification, though quality and organization vary. 2. The Internet Archive: Holds full FOIA DVD sets and individual tapes. Search terms: “NIST FOIA 09-42”, “WTCI”, or specific tape numbers. 3. YouTube Channels: Channels like Enhanced WTC Videos, September 11 Archivist, and Organized WTC Visual Databases offer deinterlaced, timed, and higher-quality versions with location notes. Easiest for casual viewing.

📼 What the Archive Contains Investigators reviewed roughly 7,000 video segments and 7,000 photographs, including: • Street-level news and amateur video (before, during, and after both collapses) • Aerial and helicopter footage • Ground Zero aftermath and following days • On-the-spot interviews and unaired broadcasts • NIST’s extracted analysis clips

(Note: The clip of the injured man in the sling at Liberty & West Street belongs to this collection, released by NIST with almost no identifying information about the individual).
⚠️ Content Warning As NIST explicitly notes, many of these clips contain graphic images of injuries, remains, people falling, and the immediate, uncensored aftermath.

🚧 Limits & What's Next Not every tape NIST collected was released. Some remain withheld, redacted, or only exist as short analysis clips. Faces were sometimes blurred on later releases, and quality ranges from broadcast Beta cam to consumer VHS dubs.
Other massive collections sit outside this dataset—including a separate video archive collected by Camera Planet recently donated to the New York Public Library. Researcher access for that collection is slated for ~2027, with online access planned later.

Looking for footage of a specific location (like Liberty/West St), a specific news station, or a named videographer? Drop a reply and I can point you to the relevant tape IDs or known public copies.

text:
I respect that you are engaging with this. You see thoughtful and trying to engage with history. (I still have to listen to your podcast episode - must do that)

I understand where you are coming from. My parents were Labour - one was even a MP candidate at one point - I was socialist for a lot of my life. But as I've got older I've become more Burkian, more nostalgic, more of a gardener than an engineer.

To me the interesting thing about the history of England (and Britain) is the accumulation of texture. Its liberties were negotiated rather than proclaimed, over centuries - admittedly sometimes as a result of force, between freemen, barons and the Crown. Nobody designed them. They were wrung from power by people who wanted particular things (a fair trial, a tax they had consented to, the right to gather wood in the forest) and who were prepared to fight for them.

What strikes me most is that England kept its thread. It had its revolution, and executed its king, yet within a generation it had repaired the break. Three centuries later it escaped the ripsaw of totalitarianism that tore through the continent. What it kept instead was a balance of forces, held in place not by a written constitution but by people, and by the practices through which they governed themselves.

English liberty is an earned inheritance. It lived in convention, duty and manners, and in the shires and boroughs, the justices of the peace, parish constables, the juries, the parishes, mutual societies, clubs and the corporations that stood between Crown / Parliament on one side and the ordinary citizen on the other. These were not the abstract rights of man, or legal code. They were ways of doing things, understood by those who did them and passed on by example.

This is the special thing about England, and it is what we have nearly lost by identifying ourselves too closely with the democratic state and the international post war catalogue of human rights: the true guarantee of freedom is culture. When the state takes over the work of the intermediate institutions, or the long march through them repurposes them, they wither. Laws cannot do what they did. A law can forbid, but it cannot create the habits of trust on which obedience to law depends - Witness what is happening with Jury trials.

The point which you identify as the birth of the nation I identify as the start of its death. The two world wars took the men who would have filled the bench, the vestry and the county council, and taught those who survived that the state could organise everything. After 1945 the lesson was applied to peace, the bonds of mutuality and fraternity loosened by the guarantee of cradle to the grave.

Modernity loosened the bonds of place, role and station that gave duty its content. The self became a chooser rather than a bearer of obligations. Multiculturalism made a principle of that choosing, since by declining to limit numbers to the rate at which they could be assimilated or to ask newcomers to respect and take up the inheritance, it offered them human rights in place of belonging.

Authority passed from custom and local judgment to courts, codes and international conventions, until "lawful" and "right" came to mean the same thing. Postmodernism completed the work by treating every inherited meaning as a mask for power. What remains is a population of rights-bearing individuals, and of interest groups organised by ethnicity and class, facing the state across the empty ground where the shires, the parishes and the juries of peers once stood.

Rights can protect freedom, but they cannot sustain it. Only culture can do that, and culture is a garden, not a design . It needs people who know and play their part in its ecology. If “our values” are reduced to something codified, if they are represented by the state, by a constitution, by a bill of human and social rights then we have lost the deep connection with this history.

Our unique inheritance has been replaced by a "design pattern" (the prevent strategy "British values" plus a hagiographic view of the NHS ) that could in theory apply to anyone anywhere.

We have divided the grounds of a stately home and attached village into lots for a new build estate. Perhaps it was unequal, perhaps it was a bit odd and old and eccentric. Perhaps people really wanted a new modern look. But forgive me if I don’t worship the new-build Barratt home with its plastic grass and patio.

Every aspect of this is outrageous. There should be a major community response.

Stanford U: Five Stanford University students who faced prison sentences and thousands of dollars in restitution in connection to a campus protest against Israel’s war on Gaza had all charges dropped on Monday.
The students also had their restitution severely reduced, ending a two-year legal saga that also saw the lead prosecutor in the case removed by the court. Part of a group of 12, the students had been charged with felony conspiracy to trespass and felony vandalism in connection to an hour-long, June 2024 occupation during which the group barricaded themselves inside the university president’s office to demand Stanford consider a student resolution to divest from Israel, among other requests. Some accepted plea deals or other diversion offers but five of the students went to trial earlier this year. The month-long trial ended with a hung jury but Jeff Rosen, the Santa Clara county district attorney, immediately announced his intention to retry the case before a judge ordered his recusal in May over a conflict of interest that, the judge said during court proceedings, would “render it unlikely that the defendants will receive fair treatment”. The case has since been taken over by the California attorney general’s office, which reached a resolution with the students. That resolution meant dropping all charges in exchange for 100 hours of community service at a nonprofit of their choosing and a total restitution of about $50,000, far less than the $1m prosecutors initially threatened them with and the $ 329,000 they each risked being found liable for at trial. The charges were the most severe handed out against students in connection to pro-Palestine protests on campus.

INDO-MIM

One of the more interesting questions around Indo-MIM is not just who its competitors are (which of course you can see in the attached image), but whether the company actually has enough differentiation to command pricing power in a highly competitive global market.

They have superior margins as one can see from their results as well.

Indo-MIM operates in the Metal Injection Molding  industry, where components are manufactured using metal powders and can be produced in highly complex geometries. Its global competitors include players such as Jiangsu Gian, CN Innovation, GKN Powder Metallurgy, Future Tech, Schunk, ARC Global and Parmatech.

So as I discussed in one of my earlier posts. IT IS NOT A PURE MONOPOLY BUSINESS.

But pricing power in MIM doesn't necessarily come from having no competitors.

It comes from qualification, process complexity, customer switching costs and reliability.

=> When a component becomes part of a customer's product, the customer typically isn't going to switch suppliers simply because another manufacturer offers the component at a slightly lower price.

The alternative supplier has to demonstrate that it can consistently manufacture the component to the required specifications, pass quality checks, complete qualification processes and maintain reliability at scale.

That creates a certain degree of stickiness.

The company has built significant vertical integration across the manufacturing process - from metal powders and feedstock to tooling, MIM manufacturing, machining, finishing.

𝐒𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐀𝐝𝐯𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬 | 𝐌𝐢𝐜𝐫𝐨𝐠𝐥𝐢𝐚: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐁𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐧'𝐬 "𝐒𝐥𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐳𝐞𝐫𝐬"?
Why do we get sleepier the longer we stay awake?
Sleep pressure builds during wakefulness, but exactly how the brain senses it, and turns it into stable sleep, is still not well understood. 

A new study published in Science Advances, led by teams from Academician Heping Cheng at Peking University and Professor Xiaochun Gu at Southeast University, offers a new answer.
The study, "Microglia stabilize sleep homeostasis via adenosine A₃ receptor signaling," reveals a surprising role for microglia in regulating sleep.
 
🔬 𝐌𝐢𝐜𝐫𝐨𝐠𝐥𝐢𝐚 𝐬𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞 𝐬𝐥𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐞
Using miniature two-photon microscopy in freely behaving mice, researchers tracked calcium activity and morphological changes alongside animal behavior, EEG/EMG, and levels of extracellular adenosine.
Microglial calcium activity closely tracked brain and behavioral states—it was found to be higher during wakefulness, lower during NREM sleep, and shifting rapidly at state transitions.
 
More strikingly, prolonged sleep deprivation increased microglial activity, which then gradually returned to baseline during recovery sleep. This suggests microglia actively respond to sleep pressure, rather than simply following changes in behavior.
 
🧩 𝐀𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐀₃ 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐨𝐫: 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐤
Adenosine is a well-established signal of sleep pressure and its extracellular levels shifted across the sleep-wake cycle in step with microglial activity.
Further experiments identified the adenosine A₃ receptor (A₃R) as a key pathway driving microglial calcium dynamics.
When A₃R was selectively deleted in microglia, both state-dependent calcium activity and morphological changes were weakened. These mice also transitioned more frequently between wakefulness and NREM sleep and showed increased sleep fragmentation—without any significant change in total sleep time.
 
🧠 𝐅𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐢𝐦𝐦𝐮𝐧𝐞 𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐬𝐥𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐫𝐞𝐠𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧
Together, these findings support a model in which microglia "read" sleep-pressure signals through A₃R, then dynamically adjust their own activity and morphology to help stabilize sleep-wake states.
In other words, microglia may act as a built-in stabilizer for sleep homeostasis.
 
🔬 𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐡𝐧𝐨𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐲 𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬
Miniature two-photon microscopy makes it possible to observe cellular dynamics at high resolution during natural behavior and throughout sleep-wake cycles in freely moving animals.
The imaging technology behind this research was developed by Academician Heping Cheng's lab and brought to market as commercial imaging systems by TRANSVISTA.
 
Read the full article: DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aef3957
Know more about TRANSVISTA: https://t.co/f491R4CFS1 
 
Figure from Zhao et al., Science Advances (2026). CC BY 4.0.

At 19, Joseph Saukulyak was serving in the U.S. Navy and preparing for the planned invasion of Japan.

Then came the news: the war was over.

Today, Joseph turns 100. 🇺🇸🎂

During WWII, he served as a storekeeper, disbursing supplies and handling payroll. He spent time aboard an aircraft carrier and later an LST that took him to Okinawa, where American forces were preparing for what they believed would come next.

Japan surrendered before the invasion took place.

Joseph later recalled being offered a choice: reenlist for another six years or go home.

“I went home and five years later I got married.”

One hundred years of life, and a firsthand connection to one of the defining moments of the 20th century.

Happy 100th Birthday, Joseph, and thank you for your service.

I’d rather wait for the volatility to settle and then see whether this zone offers a better opportunity.

ARM surged roughly 17% on Monday, closing at $322.90, as the AI and semiconductor rally pushed it to new highs.

I’m not buying into that kind of move.
My new watch zone is:

$295–$305

If it never pulls back, I’m perfectly fine missing it.
$RBRK — Rubrik Still waiting for a pullback

RBRK gained another roughly 5.9% on Monday, closing near $113.

After such a strong run over the last several sessions, my old watch zone needs to move higher.

New watch zone:
$104–$108

The faster it runs, the less interested I am in chasing it.

$TSLA — Tesla Watching: $352–$360

Tesla recently closed around $375.30.
That’s still well above the area where I’d become interested.

If it pulls back toward $360 and buyers clearly step in, I’ll start paying closer attention again.

$NVO — Novo Nordisk Watching: $38.50–$40.50

NVO fell nearly 8% on Monday, closing around $39.80, as investors reacted cautiously to the company’s latest long-term growth outlook.

So this isn’t about chasing anymore.

The bigger mistake would be:

Buying the dip too quickly just because the stock fell hard.
I want to see whether $38.50–$40.50 can gradually develop into a real support zone.

Progress around tokenized stocks and improving crypto sentiment remain catalysts worth watching.

Good news doesn’t mean a stock is worth buying at any price.
I’d rather wait for:

$110–$114
before taking another serious look.

One of the biggest mistakes in a bull market isn’t missing a rally—it’s letting FOMO push you into a stock when everyone else is already euphoric.

AI and tech are clearly strong right now.

I think the answer is to become more patient.

I’d rather miss part of a move than chase a stock after it has already gone vertical.

Studying the market and looking for opportunities is something I genuinely enjoy.

I’m never going to tell you a stock is “guaranteed to go up tomorrow.”

Save this watchlist.

European Parliament Committee delegation on Industry, Research & Energy (ITRE), led by Angelika Winzig from Austria and Raffaele Stancanelli, called on at Kartavya Bhavan.

The delegation held a wide range discussion, with focus on effective implementation of the India-EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA) and deeper cooperation with the European Union in science, technology, research and, critical and emerging technologies.

Speaking on behalf of the delegation, Angelika Winzig thanked for the meeting and said that India is a key strategic partner for the European Union. She said the delegation’s visit was aimed at gaining a deeper understanding of India’s industrial and technology policies and identifying areas for closer cooperation. She referred to shared interests in strengthening industrial competitiveness, ensuring secure and resilient critical supply chains, and advancing the green and digital transitions, while welcoming continued dialogue between India and the European Parliament on these issues.

The Indian side gave a brief about the @narendramodi government's research and innovation priorities, and the vision for Viksit Bharat 2047, with greater focus on high-impact research, translation of research into technologies and products, and increased industry participation. There was a mention of the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF) and the EUR 10 billion Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) initiative, aimed at catalysing high-risk, high-impact research and nurturing deep-tech startups.

India-EU strategic partnership offers significant opportunities for closer collaboration in areas of mutual priority, with science and research forming an integral part of the partnership.  Invited greater India-EU cooperation in frontier and emerging areas including Artificial Intelligence, quantum technologies, advanced materials, biotechnology and semiconductors, besides high-performance computing and next-generation telecommunications, including 6G.

text:
Death Is Not Health Care!

Don’t take it from me. Listen to these folks.

Three years ago Canada left a woman with stage 4 ovarian cancer and mailed her a pamphlet on how to kill herself through MAID. They told her there was no hope. They forgot her. She fled to the United States, chose Texas, and today she is still fighting. She hiked two hours up a mountain on chemo. In America doctors told her to live. In Canada they told her to die.

That is the system @AbdulElSayed wants to bring here. He wrote the book on Medicare for All. 

He campaigns on government run care from cradle to grave with no premiums, no copays, and one buyer setting the price. 

Canada already ran that experiment. Wait lists. Rationing. Doctors so strained they offer death as the treatment plan. Canadians pay for a system that, when cancer comes, hands you a suicide brochure instead of a fight.

Socialized medicine does not work. It does not save you. It manages you until you are cheap enough to discard. Even if you go broke in America, death is not the official option. Nobody mails you instructions to end your life because a bureaucrat decided you are not worth the fight.

Michigan, this is what is on the ballot. Reject the import of Canada’s death culture. Fight for care that tells you to keep living.
