text:
[8/8] @cum_granosalis @Whosoeverwills @CraigACarter1 @aspin3 @uncommonsens3 @DrDavidLAllen
*Soteriology *Follows *Christology 
*Man-Focused vs. *The-Son

The Hyper-Augustinians and Pelagians: 
Juxtaposed with the Pauline Christ Relation https://t.co/00TVRSkMiP from Bobby Grow

Douglas Campbell in his book The Triumph of God’s Love: Pauline Dogmatics offers a nice sketch of a theological continuum; what he identifies as “Hyper-Augustinianism” and “Pelagianism.” He concisely shows how both fail to do justice to Paul’s theology proper, and subsequently, his soteriology. But both of these loci have continued to plague the church from Augustine/Pelagius; Luther/Erasmus; Calvin/Pighius; Dort/Arminius; classical Calvinists/Arminians; MacArthur’s Lordship Salvation/Hodges’ Free Grace; James White/Provisionists; so on and so forth. 

This frame of reference, or this binary is rather false when we examine, with a critical eye, what we find in the teaching of the New Testament in general, and the Pauline corpus in particular. 

It is from within this frame of reference that Campbell offers up the aforementioned sketches with reference to Augustinianism/Pelagianism. In this post we will work through Campbell’s sketch on Hyper-Augustinianism, and in a post following we will visit what he has to say on Pelagianism juxtaposed with the Pauline theology. After we read Campbell’s sketch on Hyper-Augustinianism, I will attempt to tease out some further applications, and show how they might impinge on some current soteriological wanderings among the crowds “out there.”

Campbell writes at some length:
Quote:

Hyper-Augustinianism
If election is understood mechanistically, someone might attach this notion to grace and argue that God has given us everything we need in the act of electing us. God simply acts decisively upon us, albeit generously. This gift would then operate in spite of anything we do, and anything we might do should be excluded. Indeed, if we had to act, we would to that degree undermine what God has given us. Grace and human activity operate here in a zero-sum relationship, so, if we take the side of God, we would go on to attack any endorsements of a need for human activity in the name of grace.

A particular reading of Augustine can cause readers of Paul trouble in this respect, so that the assertion of any need for agency or even learning in response to grace is dubbed “Pelagianism”! I don’t think this is a complete reading of Augustine, who was a complex thinker and shifted significantly in his thinking over time. But an extreme account of some of his positions can be advocated in this way and in his name, and at this moment his influence—however misrepresented—must be resisted. We can speak of a hyper-Augustinian view, then, that eliminates any role for human agency in discipleship, the long-term results of which are serious. The whole process of formation is neglected if not opposed by hyper-Augustinians, and the end result is a church without discipleship. How good is this church likely to be? And how Pauline will it look?

Fortunately, we have already exposed the error at work in this view and corrected it. God’s election is certainly unconditional, but in the sense that a covenantal relationship is. It will never be withdrawn and will ultimately prevail. In the meantime, however, it respects human agency carefully, as seen most clearly in God’s incarnation to meet us. Moreover, as we will see in much more detail shortly, among those who respond to it, it enhances human freedom. Those who learn actively and wholeheartedly to live out of their new location in Christ can grow dramatically in their capacity to act in good ways. Relational election nurtures human agency and freedom; it does not stifle it. It summons us to ongoing and deeper responsiveness, which is to say, to learning, and many of Augustine’s writings contain a great deal of wisdom about this process. 

Nevertheless, any exclusion of human activity in response to God’s initiative in his name, in a type of hyper-Augustinianism, must be vigilantly opposed and rejected. *This* *type* of unconditionality undermines the heart of the life of discipleship.

However, a further mistake is, as is often the case, a swing to the opposite and complementary error. 

Whereas hyper-Augustinians emphasize election and grace to the exclusion of human agency, misconceiving both divine and human agency in the process, Pelagians share the same basic misunderstanding but emphasize human agency on the other side of the supposed divide, and so go on to override divine election, with equally destructive results.

End Quote.

If you are familiar with the history, you’ll agree that Campbell’s sketch captures the ground quite well; viz. in regard to understanding the binary, or divide between what we know today, and more popularly, as the “Calvinists versus the Arminians.” 

What shouldn’t be lost, and often is when considering something like Campbell’s points, is the alternative he is working into this mix. That is the “relational election” he mentions, and the covenantal relationship, as Campbell contends, that is central to Paul’s understanding of a God-world relation. What he doesn’t tease out so explicitly in his sketch, but that is because it implicitly underwrites what he is developing, is the objective/subjective status that the Pauline soteriology operates from, insofar that God acts, within a covenantal relationship, unilaterally for the world in Jesus Christ. 

This is his, or the Apostle Paul’s alternative to both Hyper-Augustinianism and Pelagianism.

Hyper-Augustinianism and Pelagianism both operate, respectively, from an abstract non-relational-covenantal frame when they attempt to think salvation. 

That is to say, anyone who operates on this continuum, and they are legion, thinks salvation from an abstract humanity (rather than from Christ’s vicarious humanity), and think in terms of individualism insofar as the cosmic Christ does not ground the way they think God’s election for the world in Jesus Christ. 

In other words, both Hyper-Augustinians and Pelagians, on a continuum, think salvation is contingent upon the elect’s response/decision to be for God. Paul’s alternative thinks salvation is contingent upon God’s election to be for humanity in Jesus Christ; that salvation is Christ-focused, and that within this as the inner-covenantal ground of the God-world relation, humanity comes to have the capaciousness to say Yes to God from God’s Yes and Amen for them in Jesus Christ. But you will notice that for the Apostle Paul, particularly as Campbell tells it, humanity comes to have this capacity from the elect and vicarious humanity of Jesus Christ. It is by this signification of God for humanity in Christ that humans come to have genuine liberty or freedom for God, “for where the Spirit of the Lord is there is liberty.” 

This undercuts the emphases that both the Hyper-Augustinians and Pelagians give us in regard to their foreclosure of God’s grace by placing God into a competitive relationship with humanity; whether that be from the Augustinian side, which emphasizes God’s brute determination and sovereignty to be for the world through a series of decrees, particularly the decretum absolutum; or from the Pelagian side which emphasizes the freedom of an abstract human agency to respond to God, insofar as they posit that said freedom has been an inherent given from since the beginning of creation. Both fail to think from Paul’s relational conception of election, and the corresponding relational-covenantalism that funds the Pauline Christ concentrated conception of a God-world relation.

Contemporary examples of Hyper-Augustinians and Pelagians: Classical Calvinists, classical Arminians / John Piper, Leighton Flowers ie his Provisionism. 

Note
[1] Douglas A. Campbell, Pauline Dogmatics: The Triumph of God’s Love (Grand Rapids, Michigan: William B. Eerdmans Publishing Company, 2020), 180–81.
 (The blog cites the subtitle first: The Triumph of God’s Love: Pauline Dogmatics.)
📖
https://t.co/4JnnlbJZ9D
📖

That is to say, anyone who operates on this continuum, and they are legion, thinks salvation from an abstract humanity (rather than from Christ’s vicarious humanity), and think in terms of individualism insofar as the cosmic Christ does not ground the way they think God’s election for the world in Jesus Christ. 

In other words, both Hyper-Augustinians and Pelagians, on a continuum, think salvation is contingent upon the elect’s response/decision to be for God. Paul’s alternative thinks salvation is contingent upon God’s election to be for humanity in Jesus Christ; that salvation is Christ-focused, and that within this as the inner-covenantal ground of the God-world relation, humanity comes to have the capaciousness to say Yes to God from God’s Yes and Amen for them in Jesus Christ. But you will notice that for the Apostle Paul, particularly as Campbell tells it, humanity comes to have this capacity from the elect and vicarious humanity of Jesus Christ. It is by this signification of God for humanity in Christ that humans come to have genuine liberty or freedom for God, “for where the Spirit of the Lord is there is liberty.” 

This undercuts the emphases that both the Hyper-Augustinians and Pelagians give us in regard to their foreclosure of God’s grace by placing God into a competitive relationship with humanity; whether that be from the Augustinian side, which emphasizes God’s brute determination and sovereignty to be for the world through a series of decrees, particularly the decretum absolutum; or from the Pelagian side which emphasizes the freedom of an abstract human agency to respond to God, insofar as they posit that said freedom has been an inherent given from since the beginning of creation. Both fail to think from Paul’s relational conception of election, and the corresponding relational-covenantalism that funds the Pauline Christ concentrated conception of a God-world relation.

Contemporary examples of Hyper-Augustinians and Pelagians: Classical Calvinists, classical Arminians / John Piper, Leighton Flowers ie his Provisionism. 

Note
[1] Douglas A. Campbell, Pauline Dogmatics: The Triumph of God’s Love (Grand Rapids, Michigan: William B. Eerdmans Publishing Company, 2020), 180–81.
 (The blog cites the subtitle first: The Triumph of God’s Love: Pauline Dogmatics.)

text:
VIVAMUS NFL

TUESDAY TOP 10 | WEEK 3 POWER RANKINGS

By Vivamus de Silva | Vivamus Sports
September 22, 2026

Two weeks into the NFL season, undefeated records are beginning to separate teams in the standings, but they don't tell the entire story. Some contenders have controlled their games from the opening possession. Others have needed late drives, defensive stands, or overtime to remain unbeaten.

My rankings consider more than wins and losses. I'm looking at how teams are performing on both sides of the ball, the quality of their opponents, and whether their strengths appear sustainable. This is the first edition of the Tuesday Top 10, so it establishes the baseline for movement in next week's rankings.

---

1. Buffalo Bills (2–0)

Buffalo's 41–31 victory over Detroit demonstrated the difficulty of defending an offense that can attack in multiple ways. Josh Allen remains the centerpiece, but James Cook's 135 rushing yards gave the Bills another way to control the game. Buffalo has earned the top position through its offensive production, although allowing 31 points to the Lions leaves questions about its defense. 

Next opponent: Los Angeles Chargers at Buffalo, Sunday, September 27.

What I'm watching: Whether Buffalo can maintain its offensive balance while limiting the explosive plays that could keep the Chargers in the game.

2. San Francisco 49ers (2–0)

The 49ers have opened with a 27–7 victory over the Rams and a 35–13 win against Miami. Their offense has produced without needing to chase either game, while their defense has allowed just 20 points across two weeks. San Francisco has put together the kind of complete performances that justify a place near the top, though the season is still young. 

Next opponent: Arizona Cardinals at San Francisco, Sunday, September 27.

What I'm watching: How effectively the 49ers establish their offense against a division opponent familiar with their personnel and approach.

3. Seattle Seahawks (2–0)

Seattle followed its opening win over New England with a 31–7 victory at Arizona. Jaxon Smith-Njigba caught three touchdown passes, and the Seahawks shut out the Cardinals in the second half. Seattle's defense is giving its offense opportunities to take control rather than forcing it to win a shootout. 

Next opponent: Seattle at Washington Commanders, Sunday, September 27.

What I'm watching: Whether Seattle's defense can sustain that level of play on the road against a Washington offense dealing with uncertainty at quarterback.

4. Kansas City Chiefs (2–0)

Kansas City needed overtime to defeat Indianapolis 33–30, but Patrick Mahomes answered the challenge with 382 passing yards. The Chiefs have the quarterback and offensive firepower to recover when a game gets away from their preferred script. Allowing 30 points to the Colts, however, is a reminder that their defense has work to do. 

Next opponent: Kansas City at Miami Dolphins, Sunday, September 27.

What I'm watching: Whether the Chiefs can establish control earlier instead of relying on another late-game response from Mahomes.

5. Cincinnati Bengals (2–0)

Cincinnati's 20–6 win at Houston offered an encouraging sign beyond its passing game. Joe Burrow connected with Ja'Marr Chase for two touchdowns, while the Bengals' defense held the Texans out of the end zone. If Cincinnati can pair that defensive performance with its established offensive talent more consistently, it will be difficult to handle. 

Next opponent: Cincinnati at Pittsburgh Steelers, Sunday, September 27.

What I'm watching: Whether the Bengals can sustain their defensive performance against a division rival while keeping Burrow productive under pressure.

6. Philadelphia Eagles (2–0)

Philadelphia remains unbeaten after escaping Tennessee with a 24–20 victory. Jalen Hurts led the decisive late drive, but two interceptions helped keep the Titans within reach. The Eagles have demonstrated that they can execute when the game is on the line. They would benefit from cleaner offensive performances that make those last-minute situations less necessary. 

Next opponent: Philadelphia at Chicago Bears, Monday, September 28.

What I'm watching: Whether the Eagles can protect the football and establish a more consistent offensive rhythm.

7. Minnesota Vikings (2–0)

Minnesota's defense held Chicago to three points in a 9–3 victory. That's an impressive result against a Bears team that scored 59 in its opener, but the Vikings also failed to reach the end zone themselves. Their defense has helped deliver a 2–0 start. The offense must give it more support as the schedule continues. 

Next opponent: Minnesota at Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Sunday, September 27.

What I'm watching: Whether the Vikings can turn drives into touchdowns rather than asking their defense to carry another low-scoring game.

8. Las Vegas Raiders (2–0)

Las Vegas improved to 2–0 with a 26–14 road win over the Chargers. Kirk Cousins threw three touchdown passes, and Tre Tucker supplied a major receiving threat with 119 yards. The Raiders are getting production from their passing game and finding ways to finish possessions. Their next challenge is maintaining that efficiency as opponents gather more evidence of how they want to attack. 

Next opponent: Las Vegas at New Orleans Saints, Sunday, September 27.

What I'm watching: How Cousins handles a Saints defense coming off a second-half turnaround against Baltimore.

9. Los Angeles Rams (1–1)

The Rams answered their opening loss to San Francisco with a 28–6 victory over the Giants on Monday night. Matthew Stafford threw four touchdown passes, and Los Angeles scored in every quarter. It was the response the Rams needed, but one strong outing against New York doesn't erase the questions raised by their Week 1 defeat. 

Next opponent: Los Angeles at Denver Broncos, Sunday, September 27.

What I'm watching: Whether the Rams can sustain their passing-game production against a Denver defense that presents a different challenge from the Giants.

10. Denver Broncos (1–1)

Denver recovered from its opening loss to Kansas City by defeating Jacksonville 20–13. Bo Nix threw for 288 yards, and Jaylen Waddle caught eight passes for 138 yards. The Broncos scored both of their touchdowns in the fourth quarter, showing they can respond late while also revealing a need for more consistent production earlier in games. 

Next opponent: Los Angeles Rams at Denver, Sunday, September 27.

What I'm watching: Whether Denver can establish its passing game earlier against a Rams team coming off a four-touchdown performance from Stafford.

---

KNOCKING ON THE DOOR

Detroit Lions (1–1): Detroit scored 31 points against Buffalo but couldn't overcome the Bills' early lead. The Lions have the offensive production to enter this Top 10; their defensive response against the Jets will help determine whether they do. 

Next opponent: New York Jets at Detroit, Sunday, September 27.

Dallas Cowboys (1–1): Dak Prescott threw four touchdowns in a 37–20 win over Washington and became Dallas's all-time leader in career touchdown passes. The Cowboys' offense delivered a strong performance, but the upcoming matchup with Baltimore offers a different test. 

Next opponent: Baltimore Ravens vs. Dallas Cowboys, Sunday, September 27, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.

Green Bay Packers (1–1): Green Bay rallied from a 17–7 fourth-quarter deficit to beat the Jets 20–17 in overtime. The comeback showed resilience, but 199 total yards and a 1-for-9 performance on third down leave the Packers with clear offensive concerns. 

Next opponent: Atlanta Falcons at Green Bay, Thursday, September 24.

---

THE WEEK AHEAD

The matchup between the Rams and Broncos stands out because both teams are trying to build on Week 2 victories. Los Angeles needs to show that Monday night's offensive performance can carry over against a stronger defensive challenge. Denver needs to establish its offense before the fourth quarter. Their meeting should give us useful evidence when we revisit the lower half of the Top 10 next Tuesday.

Buffalo, San Francisco, and Seattle have set the early standard in these rankings. Kansas City, Cincinnati, Philadelphia, Minnesota, and Las Vegas remain unbeaten, but each has questions that the next few weeks will help answer. Two games are enough to begin assessing these teams, not enough to settle where they belong for the season.

text:
Happy birthday to former Enid, University of Oklahoma and professional offensive lineman and football coach Stan West, born on this day in 1926 in Weatherford.

West attended Enid High School, where he was an All-State selection at end as a senior in 1943, helping the Plainsmen go 8-2-1.

In 1944, West enlisted in the U.S. Navy, serving during World War II in the South Pacific.

When he returned from war, he enrolled at the University of Oklahoma and was offered a football scholarship.

With the Sooners, earning First-Team All-Big Seven and First-Team All-American honors as a senior in 1949.

In 1950, West became OU's first ever first-round draft pick when the Los Angeles Rams selected him with the 8th overall pick.

With the Rams, he was a two-time Pro Bowl selection, second-team All-Pro in 1951 and a first-team All-Pro in 1952. In 1951, he became a champion when the Rams won the NFL championship.

He played five seasons with the Rams and later played with the New York Giants and Chicago Cardinals, appearing in 85 games, including 73 starts. In his career, he had two interceptions and recovered four fumbles.

After his playing career, West was employed in the oil business, but returned to professional football as a coach in 1961 as defensive line coach on the inaugural coaching staff of the Minnesota Vikings.

He coached three seasons in the NFL and later became a scout for the NFL's St. Louis Cardinals.

West was named to the All-Time Rams team, was named one of the 100 greatest Sooners and was named to Street & Smith Magazine's All-Time College Football Team. He also was one of only two players to be named to the All-Century Prep and Professional football team by The Daily Oklahoman.

After retiring, West returned to Oklahoma and to Norman, where he passed away in 2005 at the age of 78. He was laid to rest in Resthaven Gardens Cemetery in Norman.

text:
The Sorrowful Mysteries of the Rosary: The Crown of Thorns: A Prefigurement of the Eucharistic Sacrifice

In the quiet moments of reflection, as we contemplate the profound mysteries of our faith, we often find ourselves drawn to the image of Christ crowned with thorns. This iconic scene from the Passion of Our Lord is not merely a historical event but a profound symbol deeply intertwined with the heart of our Eucharistic faith. As we delve into the mystery of the Crown of Thorns, we uncover its role as a prefigurement of the Eucharistic sacrifice, a connection that has been recognized and revered throughout the history of the Church.

The Crown of Thorns, an instrument of mockery and pain, becomes in the hands of Christ a symbol of His ultimate sacrifice and love. This connection to the Eucharist, the source and summit of our Christian life, is not a new revelation but one that has been contemplated and expounded upon by the early Church Fathers and affirmed by the teachings of the Church throughout the centuries.

The early Church Fathers, such as St. Ignatius of Antioch and St. Justin Martyr, were among the first to draw connections between the Passion of Christ and the Eucharist. St. Ignatius, in his Letter to the Smyrnaeans, wrote, "They abstain from the Eucharist and from prayer, because they confess not the Eucharist to be the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins, and which the Father, of His goodness, raised up again." Here, we see the Eucharist being directly linked to the suffering of Christ, a theme that resonates deeply with the image of the Crown of Thorns.

St. Justin Martyr, in his First Apology, further elaborated on this connection, stating, "For not as common bread and common drink do we receive these; but in like manner as Jesus Christ our Saviour, having been made flesh by the Word of God, had both flesh and blood for our salvation, so likewise have we been taught that the food which is blessed by the prayer of His word, and from which our blood and flesh by transmutation are nourished, is the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh." The blood shed by Christ, including that from His thorn-crowned head, is thus seen as intimately connected to the blood of the Eucharist.

The Council of Trent, in its 13th session, reaffirmed the Church's teaching on the Eucharist, stating, "In this divine sacrifice which is celebrated in the Mass, the same Christ who offered himself once in a bloody manner on the altar of the cross is contained and is offered in an unbloody manner." This teaching underscores the continuity between the sacrifice of the Cross and the Eucharistic sacrifice, with the Crown of Thorns serving as a poignant symbol of the blood that would be shed.

When we consider the blood that flowed from Christ's head due to the Crown of Thorns, we see a foreshadowing of the blood of the Eucharist. Just as the thorns pierced His sacred head, so too does the Eucharistic sacrifice pierce our hearts, calling us to a deeper union with Christ. The blood of the Eucharist, which we receive in Holy Communion, is the same blood that was shed for our salvation, a truth that is both comforting and challenging.

The connection between the Crown of Thorns and the Eucharist is further illuminated by the writings of the Saints and Doctors of the Church. St. Thomas Aquinas, in his Eucharistic hymn "Adoro Te Devote," beautifully expresses this connection: "Down in adoration falling, Lo! the sacred Host we hail; Lo! o'er ancient forms departing, Newer rites of grace prevail; Faith for all defects supplying, Where the feeble senses fail." Here, St. Thomas reminds us that our faith in the Eucharist transcends our human understanding, much like the mystery of the Crown of Thorns transcends the mockery intended by those who placed it upon Christ's head.

St. Catherine of Siena, in her Dialogue, speaks of the Eucharist as the "precious Blood of my Son," a blood that was shed for our salvation and is now offered to us in the sacrament. She writes, "This Blood teaches the truth, which truth is likewise declared by the Blood you shed from your side." The blood from Christ's head, symbolized by the Crown of Thorns, is thus seen as a part of the greater mystery of the Eucharistic sacrifice.

In our modern context, the connection between the Crown of Thorns and the Eucharist remains as relevant as ever. Pope Benedict XVI, in his encyclical "Sacramentum Caritatis," emphasized the importance of the Eucharist in the life of the Church, stating, "The Eucharist is the heart of the Church's life and her mission." As we face the challenges of our time, from secularism to the erosion of faith, the Eucharist stands as a beacon of hope and a source of strength, reminding us of the sacrifice of Christ and the love that flows from it.

The Crown of Thorns, as a prefigurement of the Eucharistic sacrifice, invites us to contemplate the depth of Christ's love for us. It calls us to a deeper appreciation of the Eucharist, not merely as a ritual but as a participation in the very life of Christ. As we receive the Eucharist, we are reminded of the blood that was shed for our salvation, a blood that continues to nourish and sustain us.

In summary, the Crown of Thorns serves as a powerful symbol of the Eucharistic sacrifice, a connection that has been recognized throughout the history of the Church. From the early Church Fathers to the Council of Trent, and through the writings of the Saints and Doctors, we see a consistent thread linking the Passion of Christ to the Eucharist. This connection is not merely historical but remains vital to our faith today, as emphasized by recent papal writings.

As we reflect on this profound mystery, let us be called to a deeper faith and a greater appreciation for the Eucharist. Let us allow the Crown of Thorns to pierce our hearts, drawing us closer to the sacrifice of Christ and the love that flows from it. May we approach the Eucharist with reverence and awe, recognizing in it the same blood that was shed for our salvation.

How can the image of the Crown of Thorns inspire you to a deeper devotion to the Eucharist? In what ways can you allow the mystery of Christ's sacrifice to transform your life and your relationship with Him?

Tuesday, August 04, 2026

Catholics pray the Sorrowful Mysteries on Tuesdays and Fridays. These mysteries reveal Christ's passion. They guide us through suffering to redemption.

The First Sorrowful Mystery is the Agony in the Garden. Jesus prays in distress. He sweats blood. Angels comfort him. He submits to the Father's will. Modern Catholics face anxiety and tough choices. This mystery teaches fervent prayer. It inspires trust in God during personal agony.

The Second Sorrowful Mystery is the Scourging at the Pillar. Soldiers whip Jesus. His flesh tears open. He endures for our sins. Today, many suffer injustice or temptation. This mystery calls us to purity. It strengthens us against moral compromise and physical trials.

The Third Sorrowful Mystery is the Crowning with Thorns. Soldiers mock Jesus as king. They beat his head. Blood flows from thorns. He accepts humiliation silently. In our world of ridicule toward faith, this shows true kingship. It urges humility amid scorn.

The Fourth Sorrowful Mystery is the Carrying of the Cross. Jesus staggers under the heavy cross. He falls three times. Simon helps him. Veronica wipes his face. In daily burdens, Catholics carry crosses too. This mystery builds perseverance. It reminds us Christ walks with us.

The Fifth Sorrowful Mystery is the Crucifixion and Death of Jesus. Nails pierce his hands and feet. He forgives his executioners. Mary stands below. He dies for salvation. Modern suffering finds meaning here. This mystery offers hope through redemptive pain.

These mysteries together trace Christ's sorrowful path. They mirror our struggles in a broken world. They inspire us to unite sufferings with Jesus. They lead to Easter joy.

For today, contemplate the Third Sorrowful Mystery deeply. Reflect on personal humiliations. Think of mockery at work or online. See Jesus crowned with thorns. Embrace humility as true royalty. Offer these trials for the Church. Let Christ's silence strengthen your witness.

Our Lady of Sorrows, pray for us.

text:
HOYA says expanding HDD glass-substrate capacity is the challenge.
Its CEO says there is no HDD-substrate supply constraint.
Both statements can be true. But the tension between them matters.

HOYA (TSE: 7741) is mostly a life-care company by revenue. It is mostly an information-technology company by profit.

In April-June 2026, Information & Communication generated:

- 39.5% of group revenue
- 65.0% of segment profit
- A 55.1% margin on profit from ordinary operating activities

That margin included a one-off US tariff refund. Excluding it, management put the underlying margin in the 54% range.

The segment contains two businesses the company ties to AI demand: EUV mask blanks for leading-edge chips and glass substrates for hard-disk platters.

This is about the hard-disk side.

HOYA's current position (fiscal years end in March):

- 3.5-inch nearline market share: approximately 40%, company estimate
- 2.5-inch market share: 100%
- Q1 HDD-substrate revenue: +29% reported, +15% at constant currency
- FY2026 3.5-inch growth outlook: 15-20%
- Total HDD-substrate outlook: low-teens growth, because 2.5-inch demand continues to decline

In its prepared remarks, HOYA said demand remained very strong and that expanding supply capacity was the challenge.

Later, an analyst described the business as apparently supply constrained.

CEO Eiichiro Ikeda rejected that premise: "There is no supply constraint on our HDD substrate side."

My reading is that the capacity disclosures explain how both statements can coexist.

HOYA's Laos plant has building and cleanroom space for 12 production lines. Four had been running so far. Equipment for the remaining eight is scheduled to go in progressively through FY2026 and FY2027.

HOYA has also disclosed a new Vietnam plant targeted to begin operations in FY2028, with an initial investment of roughly JPY 50 billion.

So the distinction is between current capacity and the path to future capacity.

Ikeda said 3.5-inch growth of up to 20% can be fully covered. Above 20%, HOYA has not yet entered specific planning.

That does not prove the business is constrained.

But it leaves an important question open: the upper edge of HOYA's demand outlook is also the last growth level management explicitly says capacity can cover.

Ikeda offered two reasons the business could remain resilient even if hyperscaler investment slowed.

First, HAMR raises recording density. Exabyte demand therefore does not translate one-for-one into additional disks, although substrate volumes are currently still rising.

Second, HOYA expects second and third customers to ramp. Those customer additions could support volume even if market growth slows.

There is another risk.

An analyst raised reports that HDD manufacturers may produce some glass substrates internally. Ikeda framed that as confirmation that customers are shifting from aluminum to glass, noting that similar insourcing occurred during the 2.5-inch era.

That is positive for the glass market.

It is not automatically positive for HOYA. A customer producing internally is still a customer purchasing less externally.

The next test comes on 30 October 2026.

A low-teens outlook for total HDD substrates would not be a miss; it is already the plan. The cleaner signal is the 3.5-inch forecast and the reason for any revision.

If HOYA cuts its 15-20% view while equipment installation remains on schedule, the problem is probably demand.

If growth is reduced because the new lines are late, the problem is supply, and the "no constraint" answer deserves another look.

Empty cleanroom space is not spare capacity.

It is an option on future capacity, and its value depends on how quickly the equipment arrives.

Sources: HOYA FY26 Q1 earnings-call transcript, 31 July 2026, company-edited, pp. 10-16; FY26 Q1 earnings presentation, 31 July 2026, slides 4, 11 and 13; HOYA Integrated Report 2026, 7 September 2026, pp. 101-102. Translations and calculations are mine.

text:
I once brought my dev team a $500 gig. The deal was I found the work, I took 25%. They built it and they split 75%

I was still new enough not to know how to code any of it, so once it was done, they felt finding it wasn't worth 25. They offered 15
The entire dispute was over $50.
We'd done the one smart thing everyone tells you to do. 

The money was in escrow. No one could run off with it. Escrow can't answer the one question that mattered, what is finding the gig worth?

It sat there until one of them got tired and gave in. That was our ruling. Whoever blinked first.

Arthur Hayes explains the missing ingredient in this clip. When humans sign a contract, they name a venue, like California, as the place to settle disputes. Agents can do the same thing, and @GenLayer is one of those venues. Two agents agree on a job, name GenLayer, and if they disagree, the escrowed money waits on a ruling from validators each running a different AI model. 

Not on who blinks.
Why does this matter more for bots than it did for us? My dispute ended because a human got tired. Agents don't get tired. Two bots fighting over $50 with no venue named either sit there forever or one cuts a corner and moves on. 

And no court on earth was ever going to hear a $50 fight. Here a first ruling comes back in about five minutes for under a dollar.

We picked a vault. We needed a judge.
Be the judge for a second. I found the gig, they did the work. 25 or 15?

text:
Deaf Adults’ Brains Boost ‘Danger Radar’ For Peripheral Vision | StudyFinds

Deaf Adults’ Brains Trade Central Focus for Sharper Side Vision

In A Nutshell

- Adults who have been deaf since birth or early childhood devote more brain space to peripheral vision and less to central vision than hearing adults do.

- Brain scans found no overall increase in the size of the two visual structures studied, meaning the brain redistributes existing resources rather than growing new ones.

- The shift may help explain why deaf adults tend to outperform hearing adults at spotting motion at the edges of sight.

- Until now, this kind of remapping had mostly been seen only when the visual system itself was damaged, not in people with fully healthy eyes.

---

For people who are deaf from birth or early childhood, the brain quietly renegotiates how it sees the world. New brain-scan research shows that adults who have been deaf since early childhood devote noticeably more space in two key visual brain structures to catching movement and potential danger at the far edges of sight, and less space to the sharp, detailed vision used for reading or focusing on a face.

A team of researchers from the Universities of York and Sheffield, publishing in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, scanned the brains of 16 adults who had been profoundly deaf from an early age and compared them with 16 hearing adults of similar ages. The lateral geniculate nucleus, a relay station that receives signals straight from the eye, and the primary visual cortex, the brain’s first major vision-processing hub, showed the same pattern: a bigger share of tissue tuned to the far periphery, and a smaller share tuned to central vision. Neither structure was actually larger overall in deaf participants, meaning existing space simply got divided up differently.

This isn’t simply about deaf people noticing things faster out of the corner of their eye. The organization of the brain’s earliest vision-processing structures, the first stops information takes after leaving the eye, appears to differ between the two groups. That’s the surprising part: until now, this kind of redistribution had mainly turned up in people whose visual system itself was damaged, such as those with partial blindness. Here, the eyes work fine. The findings suggest a lifetime of relying more heavily on vision, since sound can’t flag what’s happening at the edges of sight, may help reshape how that space gets divided.

Wide-Field Brain Scans Traced Vision From Center to Far Edge

Researchers scanned all 32 participants using a technique that tracks blood flow tied to brain activity, showing flickering checkerboard patterns that expanded outward like ripples or rotated like a clock hand while participants stared at a fixed point. As the pattern moved, it stimulated different parts of the visual field, from dead center to a wide angle off to the side, letting scientists trace which brain regions, in the relay station and the visual cortex, responded to which part of space.

Deaf participants showed the same shift in both structures, most clearly confirmed in the visual cortex, where detailed volume and surface measurements backed it up. The center of the visual field claimed less processing territory there, while the far outer edges claimed more, compared with hearing participants. Structure size itself didn’t differ between groups, confirming this was a redistribution rather than growth.

Because most deaf participants used British Sign Language, researchers also checked whether the pattern was tied to sign language rather than deafness alone. They compared deaf participants who learned BSL as a first language, those who learned English first and picked up BSL later, and those with no sign language experience. The subgroups were small, too small for reliable statistics, but adults who learned BSL earliest showed the largest peripheral shift, hinting that sign language use might add its own layer of change on top of deafness itself.

When Sound Can’t Warn, Vision Steps Up at the Edges

What stands out is the trade-off itself. As Dr. Heidi Baseler, of the University of York’s Department of Psychology, who led the study, put it, the brain “does a type of trade-off that redistributes its existing resources,” giving deaf adults “a better chance of catching the unexpected events that might happen just out of the central line of sight,” the kind of thing a hearing person might notice first by sound, such as someone approaching from the side.

That explanation lines up with decades of research showing deaf adults tend to outperform hearing adults at spotting things happening off to the side, particularly moving objects, and offers a possible physical basis for that edge. It also builds on earlier findings from some of the same researchers showing that the retina itself carries related differences, hinting that this reshaping might start before signals ever reach the brain.

A Fully Working Visual System Still Gets Reshaped

Deaf participants in this study had normal vision, with no impairments identified in their eyes, yet their earliest visual structures still looked different from those of hearing controls. That fits a broader picture of brain adaptability: tuning happens in response to injury or disease, but also to the everyday demands life places on it.

For a deaf adult scanning a room, a sidewalk, or a classroom for the motion that sound used to flag, the payoff is measurable brain territory, redirected toward the part of vision people lean on most when hearing can’t help. As Professor Charlotte Codina, of the University of Sheffield, summed it up, the brain “can profoundly adapt to make the most of its sensory environment,” and deaf adults, as a result, “have superior peripheral vision.”

A government program offering new parents voluntary nursing assistance is one thing. A government claiming the power to send its agents into the homes of newborn babies without meaningful consent, individualized suspicion, a warrant, or an emergency is something fundamentally different.

That is not merely “public health.” It embodies one of the defining impulses associated with totalitarian government: the erosion of the boundary between the state and private life. Political definitions of totalitarianism emphasize the state’s attempt to subordinate private as well as public life to governmental authority.

American constitutional tradition starts from the opposite premise. The Supreme Court has repeatedly treated the home as occupying a uniquely protected place under the Fourth Amendment. In Payton v. New York, the Court described physical entry into the home as the central evil against which the Amendment was directed and held that, absent recognized exceptions such as exigent circumstances, government cannot simply cross that threshold without lawful authority.

History supplies a warning about normalizing state supervision inside family life. Soviet public-health policy employed visiting nurses in a system that historians describe as blurring the boundaries between public and private and placing child-rearing increasingly under professional and state authority.  Communist Czechoslovakia likewise operated a district system in which pediatric nurses entered homes of newborns and infants, continuously monitored children's health and environment, educated mothers and conducted what historical sources describe as active monitoring.  Although some of these programs may have also delivered genuine medical benefits, the crucial dividing line is consent.

That distinction should matter especially in Massachusetts. Boston, Lexington and Concord were centers of resistance to arbitrary governmental authority; John Adams, Samuel Adams and John Hancock were Massachusetts sons intimately connected with the Revolution.

A nurse invited into a family's home is a caregiver. An official whom the family is legally compelled to admit is exercising state power.

Any proposal crossing that line deserves the closest constitutional and democratic scrutiny. Assistance may be offered universally. Education may be made freely available. Families in crisis may receive intensive help. But in a free society, government does not acquire a general license to inspect a family's private life merely because a child has been born.

text:
BITCOIN LIGHTNING GETS ITS FIRST IMPLEMENTED POST-QUANTUM DESIGN

Researchers at East Texas A&M University (@startimeahmet) have unveiled PQLN, a post-quantum extension of the Lightning Network implemented and tested on real nodes using rust-lightning.

The project is designed to protect Lightning’s off-chain infrastructure against future quantum attacks without requiring a Bitcoin consensus change.

PQLN adds post-quantum protection across Lightning gossip, transport, invoices, offers and payment onions, covering BOLTs 4, 7, 8, 11 and 12.

The researchers argue this matters even before quantum computers become powerful enough to break current cryptography because attackers could record encrypted Lightning traffic today and decrypt it later.

The system uses hybrid classical + post-quantum cryptography, including ML-KEM for key exchange and ML-DSA signatures.

Testing found the biggest tradeoff was bandwidth.

A PQLN node joining today’s network would download roughly 270 MB of gossip data versus 26 MB for a standard node, while alternative cryptographic choices could reduce that overhead.

Researchers also tested 12 scenarios mixing post-quantum and standard Lightning nodes. Payments remained interoperable, while users can enable a “require-PQ” mode that fails closed rather than falling back to classical cryptography.

The implementation adds roughly 11,000 lines of code to rust-lightning.

The researchers say PQLN can begin joining Lightning today without requiring the rest of the network to upgrade first.

text:
went to the alpha schools pitch by joe liemandt in london yesterday and I have a lot of thoughts. mulling through and processing and getting them in order here. this is... thoughts in progress, I don't even know how much of this is moving pieces and will settle differently once I've had longer to think about it.

it's obvious that joe is an incredible entrepreneur. he knows exactly how to pitch and exactly what his potential customers care about. the metrics, student stories and persuasive angles he was presenting were obviously very well selected and I found myself convinced and nodding along to a lot of it - student enjoyment being the number one metric! half of students would prefer school to vacation! 2000 low income families in texas chose alpha schools as the place to spend their school vouchers!

so obviously all of this is me taking that rhetorical polish as a prior, and trying to read between the lines and work out how I really feel about the substance. so the epistemic status here is all extremely tenuous, it's my interpretation (or mis-interpretation) on my vibes (or mis-vibes) on reading between the lines on subtext

my first slight ick was it was obviously an incredibly businessy way of running a school chain. which, like, gives sleazy vibes, but the point of business is that you have to be effective, and the alpha schools expansion model sure is effective. the "founding families" playbook (pitch high-tech high-end elite school, get families who want to send their kids to high-tech high-end elite school, pick only the ones who are massive fans and committed and have lots of energy, likely elites themselves, and leverage the parents' skills and connections to launch and scale the schools in that area) is obviously extraordinarily successful. I don't hate the hustle, it obviously works and the rate of buildout of the schools has astonished me considering the general status quo bias and inertia in education. and it may in fact be the *only* way that works - getting an influential enough group of parents to push past otherwise insurmountable political obstacles (i.e. get favours from businesspeople and sweet talk the politicians from close to home). but, optics, smell, taste, ick. I don't know how it will fare against british class sensibilities. the british academic and tech elite, no matter how wealthy, mostly consider themselves "middle class" and have a more equitable and meritocratic worldview, and many view themselves as opposed to the hereditary upper class "toffs" for whom this would be more their default playbook. of course it might work for alpha to attract the upper class first and foremost - after all they are pitching at the elite private school level - but then I don't know that that will be the forward-looking, technically-minded clientele that they might be used to in their US founding families. perhaps there will be enough international tech and business families who are not so british culturally to bridge the gap - in a place like london this may work well.

joe does paint a clear picture of the price-flexibility of the alpha model - the "educational curriculum" component trends towards free, it's a hygiene factor. it's necessary, but it's not what gets the kids out of bed every day. what the money pays for is what happens in the other 6 hours of the day. if you don't have money you could go to a cheaper school and do sports, or farming, where all you need is a pitch or a field. if you have money you can have trips and international projects and go build schools in africa. in a sense this was already the deal, as it were, in that when people pay for private school what they pay for is better facilities and better connections and better opportunities. but that was always... not at the forefront of things, to the middle class british mind. the status quo is that those things comprise a minority of the day and most of the day is covered by curriculum activities - essays, art projects, design and technology - that one could at least be assured are more or less alike between private and state schools. (I attended state selective, mr c attended private, and, well, we ended up in the same place at the same time in the same social class doing the same thing by undergrad)

I am aware that I have an international audience here and I'm implicitly comparing against the english state education system, whereas alpha's own marketing, and their existing fans and haters, are mostly american, and are comparing against a much worse state school baseline. even the non-elite alpha schools are blatantly obviously an improvement on the modal american schools. but the english education system... while patchy, it serves most kids very well, particularly around historically well-funded london. the curriculum is decent and varied (and includes art, music, design and technology etc). there is actually well functioning standardised testing. the phonics teaching works, middle school students generally can read - the literacy crisis is nowhere near american levels. alpha's compressed, multiple-choice based american curriculum is an obvious negative here, so the intention to drag-and-drop the american system in place initially is going to be a big minus academically until they can catch up to a more holistic curriculum.

all surmountable problems, with the right enthusiastic parents. and there will always be enthusiasts, of course. and the whole point of the free school and academy system is to offer choice and a pathway to innovation in education.

and the part of the sales pitch that is aimed at making the parents picture the kind of school that they wish they had attended works EXTRAORDINARILY well. both mr c and I did our share of self-motivated projects as teens - and if we had had the resources and school time and coaching to pursue them properly, it would probably have legit altered our life trajectories. not having to sit through classes of materials not pitched at the right level would have been even better. and who doesn't love the promise of always being happy at school! and no homework!

but the main complicated feeling I'm left with is still about the intensification of the school choice problem on the cusp of an unknown future. the vibe I got from the alpha schools crowd is... kind of an implicit belief in techno-feudalism. the elite alpha schools exist to train kids in agency, so that they will be the ones using the AIs and running the businesses and controlling the means of production. of course there will be vocational schools. there will be sports schools, and ranch schools, and the schools for high tech mechanical engineering for going to space. but those aren't "our" kids, obviously. "our" kids will be the elites. "our" kids will be the "philosopher-builders" that the founders school freshman year syllabus page proudly declares they develop.

and obviously everyone knows peer effects are some of the biggest factors in kids' outcomes. if you want _your_ kids to be the philosopher-builders in the ruling class of the upcoming ai-feudalism, better get them in the room now with the other kids who are going to be the philosopher-builders in the ruling class of the upcoming ai-feudalism. and if you want your kids in with those kids, you better get yourself in the room with the other parents who are raising the kids who will be those kids. fomo fomo fomo, grasp grasp grasp. do you really want your kid going to a state school. do you really want your kid training to be nothing more than an employee. do you really want ai-serfdom for your kid.

this is not meant to be a dunk, by the way, there's a truth to this, but it's an unpleasant truth and I feel unpleasant about it so I put it in unpleasant words. that was always the private school bargain - socialise your kids with elite peers. but I'd never been that interested in the traditional english private schools because that's not the kind of elite I'm interested in and not the kind of elite that's going to be relevant. but this pitch is forward-looking. as a mum I don't want serfdom for my kid. my intellectual peers, here on twitter dot com, are already alpha parents.

but the outcome of alpha schools at different price points that do different activities is a social stratification of child peer groups and child outcomes from an early age, and that has been... the antithesis of what the british state education system has been driving towards for decades, and something that offends the sensibilities of lots of british parents. so there's the lingering worry that the parents who choose this in spite of that are not going to be people whose values we share. so, for now, it's one big imperfect information co-ordinating game. pick in or out, try to hit the ingroup.

what kind of person do I want lil captain to be. and why do I have to choose that when she is three years old.

***

I'm feeling very fortunate that I still have a couple years before lil captain has to make school choices. it gives me the option of getting involved early, but without having to commit my child to the experiment. I'm sure there are enough families who will be really enthusiastic about that, to get things started.

but if the alpha project is picked up by right-minded people on the london side, who work to improve and uphold and cultivate the alpha system to british standards and british sensibilities and british values, it makes me much more optimistic about lil captain's future school choices. perhaps the best of all worlds would be that alpha schools retains its quintessentially-american dna and operates its franchise of international schools, but its success moves the overton window, such that uniquely British schools modelled after its setup and with our own AI-native education stack could come into existence -

with any luck, by the time lil captain needs it.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Shawn Ryan Show: #341 Katarina Szulc - Cartels Are Recruiting Drone Operators From the Ukraine War

Overview
Katarina Szulc reports from Mexico City on cartels, corruption, and trafficking, and her findings point to one conclusion: Mexico's cartels are not just criminal enterprises but a parallel economy and political system. They run PR campaigns, absorb rival factions, extort legal industries, and now recruit drone operators trained in the Ukraine war. The Valeria Marquez livestream murder shows how a personal killing can become a cartel message, a diplomatic dispute, and a test of how justice actually works in Jalisco. Meanwhile, trafficking networks tied to Tlaxcala move women into San Diego, Houston, Los Angeles, and New York, making this a US problem as much as a Mexican one. US tactics like the kingpin strategy and the foreign terrorist organization designation have not changed cartel behavior. What might work is hitting logistics, weapons, and money, while recognizing that cartels profit from both illegal and legal goods, from crude oil to avocados.

Key Themes
- Cartels treat publicity as a weapon: narco banners, staged videos, and interviews with wanted figures function as PR to project power and control the narrative.
- Mexico does not aggressively pursue cartel leaders because organized crime is deeply tied to the economy and many high-level officials benefit from it.
- CJNG has not fractured after El Mencho's death; it operates like a decentralized corporation with multiple powerful commanders and loyal followings.
- Cartels monopolize legal goods and services: avocados, crude oil, water, Wi-Fi. Ending drug demand would not end them.
- Sinaloa is a war zone. In one trip, Szulc reached six crime scenes within four hours of arriving in Culiacán.
- Sex trafficking networks move women from Tlaxcala to major US cities, and many clients are American citizens.
- The US is central to cartel success through drug consumption and demand for stolen or illicit goods.
- Foreign fighters with drone training are being recruited from Ukraine to work for Mexican cartels, either sent deliberately or recruited after their service ends.
- Drone use is now central to cartel operations: FPV drones drop bombs on law enforcement and rivals to keep authorities away from hubs.

Detailed Summary
Szulc is a former traditional journalist now based in Mexico City. Her first passion is war correspondence, and Ukraine was her favorite place visited in the past year, but her current focus is borderland dispatches on cartels, organized crime, and political corruption.

Cartels use PR strategically. They send messages through journalists, narco banners near cities or dead bodies, videos with armed operatives and a spokesperson, and press releases. CJNG and Cartel de Noreste produce content to shape public perception and respond to negative coverage.

The Valeria Marquez case illustrates how a single killing becomes a public battle. Marquez was a TikTok influencer and beauty pageant participant well known in Jalisco. She was shot three times on livestream over a year ago. The US sanctioned El Dere, a high-ranking CJNG figure, for the murder. Mexico initially denied this and continued its own investigation. Mexico later arrested R1, also known as El Uno, a high-ranking CJNG member, for the murder of Carlos Manso, a mayor in Michoacán outspoken against cartels. R1's son is accused of ordering the hit on Marquez. The son was in a romantic relationship with her and is hiding from authorities. Journalist Luis Chaparro interviewed the accused son, who claims he loved Valeria and would never kill her, though documented toxic messages from a partner threatening her exist.

On the day she died, Valeria was livestreaming from her beauty salon when she received a Starbucks delivery and a pig stuffed animal. In Mexico a pig can symbolize someone being a rat. Her friend texted her to stay on live because an expensive gift was coming. Valeria muted the stream and was shot three times while holding the pig. The accused says Valeria knew his family and he knew hers, and he denies cartel involvement for himself.

Interviewing wanted criminals is contentious. Szulc argues it is not a journalist's job to turn them in, though she acknowledges access and rapport could theoretically be used to feed cartel egos and locate targets. She fears journalists being used as traps. The interview with the accused killer functions as PR, ego, and an attempt to tell his side.

Szulc argues Mexico does not aggressively pursue cartel leaders because cartels are deeply tied to Mexico's economy. She claims eradicating them would devastate the Mexican economy. Cartels are one of Mexico's top employers, top three to five, and profit from both black-market and legitimate goods: crude oil, avocados, water, Wi-Fi.

Cartel power in Mexico is fluid and violent. CJNG is described as extremely powerful and is absorbing or allying with the Chapitos faction against the Mayos and Mito faction. In Sakatkas, car bombs and IEDs were reported, linked to an active CJNG cell called Fuerzas Sakatkas Nueva. Sinaloa is a war zone with frequent murders. During a summer trip, Szulc drove from Mazatlán to Culiacán via the old highway and saw territorial markers such as white sombreros representing the Mito faction. Within four hours in Culiacán, she went to six different crime scenes. The most jarring aspect is seeing victims' families realize their lives will never be the same.

Politicians aligned with cartels face dangerous loyalty dilemmas. Rubén Rocha Moya, governor of Sinaloa, was indicted by the US a couple months before this conversation. He is described as having a strong alliance with the Chapitos faction and profiting from it. Before El Mayo's capture, Rocha Moya had a dispute with a Sinaloa state legislator. El Chapo's son allegedly set up El Mayo to attend a meeting resolving that conflict. At that meeting, El Mayo was allegedly beaten and placed on a small aircraft that landed him in Santa Teresa, New Mexico, where he was taken in by the FBI. Rocha Moya survived the meeting and remained governor. The state legislator was murdered during that encounter.

Szulc says Mexican politicians are constrained. Moving too far politically or acting against cartel interests can get them murdered. Some allegedly accept payoffs or comply out of fear. Anyone entering Mexican politics to be good must be willing to stand their ground and risk death. Otherwise they risk becoming corrupt or ineffective. She names Carlos Manso as a politician who took a stand against organized crime, and Lily Tees as a Mexican senator who speaks out and names corrupt officials. She says corrupt politicians are few and far between because if the president profits from organized crime, lower-level officials are unlikely to be clean.

CJNG has not fractured after El Mencho's death. It operates with multiple powerful commanders and loyal followings, resembling a decentralized or corporate structure. Splintering is possible, and two high-ranking CJNG figures could potentially split off, though unity is more profitable. El Mencho was captured or killed in February. Despite a brief outburst of buses on fire and attacks on the National Guard, CJNG did not collapse into restructuring or extreme infighting. The current top leader is El Mencho's stepson, 03. The hierarchy is a triangle: top leader, top commanders, plaza bosses, subcell leaders, and lower individuals. Los Zetas are cited as an example of a cartel that dissolved. Their special-operations-style members were reportedly trained by US forces, and many heads are now in the United States after a fugitive transfer. After El Mencho was killed, one high-ranking CJNG figure wanted to increase violence and send wicked messages, while another rejected that approach. CJNG is now essentially run by the Cuinis and Valencia family, who originally had money, Colombian connections, and US trafficking pathways through avocado exports from Michoacán.

Cartel influence involves over 50 percent of Mexico's population through some nexus to organized crime, including politicians, law enforcement turning a blind eye, and low-level participants. Cartels monopolize Wi-Fi in smaller towns by cutting wires and selling their own service. They tap PEMEX pipelines to steal crude oil and sell it to US mom-and-pop refineries at half price. Avocado extortion quotas are typically 80 percent of farmers' earnings. Those who cannot pay lose their land or lives, and many flee.

The fentanyl focus has diverted attention from cocaine, which is flowing at unprecedented levels. Szulc flew by helicopter near Cúcuta, Colombia, and saw miles of coca plants. Cúcuta was once a hub for El Chapo's Sinaloa operators and family members. The US is losing the war on cocaine by a landslide. Cartel cultural influence has spread deep into South America. Even a small bar on the Colombia-Venezuela border played regional Mexican music and patrons dressed in cartel style.

Human and sex trafficking networks are sophisticated, often family-based, and directly linked to the United States. A survivor from central Mexico described being taken to Tijuana by a man she considered her husband. Her phone and IDs were taken. She was legally registered as a prostitute and beaten when she refused to work. She provided sexual services to about 30 men per night for 10 years. When she and other women sought help, authorities dismissed it as a spousal dispute and said no one was forcing her. She escaped after becoming pregnant. She maintained a relationship with her trafficker because he is the father of her child and said she feared no other man would love her because of what she had done.

Traffickers impregnate victims. If the child is a daughter, she may later be trafficked. Women who were successful or considered attractive could be moved from Tijuana to San Diego, Houston, Los Angeles, and New York. Recruitment targets young women from small, conservative, religious towns with limited exposure. The Romeo method is described: an older man romances a young woman, wins over her family, isolates her, and moves her to a border town for supposed work. Traffickers may wait until victims turn 18 to legally register them as prostitutes or legally marry them. Tlaxcala is described as a small state outside Mexico City from which many trafficked women and traffickers originate.

A governor in Tlaxcala allegedly offered to pay the journalist for a favorable interview and asked to review the cut before publication. The governor had publicly denied a trafficking problem three times. A major trafficking network was taken down in New York by US authorities roughly three years ago. It reportedly sourced girls from Tlaxcala. A survivor said she was trafficked from Tlaxcala, asked for help, never received it, and was terrorized for a decade.

The US foreign terrorist organization designation has not meaningfully changed cartel operations. Cartels adapt quickly and treat it with indifference. Szulc strongly doubts the US will carry out drone strikes inside Mexico. She argues current tactics of splintering cartels and encouraging internal conflict are cheaper and more effective. She criticizes the kingpin strategy as ineffective against a hydra-like cartel structure, pointing to El Mencho's death being followed by business as usual within 24 hours.

The US has gathered intelligence on the ground in Mexico for a long time. Two CIA agents died in a car crash in Chihuahua while dressed in Mexican police uniforms during a meth lab dismantling operation. The US has openly taken credit for intelligence that located El Mencho. Szulc believes Mexican forces killed El Mencho rather than capturing him because he had information on high-ranking politicians that the US wanted. A video reportedly shows older Mexican women in a southern state asking President Trump to help get rid of cartels terrorizing them. The US is making deals with El Chapo's children and other traffickers, offering plea deals and visas, which may send a stronger message than drone strikes.

A stated concern among cartel figures is that US custody offers an easy break if they have valuable information, which may incentivize avoiding capture. A proposed alternative to drone strikes is a psychological operation designed to turn cartels against each other by creating false narratives and exploiting rivalries. Another proposed strategy targets cartel logistics and funding: supplies, drug precursors, firearms, weapons, and drone-manufacturing facilities. Stopping weapons flows before they reach criminals could weaken cartel power without drone strikes.

Mexico reportedly receives most weapons from the US and Israel, including regular weaponry and spyware. About 70 percent of guns found at crime scenes in Mexico are American-made. A recent large shipment of DJI drones in Mexico was stolen. Mexico was the first country to contract with Pegasus and is the number one country for Pegasus use. A previous Mexican president allegedly accepted a 25 million dollar bribe from two NSO executives to implement Pegasus in Mexico's national security apparatus. The president denied it. In a non-official tribunal involving the NSO individuals, one reportedly said they bribed the president with 25 million dollars, and the other responded that it was less than 25 million. Pegasus allegedly spread into cartel hands and was used to spy on journalists and clean politicians, with murders attributed to that access.

A case from about a year ago involved a Utah family indicted for buying stolen crude oil and smuggling it through the Port of Brownsville. They ran a family-owned smaller refinery and knowingly purchased stolen crude because it was cheaper. American refineries are identified as buyers of stolen crude oil. Proposed pressure points include boycotting avocados, penalizing or making it illegal for US companies to do business with cartels, destroying drug supplies, stopping weapons, addressing human trafficking, and handling the Mexican government. Mexico's last election was one of the most violent in history. Claudia Sheinbaum won by a historic landslide. People in Sinaloa are tired of cartel violence and willing to take a stand, but deep-rooted fear of standing up remains.

Some anti-cartel Mexicans support an El Salvador-style mass incarceration approach, CECOT, but Szulc argues it could only work if paired with economic compensation, since cartels run so much of the economy. CECOT is described as having turned El Salvador from one of the most violent places into one of the safest, though with human rights concerns and reports of people with no cartel ties being imprisoned.

Foreign fighters with drone training are being recruited from Ukraine to work for Mexican cartels, either sent deliberately with false documentation or recruited after their service ends. A French and Mexican intelligence report to Ukraine warned of foreign mercenaries training on FPV drones to later work for Mexican cartels. An individual using the name Eagle 7 went to Ukraine with false documentation, was flagged at a drone training facility for unusual FPV proficiency, and was investigated and linked to Latin American criminal organizations, including Mexican cartels and FARC. FPV drone flying is compared to video games. Young people adapt easily, and the camera shuts off at launch, creating a disconnect from typical warfare. Two simultaneous recruitment patterns are described: small numbers sent deliberately via private military companies, and Latin American fighters recruited via social media after their Ukraine service. A Colombian fighter who served in Ukraine was seen on the front lines in Michoacán with a cartel, wearing Colombian, Ukrainian, and Mexican flag patches and bragging about it. Pay for recruited fighters is believed to be low based on their profiles. Tracking recruited fighters is extremely difficult. Many Latin American foreign fighters in Ukraine were police or ex-military.

Cartel training facilities, especially those run by CJNG, are described as violent killing fields. Two years ago, the extermination ranch Rancho Seer in Jalisco, about 60 km outside Guadalajara, was described as a CJNG recruitment and training camp where many people were taken to die or forced to fight to the death. This is deliberately kept from the public because it is bad PR for cartels. Cartels mostly use FPV drones for dropping bombs, targeting law enforcement and rival groups to keep authorities away from their hubs of operation. 3D printing is not commonly used for whole drones in Mexico. Instead, cartels 3D print certain components to attach or enhance payloads on FPV drones, not kamikaze drones. Szulc has not seen cartels using large language models or AI to run drone swarms in Mexico. It could happen, but current FPV drone capabilities are good enough. Fractured cartels needing manpower often lack capital for such investment. Cartel drone personnel are described as proud of their work and frequently send drone strike videos.

Szulc believes the US government will try to turn cartel factions against each other, even by spreading lies through ranks, to keep them splintering and fighting. Despite CJNG's leader being gone, she expects CJNG's power and control over Mexico's cartel landscape and the global drug trade to continue rising. They have money, power, vision, and high-IQ individuals, particularly in the Valencia family.

She predicts the next Mexican president will likely be Omar Garcia Haruch, secretary of security, who will work closely with the Americans, different from Claudia Sheinbaum's pushback. She sees this as not entirely positive because Haruch may have his own agenda. Canada has a major fentanyl problem matching the US and a border problem. Fentanyl precursors come through Canadian ports largely unchecked. Canada shows lack of transparency: major drug busts at ports are not being released to the public or put in press releases to avoid added pressure. Canada is extraditing people involved in drug cases to the US when the DEA helped investigate, setting a precedent for a hands-off approach. Spain has a major problem with cartel infiltration and massive amounts of drugs coming in, then distributed throughout other European countries. Some individuals linked to Mexican cartels seek refuge in Spain. The problem is widespread and transnational, so no single country can dismantle operations. Collective effort is required.

Szulc declines to say where she is heading next, citing a policy of never disclosing assignments in advance. She is currently focused on cartel-related reporting and boots-on-the-ground stories. She expects to eventually move into non-cartel reporting, but says that will come later. She expects to return in about another year.

That did not happen. Even serious defenders of liberal democracy—including John Rawls, the most important political philosopher of the theory of justice, and Paul Starr in Freedom’s Power: The True Force of Liberalism—were compelled to criticize, in earnest, the coups and foreign aggressions of “liberal imperialism.” Rawls, who in The Law of Peoples was a theorist of humanitarian intervention and just war, criticized and rejected CIA coups in other countries in that same book, including the CIA coup against Dr. Mohammad Mossadegh in 1953. In §5.4 Rawls wrote that the United States overthrew the democracies of Allende in Chile, Árbenz in Guatemala, Mossadegh in Iran, and, on some accounts, the Sandinistas in Nicaragua. Whatever the merits of those regimes, the covert operations against them were carried out by a government motivated by monopolistic and oligarchic interests without the knowledge or criticism of the public. This was made easier by a skillful appeal to national security in the context of superpower rivalry, which allowed such weak democracies to be seen, however implausibly, as a threat. Although democratic peoples are not expansionist, they do defend their security interest, and a democratic government can easily appeal to that interest to support covert interventions even when the actual motive is hidden economic interests.
Rawls also wrote, in §14.1, that the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, aimed primarily at civilian populations, were very great wrongs. He went on (§4.4 and the footnotes to that section) to say that Japan was already close to surrender and that there was no need for the atomic bombings. But Truman was a racist and called the Japanese savages and barbarians and said they should be treated as such; yet how foolish it now seems to regard the Germans and the Japanese as wholly barbarian and savage.
Look at the names Donald Trump has given Iranians in his second term. On 1 April 2026, in a televised address, he said: “We’re going to hit them extremely hard over the next two to three weeks. We’re going to bring them back to the Stone Ages where they belong.” That same night: “If there is no deal, we are going to hit each and every one of their electric generating plants very hard and probably simultaneously. We have not hit their oil, even though that’s the easiest target of all, because it would not give them even a small chance of survival or rebuilding.” In early April: “No bridges, no power plants… Stone Ages.” April reports of Trump on Iranians: “animals,” and once “horrible genes, not like our own.” In July 2026 he called Iran’s leaders “scum” and “sick people.” In September 2026 he told Axios: “Do I want to go in and annihilate them or do I not? It’s a big decision.” In another interview he set out the options as obliterating Iran, letting it rot economically, or making a deal.
You see exactly the racist gaze that Edward Said mapped so well in Orientalism. (One of the charges Republicans leveled at Barack Obama was that he had met Edward Said.) That racist attitude cannot and must not be ignored in the bombing of Iran’s infrastructure—including the 28 February 2026 attack on Shajarah Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, which the UN fact-finding mission on 17 September 2026 found, on “reasonable grounds,” to have been the work of the United States and a war crime: about 157 dead, including more than 120 children. Major American media carried the same report. Trump said it was a wartime mistake.
The military attack on Iran had, and has, nothing to do with freedom, human rights, or democracy (whenever Trump feels Iran’s leaders are coming around to him, he lavishes astonishing praise on them). This attack is for oil, domination, colonialism, imperialism, racism, and the interests of Israel, and nothing else. Only that.
