text:
This is one of those historical reconstructions whose apparent simplicity is purchased only by suppressing precisely those portions of the sources which make the story difficult. Read Ibn Bishr and Mengin entire; then place beside them the early Makkan chronicle of Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr. Almost every proposition above requires either substantial qualification or outright correction.

1. “Sharīf Ghālib betrayed the peace agreement and attacked his son-in-law, ʿUthmān al-Muḍāyifī.”

Even the kinship is wrong. Al-Muḍāyifī was not Ghālib’s son-in-law, but the husband of his sister, his brother-in-law. Al-Jabartī states the matter without ambiguity:

“This al-Muḍāyifī was the husband of the Sharīf’s sister.”

Al-Jabartī further describes him as having left Ghālib, joined the Wahhābī side, gathered tribes for them and directed military expeditions.

Nor does Ibn Bishr say that Ghālib “betrayed the peace.” His actual expression is:

وفي هذه السنة انتقض الصلح بين غالب الشريف وبين عبد العزيز بن محمد بن سعود

“In this year the peace between Sharīf Ghālib and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Muḥammad b. Saʿūd broke down.”

The distinction is not pedantic. انتقض الصلح tells us that the treaty collapsed, it does not tell us, in that sentence, who first violated it.

And here an early Makkan witness becomes indispensable.

ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbd al-Shakūr al-Makkī al-Ḥanafī, d. 1257 AH/1841 CE, was a Makkan Ḥanafī historian and the author of Tārīkh Ashrāf wa-Umarāʾ Makkah al-Mukarramah. His work survives in several manuscripts; the catalogue of the Library of the Sacred Mosque records his name, his Ḥanafī affiliation, his death date and the work itself.

Why is he relevant? Because the assertion that later Makkan accounts were inventions of Aḥmad Zaynī Daḥlān rests upon the assumption that no earlier local Ḥijāzī tradition existed. Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr proves otherwise.

And his account of the breakdown of the peace is the reverse of that given. He says Sālim b. Shakhbān began acting against:

عربان الشريف الذي انعقد عليهم الصلح

“the Sharīf’s tribes concerning whom the peace had been concluded,”

and says Ghālib consequently wrote to the Saudi rulers:

يطلب منهما الوفاء بالعهود

“asking them to fulfil the covenants.”

According to Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr, Ghālib did not immediately take up the sword. Complaints were exchanged; the Saudi side denied wrongdoing and proposed that Ghālib send a trustworthy man to investigate; an investigator was dispatched; and only thereafter did the dispute deepen.

One need not canonise Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr’s every judgment to recognise what follows. “Ghālib betrayed the peace” is not a neutral datum furnished by Ibn Bishr. It is one interpretation of a disputed treaty rupture for which the contemporary Makkan tradition gives precisely the opposite account.

The same chronological sleight of hand occurs with al-Muḍāyifī. By the time Ghālib personally moved against him at al-ʿUbaylāʾ, al-Muḍāyifī had not merely whispered a private bayʿah to Āl Saʿūd and then retired peaceably to his home. He had defected from Ghālib, accepted a rival political commission, established himself at a fortified base and gathered surrounding tribes.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr further records raids upon al-Zawrān and ʿAwf, an attack upon al-ʿArj in which houses were allegedly burned and livestock seized, and then says al-Muḍāyifī left his stronghold:

قاصداً قتال الطائف

“intending to fight al-Ṭāʾif.”

Before Ghālib’s own great expedition against al-ʿUbaylāʾ, Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr already places an all-day battle between al-Muḍāyifī and the forces of ʿAbd al-Muʿīn.

And, most inconveniently for the apologetic chronology, Mengin himself says much the same thing in principle. After al-Muḍāyifī decided not to return to Ghālib, he requested troops from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz:

pour aller faire la guerre à Ghaleb

“to go and make war upon Ghālib.”

Thus the very French authority invoked places an intention to wage war upon Ghālib before the later Ghālibian assault which is being made to bear the entire moral weight of the conflict.

2. “The Wahhābīs were once again acting in self-defence.”

That conclusion is obtained only by commencing the narrative at the moment most advantageous to it.

Certainly, Ghālib subsequently besieged al-Muḍāyifī at al-ʿUbaylāʾ. There is no reason to deny what all sides acknowledge.

But history is not transformed into “self-defence” merely by beginning the clock immediately before one’s opponent strikes.

By then al-Muḍāyifī had transferred allegiance, accepted rival authority in the Sharīf’s sphere, established an armed redoubt, recruited tribes and become the nucleus of a competing political-military order. Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr additionally records actual campaigning before Ghālib’s personal attack; Mengin has al-Muḍāyifī requesting forces expressly “to make war upon Ghālib.”

What emerges from the sources is therefore not the pristine moral tableau suggested, an innocent party suddenly assaulted and reluctantly defending itself, but an escalating contest of sovereignty:

alleged treaty violations; competing tribal allegiances; al-Muḍāyifī’s defection; rival appointment; armed mobilisation; local fighting; Ghālib’s attack upon al-ʿUbaylāʾ; Saudi reinforcement; and finally the assault upon al-Ṭāʾif.

To isolate one episode in the middle of this sequence and baptise the entire campaign “self-defence” is not source criticism. It is chronological excision.

3. “Ibn Bishr says fighting broke out in the marketplaces and homes, resulting in 200 deaths.”

Here the source has not merely been abbreviated. Its grammatical structure has been altered.

Ibn Bishr says:

فدخله عثمان ومن معه من الجموع، وفتحه الله لهم عنوة بغير قتال

“ʿUthmān and those with him entered it, and Allāh opened it to them by force, without fighting.”

He then continues:

وقتلوا من أهله في الأسواق والبيوت نحو مائتين

“And they killed from among its inhabitants, in the markets and houses, about two hundred.”

And then:

وأخذوا من الأموال من البلد أثماناً وأمتاعاً وسلاحاً وقماشاً وشيئاً من الجواهر والسلع المثمنة ما لا يحيط به الحصر ولا يدركه العد

They took from the town money, goods, weapons, cloth, jewels and precious merchandise “in quantities which enumeration could not encompass nor counting attain.”

He then records the collection of the akhmās and their dispatch to ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

Observe what has happened in the paraphrase.

Ibn Bishr says:

بغير قتال

“without fighting.”

The post says:

“fighting broke out.”

Ibn Bishr says:

وقتلوا

“they killed.”

The post reduces this to:

“resulting in deaths.”

Ibn Bishr says:

من أهله

“from among its inhabitants.”

The paraphrase subtly encourages the reader to imagine nothing but soldiers dying in combat.

That is not a translation. It is an exculpatory recasting of the syntax.

One should be scrupulous even here: ahl al-Ṭāʾif does not logically prove that every one of the approximately two hundred was wholly unarmed. Ibn Bishr does not supply individual biographies for the dead. But neither does he call them an army, nor say that they fell in “fighting in houses and markets.”

He says that the final taking of the town occurred without fighting, and then says they killed inhabitants in the houses and markets.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr’s fuller narration provides the missing architecture of events.

There had indeed been bitter fighting beforehand. The walls were assaulted; artillery was used; the defenders resisted.

Then the Sharīfian coalition disintegrated.

جميع عربان الشريف تفرقوا شذر مذر

“All the Sharīf’s Bedouin auxiliaries dispersed in every direction.”

A substantial body of men left. Ghālib, hearing that a movement upon Makkah was threatened, departed toward the Holy City. Thereafter, according to Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr, the defensive order of al-Ṭāʾif collapsed. Some fled over the walls in order to escape. Men, women and children fled from the city.

Dukhayl Allāh b. Ḥurayb then reportedly overtook the Saudi-aligned army and informed it that al-Ṭāʾif had effectively been abandoned, whereupon the forces returned.

Thus there is no contradiction whatever between the two narratives:

ferocious siege combat beforehand; collapse of organised defence; final entry without a general battle; killing within the city thereafter.

Indeed, Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr renders Ibn Bishr’s terse بغير قتال far more intelligible.

What becomes untenable is the attempt to make Ibn Bishr say that the two hundred simply fell in an ordinary continuation of the siege.

And notice another convergence which is rarely advertised. Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr says that after the sack the accumulated property was carried outside, its fifth taken for the emir, and the remainder divided:

كما تقسم الغنائم

“as spoils of war are divided.”

Ibn Bishr, from the opposite camp, likewise records the vast booty, the collection of the akhmās, and their dispatch to ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. 

The Makkan chronicler and the Najdī chronicler therefore converge upon the treatment of al-Ṭāʾif’s property as war-booty, even whilst they radically differ over the moral significance of what occurred.

4. “Félix Mengin says a general amnesty was declared after the town submitted.”

Certainly.

And the word after is precisely the difficulty.

Mengin first says that when the attacking force entered al-Ṭāʾif it made short work of the Sharīf’s soldiers, adding:

il y eut aussi des habitans de tués

“there were also inhabitants who were killed.”

Only then comes:

Une amnistie générale suivit la soumission de la ville

“A general amnesty followed the submission of the town.”

His sequence is not obscure:

soldiers killed; inhabitants also killed; submission; then amnesty.

The amnesty is therefore perfectly compatible with earlier killing. One might reasonably infer that it marked the cessation or regularisation of violence after formal submission. What one cannot do is cite it as though it erased Mengin’s preceding clause.

To deploy the amnesty against reports of inhabitants being killed while omitting Mengin’s explicit statement that inhabitants were killed is a singularly unfortunate use of one’s own witness.

And Mengin, let us recall, is the same source who earlier says al-Muḍāyifī sought troops “to go and make war upon Ghālib.”

Thus Mengin simultaneously complicates both central propositions of the original post: the immaculate “self-defence” chronology and the suggestion that the amnesty somehow excludes prior killing.

5. “The stories of people at prayer, Qurʾān students, women, infants and babies being breastfed are fabrications invented by Aḥmad Zaynī Daḥlān.”

Here the argument encounters a chronological impossibility.

Aḥmad Zaynī Daḥlān was born only in 1816/17 and died in 1886. 

Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr, the Makkan Ḥanafī historian discussed above, died in 1841, and his chronicle already contains the very motifs which are being assigned to Daḥlān’s imagination. His authorship and manuscript tradition are independently catalogued.

After narrating the entry into al-Ṭāʾif, Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr says:

فقتلوهم قتلاً عاماً

“They killed them with a general killing.”

He speaks of:

الكبير والصغير

“the old and the young,”

and then explicitly of:

وعلى صدر أمه الطفل الرضيع

“the nursing infant upon his mother’s breast.”

He says the conquerors ascended into the houses searching for those concealed within them and:

فيجدون كل جماعة يتدارسون كلام رب العزة … فيقتلونهم وفي أيديهم المصاحف

“would find groups studying the Speech of the Lord of Might … and kill them while the muṣḥafs were in their hands.”

He then says they went through shops and mosques:

ويقتلون الرجل وهو راكع أو ساجد

“and would kill a man while he was bowing or prostrating.”

These are the very episodes now dismissed as “fabrications of Daḥlān.”

Whatever else one wishes to say about them, Daḥlān cannot have invented a narrative which is already present in an earlier Makkan chronicle.

That does not oblige the historian to treat every sentence of Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr as revelation. His hostility toward the Najdī movement is patent. He writes from within the wounded memory of the old Ḥijāzī order, just as Ibn Bishr writes from within the triumphal sacred history of the Saudi-Najdī cause.

But the proper conclusion from partisanship is critical comparison, not selective annihilation of the witness one dislikes.

And Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr’s narrative is considerably more discriminating than the caricature of an indiscriminate “massacre legend” suggests.

After the general violence, he separately describes armed holdouts who fortified themselves in houses and continued fighting for several days. He therefore plainly distinguishes those engaged in continuing combat from the victims described immediately beforehand.

He then narrates a formal offer of amān. Ibn Shakhbān allegedly assures one group that they are under his and ʿUthmān’s protection:

وأنكم في وجه ابن شقبان وعثمان

and binds himself to them:

بالعهود والمواثيق

“with covenants and solemn pledges.”

The result, Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr says, was:

فعند ذلك كفوا أيديهم عن القتال كافة

“thereupon they all withheld their hands from fighting.”

He then alleges that they were disarmed and that one surrendered group was subsequently taken out and executed at Daqāq al-Lawz.

A separate body was treated differently: Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr says their guarantee extended to their lives but not their goods, whereupon they were stripped, dispossessed and expelled rather than executed.

That distinction is historiographically significant. His account differentiates siege combat, flight, post-entry killing, armed resistance, negotiation, surrender, amān, alleged execution, survival and dispossession.

This is not proof that every number and every scene is exact, but it is unmistakably an early, elaborate Makkan tradition. Daḥlān did not create it ex nihilo.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr is rejected because he is partisan; yet Ibn Bishr’s plainly partisan chronicle is paraphrased so generously that “without fighting” becomes “fighting broke out,” “they killed inhabitants” becomes “200 people died,” and the enormous seizure of property disappears almost entirely.

Mengin is invoked for his amnesty, while his statement that inhabitants were killed immediately beforehand is passed over.

And then Daḥlān is accused of fabricating traditions which can be read, in substantially the same form, in an earlier Makkan Ḥanafī chronicle.

The sober conclusion is therefore much less congenial to this apologetic reconstruction.

Ghālib’s later attack upon al-Muḍāyifī is real; it is not the beginning of the conflict.

The treaty broke down; Ibn Bishr does not tell us in the cited sentence that Ghālib betrayed it.

Al-Muḍāyifī was Ghālib’s brother-in-law, not his son-in-law.

Mengin himself has al-Muḍāyifī requesting troops to wage war upon Ghālib.

Ibn Bishr says the final entry into al-Ṭāʾif occurred without fighting, after which the Wahhābīs killed approximately two hundred inhabitants in markets and houses and seized immense quantities of property.

Mengin says inhabitants were also killed, and only thereafter records the general amnesty.

And Ibn ʿAbd al-Shakūr demonstrates beyond dispute that the narratives of the nursing infant, Qurʾān readers and worshippers belong to an earlier Makkan historical tradition and were not creations originating in the pen of Aḥmad Zaynī Daḥlān.

The legitimate historical controversy concerns the magnitude of the killing, the reliability of particular atrocity reports, and the reconciliation, or irreconcilability, of the rival Ḥijāzī and Najdī traditions.

What the sources do not sustain is the immaculate modern fable in which Ghālib treacherously assaults his “son-in-law,” two hundred men merely fall in ordinary fighting, a universal amnesty follows, and the old Makkan memory of the sack is afterwards manufactured wholesale by Daḥlān.

The Wahhābī takeover of al-Ṭāʾif in 1803 was in response to the Sharīf of Makkah betraying the peace agreement and attacking his son in-law, ʿUthmān b. ʿAbd al-Raḥman al-Muḍāyifī, after the latter had declared his allegiance to Āl Saʾūd.

The Wahhābīs were once again acting in self-defense.

Ibn Bishr mentioned that after Sharīf Ghālib’s forces retreated, ʿUthmān al-Muḍāyifī’s forces entered al-Ṭāʾif, and fighting broke out in the market places and homes resulting in the deaths of 200 people.

Felix Mengin mentioned that a general amnesty was declared after the town submitted.

The so-called “civilian massacres” of people in prayer, people studying the qurʾān, women, infants and babies being breastfed are nothing but lies and fabrications by Aḥmad Zaynī Daḥlān.

In 1979 a revolutionary regime took a country and made violence a governing method. Hostages in Tehran. A war with Iraq that chewed a generation. Hezbollah in Lebanon. Plots and proxies from Buenos Aires to Beirut to Baghdad. A nuclear program built in the dark. Women beaten in the street for showing their hair. That is not a conservative talking point. It is the public record both parties used to describe when they were not scoring an American President.

“Ruled by bloodshed” is ugly language. It is also closer to how Iranian protesters talk about their own state than how a cable panel talks about it. You can hate Trump’s tone and still admit the Islamic Republic is not a normal neighbor. It funds militias. It hangs dissidents. It treats the Strait and the Red Sea as pressure valves. Democrats who backed the JCPOA did so because they thought a deal could box that behavior in. Democrats who later watched the proxies keep firing had to update. That argument is allowed. Pretending 1979 never happened is not.

Two separate files help. Iran is a people, a language, a civilization. The regime is a security caste with a revolutionary export job. Confusing them is how you get Americans cheering “the Iranian people” and then calling every sanction an attack on those same people. Pressure aimed at the Guard and the nuclear sites is not the same thing as a war on Persians. If the offer was cooperation in exchange for ending the program and the terror pipeline, a Democrat can ask whether the offer was real and whether refusal is documented. Those are fair questions. “Fanatical American regime” in the replies is not an answer. It is a mirror that avoids the map.

What a serious opposition would say next. What is the end-state. What does inspectable disarmament look like. What happens to the proxies if the money stops. What do European allies contribute besides statements. What is the cost to American troops and to oil markets if this stays a forever gray war. You do not need MAGA vocabulary to demand those answers. You need the habit of treating foreign policy as more than a clip of a man you already dislike.

Fifty-one years is his count. The revolution is forty-seven if you start at 1979. The body count does not care which number you prefer. The stage is set. Argue the terms. Do not argue that the file is imaginary.

That clip is the terms. Treat it like terms.

He said the offer was simple. Full economic cooperation if the nuclear program ends and the terror support ends. They refused. In Clausewitz that is the political object named before the force is explained. Flynn asked for the same four beats this morning: define the aim, name what stops the fighting, tell friends their share, tell the adversary the price. This is the adversary line.

Iran the nation is not the same file as the IRGC. The people under sanctions are not identical to the Quds force that built the proxy ring. A serious speech has to keep that cut or you hand Tehran a nationalism script. The refusal he describes is the regime’s, not a poll of shopkeepers in Shiraz. They chose the program and the militias over the open window. That is a choice. It has a cost.

History is not a montage. The 2015 deal bought time and cash and left the enrichment path and the regional stack in place. Maximum pressure tried the other door. The year-one offer he just recited is the third pass: trade for dismantlement, not a sunset clause with a photo. If they refused, the next sentence has to be the enforcement, not a new adjective. Energy, shipping, the proxy payroll, the enrichment sites. Name them or the hall will translate “big mistake” into theater.

Peace is not a mood at the UN. It is an inspectable end-state. No nuclear breakout. No paid chaos in the Levant, in the Gulf, in the Red Sea. Allies who want the umbrella pay into the same object. Adversaries who want the old model hear the terms twice. Once as an offer. Once as a clock.

DID YOU KNOW??

Before becoming YouTube's undisputed king, Felix Kjellberg (PewDiePie) dropped out of a prestigious degree in Industrial Economics and Technology Management at Chalmers University to sell hot dogs on the street to fund his early channel, after his parents refused to support him financially.

​In 2011, Kjellberg decided to walk away from his degree at one of Sweden's top engineering universities because he felt unfulfilled. His parents were so disappointed that they refused to offer him any financial backing for his YouTube ambition.

​To buy a gaming computer and basic editing gear, Felix took a job working at a hot dog stand in Gothenburg, while also selling his own Photoshop artwork online. The gamble paid off: by August 2013, he became the most-subscribed creator on YouTube, held the individual creator title for nearly a decade, and transformed digital entertainment forever. Walk with me 👇🏾👇🏾 

The Four Phases of the PewDiePie Arc:

​Felix Kjellberg's career represents the evolution of online creator culture from its wild west roots to mainstream global media:

1. The Hot Dog Stand & Horror Games
2010–2012:
Felix drops out of college, works odd jobs, and gains massive traction playing indie horror games like Amnesia: The Dark Descent, pioneering high-energy commentary and webcam reactions.

2. The YouTube Titan
2013–2017:
He becomes the #1 most-subscribed channel on YouTube, building an army of over 50 million "Bro Army" subscribers and turning gaming Let's Plays into a multi-billion-dollar industry.

3. The Great T-Series War
2018–2019:
A global internet cultural movement emerges as fans rally under the "Subscribe to PewDiePie" banner to keep an individual creator ahead of corporate Indian music giant T-Series, spawning viral billboards, songs, and mainstream media coverage.

4. 'Soft Retirement' & Japan Move
2020–Present:
After surpassing 100 million subscribers, Felix transitioned into a relaxed vlog and commentary style, officially moving to Japan with his wife Marzia and starting a family away from intense algorithm chasing.

More Surprising Facts About PewDiePie:

A. ​Forgotten Password Created the Name: His original YouTube account was actually named "PewDie" ("pew" for the laser sound, "die" for death). After forgetting the password to that original account, he created a new one in 2010 and added "Pie" to the end, creating the legendary handle.

B. ​The "PewDiePie Effect" on Indie Games: In his prime, playing an indie game for just 10 minutes could instantly turn an unknown developer into an overnight millionaire. Games like Flappy Bird, Goat Simulator, and Slender: The Eight Pages owed much of their massive viral success directly to his videos.

C. ​The First Individual to Hit 100 Million Subscribers: In August 2019, he became the first solo creator in YouTube history to reach 111 million subscribers and receive YouTube's custom Red Diamond Play Button.

SUMMARILY! 
​PewDiePie dropped out of a prestigious Swedish university and sold hot dogs to buy his first gaming rig, eventually becoming the first individual creator to reach 100 million YouTube subscribers.

Hopefully you've learnt something new today?

text:
Brian Evans is not a random YouTube guy. He is a Las Vegas lounge singer who used to open for Carrot Top. Then the friendship went into Florida court. Everything below is allegation plus docket, not a verdict.
Who he is
Late 1990s he was the crooner at the Desert Inn Starlight Lounge (the hotel that became Wynn). Cut Live at the Desert Inn. Years later he worked Thompson’s Luxor residency: opened the Atrium in 2014 and 2015, shot videos with him (Creature at the Bates Motel, then a 2021 soccer-jazz clip Thompson appeared in). Radar bills him as a Billboard-chart singer. He also ran as a Republican congressional candidate out of Hawaii. After the 2023 Maui fires he says he was treated for PTSD, anxiety, depression, insomnia. That diagnosis is the hook he now uses to try to void a 2024 deal.

How they got here
Evans says that around 2022 or 2023 Thompson sent him an unsolicited explicit video. He says he was shocked, deleted it, then found it in iCloud. June 2024 they signed a confidential settlement (July addendum). Evans now says he lacked capacity to sign because of the Maui trauma, and that Thompson dangled future work. He wants that paper torn up. Thompson’s camp treats the settlement as closed and Evans as a serial filer.
The docket war, 2026

July 8: Evans sues Scott Thompson in federal court, Southern District of Florida.
Judge denies his emergency injunction.

Aug. 6: Evans voluntarily dismisses the federal case without prejudice and refiles in Broward County.
Same stretch: he is also fighting CAA and agent Steve Levine, claiming they blacklisted him after he reported the video.
A federal judge noted he had filed no fewer than 15 pro se cases in that district since 2025 that “appear frivolous.” That is the “vexatious” tag he is yelling about in your clip.
The $500k / $2M fight
Sept. 3, Thompson’s lawyer Ronnie Bitman filed “Communications Demonstrating Plaintiff’s Extortion.” The exhibit is an Evans email: Path A is $500,000 in immediately available funds to resolve all claims against Thompson, or he proceeds with a motion for leave. Bitman says that means the USB goes in the public file for the press. Evans says he never threatened to post a tape for cash, the file was already deleted under the old settlement, and the email is Rule 408 settlement talk being spun. Sept. 7 he sued Bitman and another lawyer for calling it extortion. TMZ later posted a separate $2 million global-settlement ask from last week, days before Thompson hit the hospital. Evans still denies a leak-for-money plan.
The other name in the pile
Zachary Defazio, 25, filed a sworn declaration in the Broward fight. Separate civil claims about meeting Thompson on Grindr at 19. His former lawyers once sent a $7.5 million confidential demand. That is not a criminal case and it is not proven. Do not weld Defazio and Evans into one story.

What the hell
Two Strip acts who used to share a stage. A 2024 hush deal Evans wants undone. Money emails the lawyer calls extortion and Evans calls settlement. A judge who already branded him a problem filer. A YouTube clip where he offers a polygraph and says “I’m not that guy.” Then Thompson is hospitalized and every outlet slams the two files together. None of that is a finding that Evans extorted anyone. None of that is a finding that Thompson did what the complaints describe. Broward still has the paper. Tape stays off this feed.

text:
1. $SPCX (Space Exploration Technologies / SpaceX)

Business: Three segments — Space (reusable rockets/launches), Connectivity (Starlink), AI (xAI/Grok + compute infrastructure). IPO'd June 2026. Market cap ~$2.06T.

Revenue: TTM ~$23.0B (+122% YoY). Q2 2026: $7.8B (+92% YoY) — Connectivity $4.3B, AI $2.6B (+247%), Space $0.96B.

Gross Profit / Net Income: TTM gross margin ~52%. Q2 gross profit ~$4.3B. Still net loss (TTM ~–$8.9B; Q2 –$541M) due to heavy AI CapEx and R&D. Adjusted EBITDA strong (Q2 ~$3.5B).

Outlook: Starlink subscriber + enterprise/government growth continues. New multi-year AI compute deals accelerating. Heavy CapEx (AI alone >$23B in H1) pressures near-term profits, but vertical integration (rockets + satellites + AI) creates a long-term moat. Analyst PT mid-point ~$222 (+46%). Risks: valuation, execution, regulation.

2. $CRDO (Credo Technology)

Business: High-speed copper & optical interconnects for AI data centers (AECs, DSPs, ZeroFlap optics, silicon photonics). Serves hyperscalers.

Revenue: FY2026 (ended May 2026) $1.34B (+206% YoY). Q4 $437M (+157% YoY). Q1 FY2027 ~$479M.

Gross Profit / Net Income: Gross margin consistently 67–68%. Non-GAAP net income FY2026 ~$662M (5x+ growth), net margins ~50%. Strong FCF and ~$1.4B cash.

Outlook: Optical ramp expected to exceed $600M. FY2027 guidance implies another ~80% growth. High-quality, self-funding growth with expanding product suite. Valuation has compressed; PEG looks attractive. Risks: customer concentration, sequential growth moderation.

3. $NBIS (Nebius Group)

Business: Full-stack AI cloud (GPU clusters + platform). Former Yandex spin-out; also owns Avride and TripleTen.

Revenue: TTM ~$1.36B (+500%+). Q2 2026 $582M (+454% YoY), almost entirely AI cloud.

Gross Profit / Net Income: Gross margin 74–77%. Q2 Adj. EBITDA $236M (41% margin). GAAP still volatile (Q2 net loss ~$190M) due to interest and non-cash items.

Outlook: Large multi-year contracts (Microsoft, Meta, etc.), NVIDIA investment, 2026 ARR target $7–9B, full-year revenue $3.0–3.4B. Aggressive CapEx ($20–25B) to scale power capacity to multi-GW. Risks: high leverage/interest expense, execution, competition.

4. $IREN (IREN Limited)

Business: Vertically integrated AI cloud data centers + Bitcoin mining, rapidly pivoting to AI. 100% renewable power; >5 GW pipeline.

Revenue: FY2026 (ended June 2026) $707M (+41%). AI Cloud $129M (8x growth), Bitcoin mining $578M.

Gross Profit / Net Income: Gross margin ~69%. Adj. EBITDA ~$246M. Net loss ~$703M (mainly non-cash impairments of $639M). Operating ARR already ~$1B; contracted ARR ~$4B for 2026 capacity.

Outlook: Microsoft and other large contracts; major GPU orders. 2026 capacity largely sold out; 2027 discussions ongoing. Risks: impairments, Bitcoin price exposure, high CapEx and debt.

5. $CRWV (CoreWeave)

Business: Purpose-built AI cloud platform (GPU clusters + software stack) for AI labs and enterprises.

Revenue: TTM ~$7.59B. Q2 2026 $2.58B (+112% YoY). Revenue backlog ~$104B.

Gross Profit / Net Income: Q2 gross profit ~$1.70B (gross margin ~66%). Adj. EBITDA $1.51B (59% margin). Still net loss (Q2 –$626M) driven by interest and depreciation.

Outlook: Explosive demand and massive backlog support multi-year growth. Operating leverage should improve with scale. Risks: high leverage, interest expense, intensifying competition.

Overall Future Trajectory

All five sit at the center of the AI compute, networking, and power build-out.

$SPCX has the broadest long-term optionality via vertical integration.

$CRDO offers the cleanest profitability and highest-quality growth.

$NBIS, $CRWV, and $IREN are high-growth "neo-cloud" plays — capital-intensive with near-term losses but rapid revenue scaling.

Secular drivers (hyperscaler CapEx, GPU scarcity, power constraints) remain intact into 2027–2028. Near-term volatility will be high due to valuation, interest rates, and execution risk. Medium-term upside looks substantial as scale improves margins.

text:
JD Hall's screed is what you get when someone skims Leviticus 16, watches a viral chicken video, and decides they have uncovered an 1,800-year fraud. Confident, punchy, and sloppy.

Nobody serious thinks kapparot (the custom of waving a chicken or money over the head as a symbolic atonement) is Yom Kippur. Swinging a chicken is a later minhag (custom), not written in the Torah and not established in the Talmud. It shows up clearly in Geonic sources centuries later, and major poskim (halachic authorities) argued over it. Some communities keep it. Many use money. Many skip it. Treating a disputed custom as the definition of the day is like watching mall Santa photos and announcing that Christmas is the mall.

"Made up circa 200 AD" is just a bad reading of the Mishnah's date. Tractate Yoma (the Mishnah section on "the Day") is not a new holiday. Most of it records the Avodah (Temple service) of the Beis HaMikdash (the Holy Temple): the Kohen Gadol (High Priest), the two goats, the blood, the scapegoat. Chazal (the Sages) were preserving the Torah's Temple service after it could no longer be performed, not inventing a replacement day and slapping the old name on it. The last chapter sets out the personal innuy (self-affliction) of the day (no eating or drinking, no washing, no anointing, no leather shoes, no marital relations). That is how the Torah's command to afflict your souls was applied to each person. It is not the invention of Yom Kippur in the year 200.

The day is from the Torah: the tenth of Tishrei, no work, affliction of the soul, and atonement. While the Temple stood, the central avodah (service) was the Kohen Gadol's service. Philo and Josephus already describe Jews fasting and praying on that day. After the churban (the destruction of the Temple), the sacrifices stopped because there was no Temple. The date did not stop. The fast did not stop. Teshuvah (repentance) did not stop. Chazal themselves say the point out loud. Rabbi Yehoshua mourns that the place which atoned for Israel is destroyed. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai answers that gemilus chasadim (acts of loving-kindness) remains. That is not a cover story for a fake holiday. It is the Jewish response to losing the altar.

The claim that none of this is "in the Christian Old Testament" is just as weak. The written Torah already commands the day. Hosea 14:2 is also in Tanach (the Hebrew Bible): take words with you, return to Hashem (God), and offer the words of your lips in place of bulls. Jewish sources use that verse for a reason. Prayer, confession, and repentance are not a 3rd-century product listing. What changed after 70 CE was not the existence of Yom Kippur. What changed was that the nation could no longer bring the korbanos (sacrificial offerings) the Torah assigns to the Temple.

The Christmas analogy fails for the same reason. A commanded day does not become counterfeit because its Temple form is suspended. Jews lost the Mikdash (Temple), the Kohen Gadol's Avodah, and the scapegoat. They kept the tenth of Tishrei, the fast, vidui (confession), teshuvah, and the recitation of the Temple Avodah in shul (synagogue). That is how the day is observed in exile. It is not "Temu-Hebrew." It is Yom Kippur without a Temple.

"Pharisee cult invents rabbinic Judaism" is a slogan, not a source. The Torah's day remained. The Oral Law explains how it is kept. After the Temple fell, that is what could still be done. Calling the result a fabrication because it no longer looks like the Kohen Gadol walking into the Kodesh HaKodashim (Holy of Holies) only shows the poster does not know the difference between the Avodah of the Mikdash and the mitzvah (commandment) of the day.

The Temple service and the synagogue fast are not identical. That part is obvious. Almost every date and label used to turn that into "they made the holiday up in 200 AD" is wrong. The korbanos ceased. Yom Kippur did not.

text:
The "it’s a privilege, not a right" argument misses how constitutional law actually works.

Driving a car or holding a professional license is legally a privilege, not a constitutional right—yet the government cannot revoke your driver’s license simply because it dislikes your political speech or without basic due process.

The exact same principle applies here. Under binding precedent (Sherrill v. Knight), once the White House chooses to establish an accredited press corps, credentialed journalists hold a protected liberty interest. Revoking that access arbitrarily or as retaliation for critical coverage violates both the First Amendment (unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination) and the Fifth Amendment (deprivation of access without clear notice, published standards, or due process).

The government isn't required to offer every benefit in the first place, but once it does, it cannot weaponize that benefit to reward praise and punish criticism.

BREAKING: @a16z is launching Horowitz Andreessen Academy

A new post-high school program in SF built for young people who want to start companies or work in tech.

CEO @gaganbiyani says they are rethinking what college could look like if it were designed for the AI era:

“In the AI era, you can learn whatever you need to learn on the job. Therefore, it's much more effective for students to go & just build things.”

Instead of organizing education around credits & classes, HAA is project-based:

“They'll go & literally travel to the big manufacturing facilities around the country or maybe even in the world, & deeply try to understand how it works while simultaneously, maybe studying robotics, the technical side of robotics via both self-driven learning but also via online courseware or courses that we offer at the academy.”

“You can imagine a world in which this student is visiting factories in Shenzhen, or maybe they're visiting factories in Austin or LA, & simultaneously studying online through our diverse network of faculty, robotics, & they're also building an actual robot from scratch.”

“This is the type of experience that we wanna create for the student who comes to Horowitz Andreessen Academy.”

text:
Starlink on United is Internet

Compare Starlink vs. ViaSat.

Starlink delivers average download speeds of ~90 Mbps while ViaSat is ~13 Mbps.

Starlink offers latency in the ~30 ms range while ViaSat can be around 770 ms.

That latency difference is the killer.

ViaSat, Anuvu, Panasonic and the other traditional satellite systems rely heavily on geostationary satellites roughly 22,000 miles above Earth. You can optimize the network around that, but you can't optimize away the distance.

It's physics.

At 35,000 feet, a Starlink satellite is hundreds of miles away, not tens of thousands. The speed of light is an unforgiving constant.

That's why Starlink isn't just better Wi-Fi on an airplane.

It's a fundamentally different network.

Measurements from my network testing app NetP. Available at https://t.co/PNDdxI1z3v.  Try it on your next flight.

text:
Trump’s UNGA speech is today (Sept. 22, 2026). 

(The White House has not posted an official full transcript yet. Below is the most complete reconstruction available from contemporaneous reporting of the delivered remarks, mainly from the Jerusalem Post’s running quotes and NYT live coverage. Treat this as a near-complete news reconstruction, not a certified White House text. ￼)

President Donald Trump — Address to the 81st UN General Assembly
United Nations Headquarters, New York — September 22, 2026

While others have talked, I have acted. While others have spoken of peace, I have made it. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them. While others have talked of courage, America has shown it. While others have promised strength, I have used it to make America the most powerful country in the world.
Our economy is the envy of the world. Our military is the most powerful on earth. Our technology is second to none, and we are leading in virtually everything.
There is no better example of a danger that was allowed to gather strength at the world’s peril than the number one sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic.
For 51 years, the fanatical Iranian regime has ruled by bloodshed and mass murder, spreading death and carnage and chaos across the entire Middle East and beyond. They were the bully of the Middle East, but they are the bully no more.
From the first day I entered the political arena, I have been unwavering. I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon. Upon taking office last year, I immediately opened negotiations with Iran and offered them full economic cooperation in exchange for ending their nuclear program.
But they refused. They absolutely refused. That was a big mistake. Then in Operation Midnight Hammer, the US military obliterated their nuclear program beneath mountains of rubble. And again, I urge Iran to make a deal. And again, they refused.
The regime continued building a vast missile and drone stockpile and threatened the security of every American service member in the region and everyone else in the region. They also made a missile that was capable of hitting Europe, and they were very proud of it.
If they had succeeded, that wicked regime would have been free to spread terror and death forever, knowing that any attempt to stop them would face an arsenal of nuclear annihilation.
In America, we just marked the 25th anniversary of the worst terror attack in history, September 11th, which killed 3,000 people a few miles from here. In two weeks, we will mark the third anniversary of the October 7 attack in Israel, where terror is funded by Iran, tortured, mutilated, and killed 1,200 very innocent civilians, including dozens of Americans and many babies, little, tiny, beautiful babies.
Iran’s supreme leader celebrated that massacre and called it a service to humanity. The same regime slaughtered over 72,000 of its citizens this year. Recently, 10,000 were killed for protesting.
Just imagine such a vile regime were ever empowered to carry out large-scale terror attacks from behind a nuclear shield. This was the reality we had to confront — a reality that far too many preferred to ignore. They all ignored it. Many presidents and many others just wanted to ignore it. They were unwilling to do anything about it, but they knew the problem.
As a result of Operation Epic Fury, all 159 ships of their navy are now lying at the bottom of the sea. Likewise, their air force is gone, their radar is gone, their anti-aircraft equipment is gone, their missiles and drone manufacturing capacity is almost gone.
Their economy is gone. The only thing that isn’t gone is inflation, which is destroying their country, and is now well over 300 percent.
Yet even after we agreed to a ceasefire for nuclear discussions, Iran promptly violated it with brazen acts of terrorism against civilian ships from other countries.
I want to thank the UN Security Council for voting overwhelmingly to pass a resolution condemning Iran’s despicable terrorist attacks on commercial shipping. That resolution, I’m pleased to say, received more co-sponsors from UN member nations than any Security Council resolution in history.
The United States Navy has recently escorted more than 1 billion barrels of oil out of the Strait of Hormuz, and more oil is flowing than at any point since the start of the war.
But I have a big decision to make. Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world. Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?
Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations? But I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to. They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.
They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don’t realize is that I’m not running. I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran. It doesn’t even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.
The cowards and traitors would love to say the United States is low in munitions, but that’s not true. We have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using, and we’re building them at levels that we have never done before.
I call on all nations to join us in enforcing the complete economic isolation of Iran until they stop their attacks on commercial shipping, relinquish their nuclear ambitions, and cease their support of terror.
The terrorist regime is behaving badly, badly, not because they are strong and confident, but because they are weak and desperate.
If we stand united, we will soon see a world free of the last 51-year menace of Iranian terror.
One year ago, when I addressed the great leaders in this hall, the war in Gaza was still raging brutally. The hostages were still deep in Hamas tunnels, and there was no end in sight. It was never going to be resolved. But here, on the sidelines of the General Assembly, we took the first steps that changed everything. A few weeks later, we ended the war in Gaza, saving untold thousands of lives. We also brought home all remaining hostages, both living and dead. Every single one of them.
I want to express my gratitude to the United Nations Security Council for their unanimous endorsement of our 20-point Gaza peace plan, and for officially approving the Board of Peace.
We’re thankful to many of those member nations for contributing billions and billions of dollars to relief. And it goes right to the rebuilding and relief of Morocco and Bahrain. These are the countries that gave: Qatar, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Afghanistan, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Uzbekistan, and many more.
I also want to thank those who have committed troops, police, and training to help stabilize Gaza, including Indonesia, Morocco, Albania, Kosovo, Kazakhstan, Egypt, Jordan, and more.
We’ve invested more money in the United States military in the past 12 months than ever before, and this term it’ll be 1.5 trillion dollars.
To the victor belong the spoils. [On Venezuela / Maduro operation.]
Communism will never be coming to America, but freedom will be coming to Cuba. We will not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep.
The cartels are the ISIS of the Western Hemisphere. They are enemies at war with civilization, using murder, rape, torture, and extortion as instruments of terror.
The Cuban regime has also spent decades coordinating with left-wing radicals and Communist networks here in the United States. As our State Department has detailed, they have cultivated ties to subversive and radical groups such as the Communist Party USA, Antifa, and the Democrat Socialists of America. There is no global government, and while I am President, there will be NO GLOBAL TAXES. Freedom was not a gift that Americans won easily, and after 250 years, it is not one we will ever surrender.
As I announced just days ago, the United States has also reached an unprecedented agreement regarding the northern frontier of North America, the large and strategically vital piece of land known as Greenland.
This agreement, made with the Kingdom of Denmark, an incredible, beautiful country, and the Greenland people themselves, gives the United States permanent control over security and all of the needs on that territory. We will have the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent and also Europe and other places.
No US adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland anymore, or make sensitive investments there without our express written approval. We will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations. We’ll be building two very major military bases.
This agreement will be signed later today, and I look forward to working with the wonderful people of Denmark and Greenland.
I was forced to intervene to stop an obscure U.N. body, the International Maritime Organization, from establishing a first-ever global carbon tax, a very expensive tax.
The United States rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control artificial intelligence. From this point forward, all of the United States documents and, hopefully, the world’s will be changed to use the much more accurate term “super” as opposed to artificial. So it’s super intelligence. SI.
The United States leads the world in superintelligence, and we’ll continue to do so safely and responsibly. Americans have never been a nation that retreats from a frontier or shrinks from a challenge. We will only encourage super intelligence. We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in.
Warnings about the dangers to humanity of A.I. were coming from the same group of people who promoted the Russia hoax.
I call on all members of the International Criminal Court to resign immediately. It is a rogue institution.

Note: This is assembled from quoted passages in live reporting. Opening greetings, some transitions, and closing lines may still be missing until the White House posts the official remarks. If you want, I can pull the official transcript as soon as it goes up.

As diesel demand continues to rise and supplies tighten, biobased diesel is helping stretch every gallon further.

Biodiesel and renewable diesel add billions of gallons to America’s fuel supply—meeting approximately 9% of U.S. on-road diesel demand in 2024. These fuels supplement limited petroleum diesel inventories while keeping trucks, buses, farm equipment, emergency vehicles, ships, and other essential operations moving.

With U.S. distillate inventories well below the five-year seasonal average and increased demand expected from the fall harvest and winter heating season, every additional gallon matters. Biobased diesel offers a practical, domestically produced solution that works with today’s engines and fueling infrastructure while reducing lifecycle emissions and supporting American farmers, fuel producers, and rural communities.

Biobased diesel cannot resolve today’s global supply challenges by itself—but without it, supplies would be tighter and consumers would face even greater pressure.

It isn’t a future solution. It is strengthening America’s fuel supply today.

text:
THE EVIDENCE™

NICK EMMANWORI: SEATTLE'S ONE-OF-ONE DEFENSIVE WEAPON

Nine snaps offered only a glimpse. What happens when Mike Macdonald fully unleashes a player Julian Love has already flagged as one of the rarest pieces on the roster?

The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

Nick Emmanwori returned Sunday against Arizona and played only nine defensive snaps, recording one tackle. On the surface there is almost nothing there from which to build an argument, and that may be the most useful place to begin. Seattle did not need Emmanwori to dominate the game — the Seahawks beat Arizona 31-7, outgained the Cardinals 381-151 and controlled the ball for more than 36 minutes. Emmanwori was returning from ankle surgery after missing training camp and the season opener, so Seattle placed him on a snap count and resisted any temptation to accelerate the process. Macdonald confirmed afterward that Emmanwori could have played more, but the plan called for roughly six to eight plays to ease him back in, and Pro Football Focus counted the total at nine. Macdonald's own postgame framing left little ambiguity about what comes next: "It was great for him to get the confidence back, get him moving. He got a couple rushes in, which was cool. So we should be really accelerating into next week." Emmanwori echoed the sentiment from the other side of the ball, saying he hoped this was the last time all season he carries any kind of designation next to his name.

Nine snaps, then, should not be treated as a performance sample so much as an introduction to a more interesting question: what does Seattle's defense become once Nick Emmanwori is fully back?

Julian Love has already provided part of the answer. During Seattle's offseason program, Love described Emmanwori's value in structural terms, explaining that his versatility lets the Seahawks use him as an outside linebacker, a linebacker, a nickel or a corner depending on what the moment demands. After Sunday's win in Arizona, Love's commentary shifted from description toward consequence, pointing at the larger role Emmanwori is stepping into now that Seattle has lost a starter from its Super Bowl secondary in free agency. Love is not talking about adding another productive safety to an already strong defense — Seattle already knows Emmanwori can produce. The larger issue is what his presence allows Macdonald to ask of everyone else around him, and that distinction is where this investigation begins.

VERSATILITY IS ONLY THE FIRST LAYER

The easiest way to describe Emmanwori is versatile, but that description is incomplete. At the 2025 NFL Combine, Emmanwori measured 6-foot-3⅛ and 220 pounds, ran an official 4.38 forty, posted a 43-inch vertical and broad-jumped 11 feet, 6 inches. Those numbers are extraordinary on their own; their intersection in one defensive player is what changes the discussion. Seattle discovered during his rookie season that those traits could be converted into assignments that usually belong to several different positions, lining him up at safety, in the slot, at linebacker depth and directly on the line of scrimmage. By season's end, Next Gen Stats had him among the league's rare few defensive backs who aligned in the box on 45-plus percent of his snaps, at edge rusher on at least 10 percent, and in the slot on at least 30 percent — a combination shared with almost no one else except Baltimore's Kyle Hamilton, the safety Macdonald built into an All-Pro during his years as the Ravens' defensive coordinator. Hamilton has since said he watches Emmanwori closely and sees the same blueprint at work.

That is the distinction worth sitting with: versatility describes the player, since Emmanwori can perform several jobs, while multiplicity describes what the defense can do because he can perform them. An offense can identify a conventional safety and begin narrowing the range of assignments available to him, but Emmanwori complicates that exercise because his body type does not reliably disclose his responsibility. For an offense, personnel ordinarily provides clues, and Emmanwori makes some of those clues less useful.

THE ROOKIE SEASON ALREADY ESTABLISHED THE FLOOR

There is another reason to treat Sunday's nine snaps cautiously: there is already a much larger body of work behind it. Emmanwori suffered a high-ankle sprain four defensive snaps into his NFL debut and missed three games, and as soon as he returned Seattle began expanding his responsibilities. He started 11 of 14 regular-season games, finished with 81 tackles, nine tackles for loss, 2.5 sacks, 11 passes defensed and an interception, and closed the year holding up his end of a Super Bowl-winning defense, finishing second in Defensive Rookie of the Year voting despite the missed time. Those numbers establish production, but they still do not fully explain why Seattle appears so interested in expanding his role further.

Consider what Sunday itself revealed about where that expansion is heading. Of Emmanwori's nine snaps, PFF logged six with him lined up on the line as a rusher, one in the box and two in the slot, a workload weighted toward the pass rush rather than the coverage responsibilities that defined his rookie profile. Emmanwori confirmed the plan was intentional, saying the coaching staff had specifically worked that week on lining him up at edge and defensive end and having him blitz, and that it had gone well. Coaching staffs do not build a game plan around a returning defender's pass-rush reps as a ceremonial exercise, and Seattle used a limited window to test exactly the layer of Emmanwori's game that offenses have the least existing film to prepare for. Macdonald's problem is gradually becoming a favorable one: how many different jobs can one player absorb before the offense stops being able to determine which one is coming?

WATCH WHAT HAPPENS TO THE OTHER TEN PLAYERS

This may be the most important part of the Emmanwori discussion, because his value cannot be measured only by counting his tackles, sacks or passes defensed. His alignment affects the assignments available to the other ten defenders. Start with Julian Love, who played a full defensive snap count against Arizona while Emmanwori worked in on a pitch count. If Emmanwori can handle work closer to the line, over a tight end or in the slot, Love can spend more snaps operating from the positions Macdonald wants him in rather than rotating downward because the defensive structure requires it. Then consider Devon Witherspoon, already one of Seattle's most flexible defenders. Adding a healthy Emmanwori gives Macdonald another defender who can absorb responsibilities that otherwise might require Witherspoon to stay in one location, so Witherspoon can be reassigned without automatically creating a vacancy somewhere else.

That pairing is where Seattle's personnel becomes particularly difficult to read. An offense can see Love, Witherspoon and Emmanwori on the field and know exactly which three players Seattle has deployed, but it does not necessarily know where those three players will be when the ball is snapped or which responsibility each will carry once the formation shifts. Macdonald can move the jobs while leaving the personnel intact, and that is harder to diagnose than a defense that must substitute every time it changes its structure.

THE OFFENSE HAS TO SOLVE THE PICTURE

Modern NFL offenses spend enormous resources trying to identify defensive intent before the snap, and a defender such as Emmanwori introduces uncertainty into that process because his location does not provide a clean answer. Sunday supplied a live example. In the final minute of the first half, on third-and-4, Emmanwori blitzed off the edge and drew two blockers, star tight end Trey McBride and right tackle Elijah Wilkinson, both peeling off their assignments to account for him. Quarterback Jacoby Brissett had to climb the pocket and throw the ball away, meaning one rookie-caution blitz on a limited snap count forced two Arizona players to abandon their plan and cost the Cardinals a down.

That is the mechanism at work before Emmanwori ever touches the ball carrier. Put him near the line and the quarterback still has to determine whether he is rushing, setting the edge, carrying a tight end or dropping. Move Witherspoon toward the box at the same time and the protection problem changes again, and leave Love deep and the defense can present one structure before the snap while retaining several different answers after it. Former NFL quarterback Brock Huard, reviewing the tape afterward, put it plainly: even without a finished pass-rush move, Emmanwori got upfield in a hurry, and Brissett clearly felt him. On the snaps where he wasn't rushing, Huard noted, Emmanwori was simply taking away space from his big-nickel alignment, value that shows up nowhere in a box score. Macdonald gains something before Emmanwori makes a tackle — he gains uncertainty about the assignment.

THE PHYSICAL PROFILE CHANGES THE MENU

There have been large safeties before, fast safeties before, defensive backs who blitzed and linebackers who could cover. Emmanwori's value to Seattle comes from the number of those characteristics concentrated in one player. A 220-pound defender who runs 4.38 creates a different set of options than a traditional safety because Macdonald does not have to choose as sharply between size and range. If Seattle wants more physicality near the formation, Emmanwori can provide it without automatically surrendering defensive-back speed, and if Seattle wants to threaten pressure, it does not necessarily have to remove a coverage player to introduce another rusher. That is where the term multiplicity earns its place, since the same personnel grouping can produce several defensive structures.

There is risk in that approach, because giving a young defender too many responsibilities can slow recognition and turn flexibility into complexity for its own sake. Seattle appears aware of that boundary, and Love has credited Macdonald with introducing Emmanwori to concepts gradually as a rookie rather than overwhelming him with the entire package at once. Year Two changes the equation because the introductory phase has already occurred, and the question now is how much more Macdonald can install.

NINE SNAPS MAY HAVE TOLD US SOMETHING AFTER ALL

Sunday did not answer that question so much as establish the starting point. Seattle had a player coming off ankle surgery, with no training camp and no Week 1 game action, and deliberately restricted him to a handful of plays. Macdonald says the plan now is to accelerate his workload heading into Week 3, which gives us a useful benchmark for what follows. Watch where Emmanwori lines up, and whether the six rush snaps from Arizona become a standing feature rather than a one-week experiment. Watch whether his presence changes Love's alignment, and how often Witherspoon is freed for pressure or moved elsewhere in the formation. Most important, watch whether Seattle can change those assignments without changing personnel.

The box score will tell us how many tackles Emmanwori makes. The formation will tell us something far more interesting about what Macdonald is building. Julian Love's characterization of Emmanwori as a rare, multi-position piece was an evaluation of the player; his comments after Arizona point toward the broader consequence for a defense replacing a departed starter. The first statement concerns Nick Emmanwori. The second concerns the Seattle Seahawks defense, and that is the investigation worth following.

Nine snaps were never going to provide the answer — they placed the player back on the board. Now Mike Macdonald gets to start moving the pieces.

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

text:
🏬 What Actually Killed the Malls

The dead-mall phenomenon is real, and it wasn’t an accident. It was a pincer movement.

Amazon’s side (We won’t get into Amazon being subsidized by the intelligence apparatus/deep state)

- E-commerce didn’t just take a slice of retail—it took the anchor-adjacent traffic. When people stop going to Sears and JCPenney, the small inline stores lose their foot traffic too. The whole mall model was built on anchors as loss leaders.

- Amazon ran deliberately thin margins for years, subsidized by cheap capital and tax advantages that brick-and-mortar couldn’t touch. That’s not “better service,” that’s asymmetric warfare.

Private equity’s side:

-  This is the part people underrate. PE firms bought mall REITs and retail chains, loaded them with debt, extracted management fees and dividends, then let them collapse under the leverage. When they hit financial turmoil, Uncle Sam was there to bail them out. The goal was all a small part of the plan to destroy the family unit.

-  Toys “R” Us, Sears, Payless, Claire’s, Nine West—the pattern is identical. Buy, lever, strip, bankrupt. The stores die not because they were unprofitable as businesses, but because they were made unprofitable as debt vehicles. They were gutted by modern-day pirates!

-  When the retail tenant dies, the mall’s rent roll collapses. Then the PE-owned mall gets sold for land value or bulldozed.

It’s not a natural market death. It’s engineered extraction. With ties to communism. 

🧠 “Corporatism Is the New Communism”?

I’d sharpen this statement rather than dismiss it. The frame is imprecise, but the intuition is sound.

Both systems concentrate power in a small class and route the state toward serving that class. The difference is the mechanism:

-  Classical communism: the state owns the means of production; party cadres allocate.

-  Corporatism: private entities own the means of production, but they capture the state—regulatory capture, revolving doors, subsidies, bailouts, tax carve-outs.

The outcome converges: a small, connected elite; a hollowed-out middle; a dependent population; and a managed narrative that says this is all just “the free market” or “progress.” The revolving door is the tell. When the regulator used to work for the regulated, you don’t have capitalism—you have a cartel with a flag.

⚠️ Where I’d Push Back on the Traditional Framing

Two caveats, because the “Amazon killed everything” story is incomplete:

1.  Malls were already dying of self-inflicted wounds. Overbuilding in the 80s–90s, terrible mall design, high rents on inline tenants, and the retail apocalypse were predicted before Amazon was a threat. Amazon accelerated a structural decline; it didn’t invent it.

2. PE didn’t kill malls—it killed the tenants. Those are different claims with different villains. The mall landlord was often the victim too.

🎯 The Real Point—This Is VERY Important. It Was Exactly How They Controlled The Population During COVID!

What died wasn’t just retail square footage. It was third places—the unplanned, non-transactional public spaces where Americans used to run into each other. Malls, bowling alleys, diners, Main Street. They must separate us. Divide us. United, we threaten their agenda.

That loss has measurable downstream effects: declining social trust, rising loneliness, and a population that increasingly interacts only through screens. Amazon and PE didn’t set out to destroy community (the EU, Brussels and the WEF did)—they set out to extract value, and community was collateral damage. But the effect is the same.

The replacement of in-person commerce with algorithmic delivery and of public space with private feeds is one of the biggest quiet transformations in American life. It got sold as convenience. It functioned as enclosure.

text:
FOREIGN HACKERS BREACHED TWO COLORADO WATER UTILITIES, ALTERED PUMP CYCLES AND DISABLED ALARMS

Two privately owned Colorado water utilities were breached by foreign hackers in August, with attackers changing equipment settings, disabling alarms and remote access, and altering pump cycles, according to reporting from FOX31.

The Colorado governor’s office said the two affected utilities are small systems serving fewer than 200 people. Officials have not publicly identified the utilities or said which foreign actors were responsible.

Eric Maruyama, a spokesperson for Gov. Jared Polis, told FOX31 that the breaches were quickly addressed by the utilities.

According to the governor’s office, treatment processes and water quality were not impacted at either provider.

The incidents involved more than simply accessing computer networks. The hackers reportedly changed equipment settings, disabled remote access and alarms, and altered the cycles of pumps used by the systems.

State officials said they checked with the affected utilities to ensure the problems had been resolved and offered technical assistance. Colorado is also working with national partners and asking water providers to review their cybersecurity measures.

The incidents come amid broader concerns about cyberattacks targeting water infrastructure across the United States. FOX31 reported that the EPA says high-profile attacks have targeted more than 100 drinking water and wastewater systems across 12 states this year.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has also warned that Iranian-backed groups have attempted to gain access to U.S. drinking water and wastewater systems. Colorado officials, however, have not identified the actors behind these two breaches, so there is currently no confirmed connection between those warnings and the Colorado incidents.

Melissa Grove, deputy director of technology for Aurora Water, told FOX31 that utilities must remain constantly vigilant because automated systems are used throughout water treatment and distribution.

“Customers should know that the threat is real. It’s out there,” Grove said, while emphasizing that utilities have detection systems and partnerships in place to defend their infrastructure.

Neither of the breached Colorado utilities has been publicly identified.

Source: FOX31/KDVR, citing the Colorado governor’s office, EPA, CISA and Aurora Water.

text:
Step into the elegant world of early 19th-century Salem at the Gardner-Pingree House in Massachusetts. Built in 1804, the Federal-style mansion was designed by renowned architect Samuel McIntire, whose graceful woodcarving and carefully balanced interiors helped define the architectural character of historic Salem.

The house is especially notable for its finely crafted staircase, carved mantels, decorative woodwork, and period rooms that reflect the wealth created by Salem’s maritime trade. Today, it is preserved by the Peabody Essex Museum and offers visitors a remarkable look at the craftsmanship and domestic life of the Federal era.

Little-known fact: The house was the scene of one of Salem’s most notorious crimes. In 1830, wealthy ship captain Joseph White was murdered there, and the sensational case drew national attention—Daniel Webster even took part in the prosecution.

text:
At San Antonio station, passengers dozed beneath the glow of fluorescent lights. An old black-and-white film played on a television bolted high against one wall.
Then alarms began to ring.
Railroad employees rushed into the waiting room and ordered everyone out. Others sealed the platforms with barricade tape.
The passengers were furious. They had planned their trips; changing them wasn’t easy.
The station employees could offer no explanation. They had received emergency orders. Everyone had to leave. Tickets would be fully refunded.
The passengers resisted.
They had families waiting. Meetings in the morning. Vacations already paid for. A full refund would not restore a missed wedding or replace a lost day of work.
Police arrived minutes later.
They were not there to settle the argument.
They were there to clear the entire station—including the railroad staff.
"You can't just cancel my train! Who's paying for my hotel?" a man shouted at a heavily armed cop.
The television picture vanished.
A solemn anchor appeared.
“We interrupt our program with breaking news. Approximately two hours ago, an express train traveling from Florida to California was seized near Houston by an unidentified group of heavily armed hijackers. Their motive is not yet known. The train is believed to be carrying approximately five hundred passengers and is now approaching San Antonio. We will bring you further details as they become available.”
The waiting room erupted, instantly descended into absolute pandemonium as people scrambled for the exits.

text:
The frustration about low voter turnout is understandable. The analysis is not.

Blaming non-voters for high gas prices while ignoring that energy policy is set by regulatory agencies, commodity markets, refinery capacity decisions made by corporations, and OPEC production agreements — none of which are controlled by midterm election outcomes — is not serious political analysis. It’s scapegoating.

The 70% figure also requires context. Structural barriers to voting in America are well documented — polling place closures, lack of paid time off to vote, gerrymandered districts where outcomes are predetermined, and a two party system that offers millions of voters no meaningful representation of their actual interests. Calling people lazy for not participating in a system that demonstrably does not represent them is not a compelling argument for participation.

The deeper problem with this approach is that shaming and insulting people has never once in recorded history been an effective strategy for motivating behavioral change. Calling 70% of registered Republicans lazy and stupid is more likely to produce defensiveness and disengagement than civic participation.  This is exactly the behavior Pres. Trump has engaged in.

If the goal is actually higher voter turnout the research is clear — people vote when they believe their vote matters, when barriers to participation are removed, and when candidates give them something worth voting for.

None of that is addressed here or in the current crop of candidates for November.

Now to the point:
the relationship between the US and Israel is described as a two-way street, not just aid from the US to Israel. 

Based on recent reports and social posts, here’s what Israel provides:

1. Strategic military & security value • Foothold in the Middle East: 
Israel gives the US a reliable, heavily armed partner in a region with key oil routes, counterterrorism concerns, and Iranian influence. Ports like Haifa and Ashdod serve the US Navy and house emergency military stockpiles.   

• Intelligence & counterterrorism: Israel shares extensive intelligence on terrorism, cyber threats, and nuclear proliferation. Israeli officials and commentators cite intelligence as saving American lives and helping protect US troops. 
A Netanyahu interview cited a quote that Israel was worth "five CIAs" to the US.    

• Battle-tested defense tech: Joint development of missile defense like Iron Dome, David’s Sling, and Arrow. The US has also purchased Israeli systems: Trophy APS for M1 Abrams tanks, Iron Fist for Bradleys, F-35 pilot helmets, and more.   

• R&D multiplier: Since 1967, US-Israel cooperation has been described as generating >1,000% return on investment. Israel was the first to use the F-35 in combat, and fixes/improvements from Israeli experience were shared with Lockheed-Martin, saving ∼10-20 years of R&D.    

2. Technology & economic ties 
• Innovation hub: Israel spends ∼6% of GDP on R&D and hosts major centers for Intel, Microsoft, Google, Nvidia, Apple. Technologies like Waze, PillCam, Face ID/PrimeSense, drip irrigation, and cybersecurity firms Check Point, CyberArk, Palo Alto Networks are cited as Israeli contributions.   

• Trade & jobs: ∼$55B in annual bilateral trade, with the US exporting over $24B in goods/services to Israel. Israeli investment in the US exceeds $36B, with 2,500+ Israeli-founded companies supporting 250,000+ American jobs. 

• Defense industry integration: The US buys billions in Israeli defense exports annually. A new startup, Covenant, is building cruise missiles with plants in Israel, Texas, and Germany to supply the US Navy.    

3. Operational support 
• Past wartime cooperation: During the 1991 Gulf War, Israel offered military/hospital facilities, Haifa port support, and detailed tactical intelligence on Iraq.   
• Regional actions: Israel destroyed Syria’s nuclear reactor in 2007, preventing a potential US intervention. 

In 1970, Israel helped deter Syria from invading Jordan at US request.    

4. Current political proposals: “From aid to partnership”

text:
I've been thinking about immigration today, and I think sometimes Americans forget our own story.
Native Americans were already here.
Black Americans have a unique history because millions of their ancestors didn't immigrate here looking for opportunity. They were brought here by force through slavery.
But generation after generation of other Americans came from somewhere else.
English and other Europeans came seeking religious freedom.
Irish families fled famine.
Germans came amid economic hardship and political upheaval.
Italians, Poles, Russians and other Eastern and Southern Europeans came looking for work, safety and opportunity.
Chinese immigrants crossed an ocean looking for opportunity and helped build the country while facing enormous discrimination.
Indians have come seeking economic, educational and professional opportunities.
Mexicans, Central Americans, Caribbean families and people from across Africa have come for different combinations of work, safety, family and possibility.
Ukrainians are fleeing war today.
These stories aren't identical. Some people fled war or persecution. Some fled hunger or poverty. Some simply believed their children could have opportunities here that they couldn't provide at home. And sometimes people are fleeing instability in which American foreign policy has itself played a role.
And yes, countries need immigration laws. Understanding why someone comes doesn't mean everyone who arrives has a legal right to stay.
But I wish we'd leave a little room for compassion.
Leaving home isn't necessarily the dream.
Sometimes the dream is staying home. But through no fault of their own, home no longer offers the safety, stability or opportunity they need to build the future they want for themselves or their children.
So they take a chance somewhere else.
And America has benefited from generations of people taking that chance. They became workers, business owners, scientists, inventors, teachers, artists, neighbors and Americans. They brought languages, food, music, skills, ideas and traditions that became part of this country.
America isn't one thread.
It's a quilt.
Different pieces, different histories, some of them extraordinarily painful, sewn together over generations into something none of those pieces could have made alone.
