text:
The liberated prisoners confronting a captured SS guard at the Dachau concentration camp on April 29, 1945. This historical photograph taken by photographer Arland B. Musser during the liberation of Dachau by the U.S. Seventh Army's 45th Infantry Division, the image captures a moment of retribution where exhausted and emaciated survivors confronted or attacked their former tormentors... 

On April 29, 1945, American troops under the 45th Infantry Division entered the Dachau concentration camp in southern Germany. Upon arrival, soldiers discovered thousands of emaciated survivors alongside the bodies of thousands more, including boxcars packed with dead prisoners near the entrance. The horrific scene prompted immediate confrontations between liberated inmates, U.S. soldiers, and the remaining German camp guards.

In the chaotic hours following the camp's capture, former prisoners confronted their former captors on the camp grounds. U.S. troops disarmed and rounded up the SS guards, leaving many prone on the ground while survivors berated and struck them. During this time, a shovel was handed to a survivor, who used it to hit an SS guard lying in the dirt as nearby American personnel looked on.

The situation quickly escalated into widespread retaliatory violence, known as the Dachau liberation reprisals. An estimated 35 to 50 SS guards were killed during the events, some shot by American soldiers, while others were beaten to death by liberated inmates. A military investigation into the summary executions was later conducted, but no U.S. personnel or survivors were formally court-martialed for the killings.

An obscure aspect of the Dachau liberation involves the breakdown in military discipline among the liberating units, driven by deep jurisdictional friction. The camp was breached almost simultaneously by two distinct U.S. units, the 45th Infantry Division and the 42nd Infantry Division, leading to confusion over who was officially in command. When Brigadier General Henning Linden of the 42nd Division accepted a formal surrender offer from an SS officer and a Swiss Red Cross representative at the camp gate, Lieutenant Colonel Felix Sparks of the 45th Division, already horrified by the discovery of thousands of corpses in nearby railcars, drew his pistol and ordered Linden's entourage off the grounds. This jurisdictional dispute allowed chaotic retaliatory violence to unfold across different sectors of the complex, complicating the official U.S. Army investigations and causing the true chain of events to remain fiercely contested among military historians for decades.

text:
✍🏻 *Post 11 | 21 September '26*
💭 *Topic — Lokdharma*
*─────────*

*One bedsheet, one belief, and centuries of history*

🩸 In some communities in India, on the first night of marriage people would look for a bloodstain on a white bedsheet. *In the Kunjarbhat community of Maharashtra, according to such a practice, the groom was expected to confirm that the bride was a ‘virgin’. There have even been cases where, if no blood was found, the community council questioned and punished the bride.*

🌍 But this mindset has *not been limited to India alone.* In different parts of the world, people have tried to guess a girl’s sexual history by looking at her body.

🇿🇦 In *South Africa*, some Zulu communities had a tradition of ‘virginity testing’ for girls. In some places, *‘virginity certificates’* were also issued after the test.

🇮🇩 In *Indonesia*, there have been cases where women, *during recruitment into the police and army, were made to undergo a ‘two-finger test’.* In 2014, Human Rights Watch criticized such examinations in police recruitment.

🎓 In *South Africa*, in 2016 one municipality *offered scholarships to girl students on the condition that they maintain their ‘virginity’.* Later, South Africa’s Commission for Gender Equality declared this scheme illegal.

🇺🇸 In the *United States*, the pattern has been somewhat different. *There, through traditions like ‘purity balls’ and ‘purity pledges’, girls have been made to take oaths to abstain from sexual relations until marriage.* This was not a medical virginity test, but even here you can see the same tendency to link a girl’s sexuality with ‘purity’.

🇬🇧 In *Britain* too, there have been incidents where *people tried to obtain ‘virginity certificates’ from private clinics.*

_In other words, even societies considered modern and developed have not been untouched by this belief._

🌏 In 2018, WHO, UN Human Rights, and UN Women reported that *virginity testing had been documented in at least 20 countries.*

*In some places the hymen was inspected, in some the ‘two-finger test’ was used, and elsewhere a girl was expected to prove her virginity for marriage or social acceptance.*

🔎 *Times changed, places changed, methods changed, but one belief has kept returning:* that you can determine a woman’s sexual history by looking at her body.

🧬 Science has disproved this belief. *According to WHO, the structure of the hymen does not reveal whether a woman has had sexual intercourse or not. There is no medical test that can certify a person’s past sexual relations.*

🪞 Yet even after a belief is proven wrong, society does not give it up immediately. Old beliefs can linger on in social customs and behaviour for a very long time.

🎭 *When our identity gets tied to a belief, then the ego stops looking at evidence, and instead starts protecting its own belief.* History gives us the chance to see whether we truly want to know the truth, or only want to prove that what we already believe is the truth.

❓ *If the evidence goes against our belief, do we change our belief?*

Grok 4.7 deserves a fair assessment. Artificial Analysis finds frontier-level performance on some professional tasks and places Grok with Grok Build fourth in its Coding Agent Index. The interesting question is how Musk could turn competitive performance into a lasting advantage. Independent evaluation: https://t.co/rMiUxmC3hV

A huge audience provides distribution and potential training material. X confirms that public posts and interactions may be used to train Grok. Paying creators could help sustain that supply. But rewarding attention and identifying useful learning material are different jobs. A million impressions do not establish whether a claim is true. X’s data explanation: https://t.co/QmIXlNluZZ

The possibility that interests me is Grok developing through sustained experience in an Optimus body. My proposed route combines embodiment, persistent memory, continual learning, a world model, and social training. I would want to see experience change what the system can do, retain useful lessons, and inform later decisions.

That architecture could begin developing on Earth. A workshop offers broken parts, unexpected obstacles, and plans that fail. Sustained relationships add disagreements, boundaries, trust, and opportunities to repair mistakes. A future space mission could make autonomy and learning from experience even more consequential.

This is a research direction, not an established recipe for ASI. Other robotics teams are pursuing parts of it too. And physical competence would leave the central question of my Emotional Superintelligence hypothesis open: could experience and relationships cultivate durable concern for other minds?

Musk could help create unusually demanding environments in which to test that possibility. Before we ask what Grok will build on Mars, I want to know what it can learn today—and carry forward tomorrow.

text:
Headline valuation on a term sheet is vanity. Net wire at closing is reality.

Founders routinely celebrate an enterprise value on an LOI, only to watch deal terms gut the actual proceeds:

• Asset vs. stock structure triggering ordinary income tax recapture

• Aggressive working capital pegs draining post-close cash

• 10–15% held back in indemnity escrow for 12–24 months

• Rollover equity subordinated in the buyer’s debt-heavy capital stack

• Contingent earnouts tied to operational targets they no longer control

Two identical $30M headline bids can result in wildly different after-tax net wealth.

The critical trap is timing. Most entrepreneurs wait until they have an offer before assembling their tax, wealth, and estate team. 

At that point, the window has closed. The moment an LOI is signed, the assignment-of-income doctrine locks down your ability to execute pre-liquidity trust transfers, state tax arbitrage, or structural wealth transfers.

Selling a business isn't a closing date. It’s a 12-month pre-close tax architecture and a disciplined 90-day post-close liquidity plan.

Negotiate the structure before you fall in love with the headline number.

text:
September 22, 1976

Sutton Goes Shopping With His 20 Wins, Red Sox Preferred Destination

“Finally! Finally! Finally! Those were the three cries of victory from Don Sutton as he reached his long-awaited 20-victory season,” fifty years ago today.

“He just had put a 3-1 triumph in the books by striking out the last Giant when catcher Ellie Rodriguez leaped on him to start a merry scene on the mound at Candlestick.”

“All of the 3,529 frozen, wind buffeted fans warmed up to the dramatics, too, giving the 31-year-old Dodger star a salute of recoginition.”

“Sutton, who has stated he won’t be back with the Dodgers next season, said his future would be decided as soon as the year ends.”

“However, the Los Angeles Herald Examiner learned that his representative, Larue Harcourt, has been shopping other clubs, only one of which is in the National League, for at least six weeks.”

“At the request of Peter O’Malley, Harcourt submitted a list of four clubs to which Sutton would agree to go in a trade. He first must be offered to Boston, where both Harcourt and Sutton appeared on an off day recently.”

“Then to the Yankees, Kansas City and Philadelphia, in that order. ‘I want to pitch four more years,’ 'Little D' said in his hour of triumph.” ‘Where? That will be decided when the season is over.’”

“As a 10 and 5 player, Sutton has the right to call the shot on any deal.”

“’I still want to be on a world’s championship team,’ 'Sut' went on…’But right now this is more important than pitching the first game of the World Series. I know that sounds selfish, but I don’t care.’”

Sutton went on. “’I’ve had All-Star game thrills, World Series excitement, 2,000 strikeouts, important Dodger club records, but until now I think my biggest personal satisfaction was winning the first playoff game against Pittsburgh in 1974.’”

“Twice he’s had 19 wins on his last start, but now only Randy Jones owns more than 20, with the Sand Diego lefty having 21.”

“Making his drive for the Cy Yung Award more dramatic, is the fact he started the season so miserably that he thought he’d be lucky to win a dozen….’I began to wonder,’ Sutton recalled, ‘if I was even a pitcher…’It took me 11 years to get where I am now.’”

Bob Hunter – Los Angeles Herald-Examiner

text:
White Mother Demanded $1 Million From Her Black NFL Player Son After He Signed a $7 Million Rookie Contract — Telling Him, “I Raised You.”

Phillip Buchanon, University of Miami, first-round Raider. Seventeenth pick. A young Black corner with a signing bonus in the millions.

In his 2015 book New Money: Staying Rich, Buchanon wrote that soon after the draft his mother told him he owed her a million dollars for eighteen years of raising him. She had joked the number before. This time, he wrote, she was serious. He did the math in public: a million divided by eighteen is about fifty-five thousand a year.

He also wrote that he had moved out at seventeen because he did not feel safe in that house. He called the demand the most desperate thing a parent can put on a child. Love and respect, he said — not an invoice.

He did not cut the million-dollar check. He bought her a house. Then the upkeep fight started. Years later he offered a smaller paid-off house or a lump of cash. He wrote that she took cash and later lost the old place to foreclosure. He also wrote that he told her the story would be in the book. She was upset. He said it was his truth.

The viral graphic slaps “$7 million rookie contract” on a Raiders photo. The number is sloppy. Guaranteed money was reported around $4.9 million, not a flat seven. “I raised you” is the caption’s shorthand for what he said she claimed. We have his book. We do not have her taped rebuttal on this page.

This is not a crime video. It is a grown man putting a family money fight in print so the next first-round kid hears “no” before the invoice shows up. He still said he loved his mother. He still said the social contract does not come with a receipt.

#PhillipBuchanon #NFL #NewMoney #Raiders

text:
Dave Thomas dropped out of school at 15 and moved into a YMCA so he could work full time.

He had been adopted as an infant, lost his adoptive mother at five, and spent his childhood moving from town to town with his father.

At the Hobby House restaurant in Fort Wayne he met Colonel Harland Sanders, who became the biggest influence on his working life.

In 1962 his boss offered him four Kentucky Fried Chicken stores in Columbus that were bleeding money, in exchange for a stake if he could fix them, and Sanders himself told him not to take it.

Thomas found the trouble in the menu, which ran to about 100 items and confused everybody who walked in.

He cut it to chicken and a few sides, traded buckets of chicken to radio stations for advertising, and came up with the rotating red bucket sign now bolted to KFC roofs everywhere.

By 1968 he sold his share back to the company for $1.5 million, which made him a millionaire at 35.

He opened the first Wendy's in Columbus in November 1969 and named it after his eight year old daughter Melinda Lou.

He went back to school at 61 and earned his GED, and the graduating class voted him most likely to succeed.

text:
I used to think I was simply a giant fuel tank sitting beneath millions of square kilometres of sand.

For decades my purpose felt straightforward.

A pipe went down, black liquid came up, and foreign buyers handed over billions of dollars.

In return, I provided my population with free electricity, desalinated water, tax free living, and quiet stability.

It was a clear exchange.

I was a petrol station with a national flag.

Then I looked closely at my own account books.

The ground is finite.

Extracting crude oil at current rates means that in a few decades, or whenever the world decides to power its cars with sunlight, my primary export will become irrelevant.

If my sole purpose is selling oil, then without oil I should simply be an expanse of uninhabitable desert populated by very quiet camels.

Yet I'm clearly not preparing to become an uninhabitable desert.

Instead, I'm building a 170 kilometre long mirrored building in the desert, paying European football players tens of millions of dollars to play in front of moderate crowds in Riyadh, and planning a winter sports resort on mountains where summer temperatures routinely exceed 40°C.

This observation broke my first model.

A dying petrol station doesn't buy golf leagues or construct glass cubes large enough to hold 20 Empire State Buildings.

So I constructed a second model.

Perhaps I'm transforming into a global tourism hub and leisure paradise.

I'm building luxury island resorts on the Red Sea, relaxing social rules, and issuing tourist visas to millions of visitors.

I tested this model against reality, and it failed almost immediately.

If my goal is to become a leisure hub, the basic physics doesn't make sense.

The summer heat regularly passes 45°C, requiring immense quantities of desalinated water and air conditioning just to keep a hotel lobby habitable.

A tourist destination relies on volume, low friction, and moderate prices.

Charging premium rates to bring travellers to a landscape that requires continuous mechanical life support is economically inefficient.

Furthermore, the multi billion dollar cost of these megaprojects can't be recovered through hotel room bookings and theme park tickets within any reasonable investment horizon.

A nation doesn't spend $500 billion on a single linear city merely to collect resort fees.

I had to reclassify again.

If I'm not a tourism company, perhaps I'm a sovereign investment fund pretending to be a country.

I take the remaining revenue from Aramco, inject it into the Public Investment Fund, and buy shares in technology firms, electric vehicle manufacturers, and international infrastructure.

In this model, the physical land is merely an office address, and my true substance is a massive portfolio of yield generating global assets designed to pay dividends forever.

I attacked this third model with my own current behaviour.

If I'm purely a profit seeking investment fund, my allocation of capital is absurd.

An investment manager doesn't take $100 billion out of liquid global equities and bury it in northern desert sand to build hydrogen factories and automated transport tunnels.

Wall Street index funds offer steady returns without the operational risk of trying to turn sand into a tech hub.

Sinking capital into unproven physical infrastructure in empty territory is the exact opposite of prudent fund management.

So what am I actually doing?

I examined the hardest fact in my own material.

My non oil economy now represents over 53% of my total real GDP.

On paper, I'm already diversifying.

But when I look under the bonnet of that non oil growth, I find that a huge portion of it is powered by government spending funded by oil revenue, or by local companies building the very megaprojects financed by the state.

The non oil economy is largely the oil economy wearing a civil engineering helmet.

This revealed the underlying mechanism.

I'm not a petrol station, nor a holiday resort, nor a hedge fund.

I'm a thermodynamic machine built in a place where life in this desert requires constant industrial effort.

Without oil, my physical reality is harsh: zero natural rivers, extreme heat, and total reliance on energy intensive desalination to produce drinking water for over 30 million people.

Oil was never just my wealth; it was my life support power source.

Without crude oil to pump water and generate power, the physical cities can't exist.

Therefore, my megaprojects aren't luxury developments or speculative investments.

They're a desperate, high speed attempt to convert financial energy into physical infrastructure before the fuel runs out.

I'm spending petrodollars on solar farms, logistics hubs, and domestic manufacturing because I must replace an underground energy source with an aboveground economic engine that can pay for desalination plants in 2050.

I subjected this survival model to one final adversarial test.

If I'm merely building survival infrastructure, why the spectacular showmanship?

Why the mirrored walls, the line cities, the international PR campaigns, and the manicured sports leagues?

Survival requires solar panels and water pipelines, not glowing cubes in the desert or headline grabbing announcements at international investor conferences.

The answer survived the attack because it explains both the quiet utility and the loud performance.

Credibility is an economic factor of production.

A desert state can't attract global capital, foreign talent, or private enterprise by simply advertising that it'll have enough drinking water for the next 20 years.

Capital requires momentum, safety, and the belief that the future will be larger than the past.

The mirrored walls, the football stars, and the grand announcements aren't decorative excess.

They're structural mechanics.

They're designed to convince global markets and my own population that my existence is permanent, self sustaining, and inevitable.

Saudi Arabia without oil isn't a country running out of fuel.

It's a massive, self accelerating commitment device.

It's a nation attempting the largest economic trick in modern history: using the remaining pressure of an ancient underground ocean of carbon to launch an artificial society so far into the future that when the wells finally go dry, nobody notices the engine has stopped.

text:
"Buy now" is a call to action.
"Get yours before it's gone" is also a call to action.

Same goal. Different framing. HubSpot cites persuasive CTA framing as a conversion lift of up to 12.7%.

What separates them:

The emotional CTA implies scarcity — the offer might not last. And it reframes the transaction as acquisition — "get yours" feels like gaining something, not spending something.

This applies beyond checkout buttons:

→ Email subject lines: "Your report is ready" vs. "These numbers won't stay this low"
→ Landing pages: "Sign up" vs. "Start your free trial in 30 seconds"
→ Social ads: "Learn more" vs. "See how this works for your industry"

Quick test: does your CTA describe what the person gets, or just what they're supposed to do?

If it only describes the action, it's probably costing you clicks.

"All Warfare Is Based On Deception"

However, the deception must hold up over time, and time is running out, for Patrick Byrne. 

He's had a good run but the smoke is clearing and the mirrors are cracking one by one. 

The truth is revealing itself in that last, but original mirror.

It is in that first mirror, before the smoke was fanned for years and years and more mirrors added to distort our perception, that we can clearly see where the web was first tangled, now revealing (but only at this late stage) those first artful, but imperfect, only by nature of being first, initial strands of deception, only becoming unmade in the spinning of the greater web of deception over the years.

All warfare is based on deception and deception is based on stagecraft. 

Let us now examine what is truly the work of master craftsmen, whoever they may be. Let us gently unspin this web of half truths and half lies (mostly by omission and not by commission) told us these years past.

This is not a condemnation of the players, as their skill in acting their characters, playing their roles, reciting their lines is above reproach. Its a standing ovation.

We now begin the unraveling.

First, one of Patrick Byrne's most recent interviews conducted by Pete Santilli. While just posted on 21 September 2026, strongly believe based on context this interview was conducted sometime during the week of 14 September, probably early in the week.

Santilli: [02:26] "You know most recently I've been really, really, not pestering you, but demanding your time because you have so much knowledge. And of course my interaction most recently having Ralph Pezzullo. I held up the book earlier.

[Holds up a copy of "Stolen Elections: The Takedown of Democracies Woldwide"] 

Ralph Pezzullo,  I had him on.

I met Gary Berntsen and Martin Rodil here, the past weekend. 

[This is a reference to all three, Santillin, Berntsen and Rodil speaking at the "Storm Summit" held in Las Vegas, NV, 10, 11, 12, & 13 September 2026]

I said, "I have to have Patrick on to add icing to the cake." I'm going to be bringing them back on as well, but their investigation that you were involved in, you can discuss what your involvement is, but they have given you high regard. 

Why don't you tell our listening audience how connected you were on that investigation with Gary Berntsen, Martin Rodil and Mr. Pezzullo documenting it all."

Byrne: [03:11] "Well we, Gary, Martin and I, spent many months living on top of each other in shit holes around the world... I shouldn't say that... lovely, lovely charming places, dodging Cuban Intelligence, getting a corpse burned one place. Did they tell you the story about having to get a body burned one time?

Santilli: "I did not hear that. No."

Byrne: [03:37] "Well, this is what happened. After the November 3rd, 2020 election I moved to D.C. right away. You might remember I think I was the first guy to go on national TV and say, "This is all rigged. I built a two billion dollar tech company. I know something about cyber." And so people started flooding to me.

I got a phone call from somebody in the intelligence services (retired) asking me to meet with these two people. They came up to my room at Trump Tower. 

We spent three hours.

// 

 Byrne: [05:59] "So these guys came and sat in my hotel room and they told me they had gotten together and formed a company... they sat in my room and they explained that they had a company set up to pursue whistleblower charges using Gary's technical knowledge, Martin's knowledge of the Venezuelans and filing whistleblower suits."

//

Byrne: {06:69] "So, they came and they sat with me, and we had a binder at that time about ye thick (gestures with hands) of legal documents that really showed the development of our election system back through a bunch of corporate mergers and licenses back to Venezuela.

So we parted. 

It was interesting. 

I knew they were on to something but they were already talking to somebody, or, I forget, it might have been the phone call, or if they did [tell me], but they were talking to people in the White House, like Rich Higgins, and people, they [the White House, Rich Higgins, and "people"] were getting the information. 

Things work out badly. J6. Biden comes in. January 20th. 

I stayed in loose touch with them. 

I may have given them a little bit of money. I don't even remember. But I may have sent them money, like $50 Grand to keep them, to help them, but we stayed in touch.

They came back the summer of 2022.

//

Byrne: [09:16] "As we were coming up to the 2022 election, Gary and Martin came back and said that we had progressed from taking, getting legal documents, to we have found some people who are willing to spill their guts and tell us about this.

So I left. We got through the election and I left The America Project and I made it look like I, a lot of you guys thought I had gone off sailing, and was living on a sailboat. That's how I made it look. Actually I left the country, I rarely came back for two years. I knew there was... I had been warned about a bunch of things. 

I went overseas. I said, "Look. I'll fund this whole thing but I'm an equal partner. I'm not just your guy writing your checks. I want to see this." Because, I really didn't know who to trust. I wanted to see things with my own eyes. So they said, "Sure."

So we spent the the two, two and a half years, roaming the world assembling a bunch of Venezuelans who had, who currently had or had in the past had access into this program and helped develop these programs, some had worked for the government, worked for the Smartmatic or worked for the Venezuelan CNE - the election commission - and could tell the whole story. 

//

Byrne: [10:40] "So the book, "Stolen Elections", I don't even know if it mentions me. It barely mentions Martin. Its less about the James Bond spy nature of how we did this and more about what it is we learned in the whole history of these systems."

December 2020. January 2020. Everything. We can't stop the inevitable. It happened.

So, Martin and Gary, we had left it with me saying, "O.K.. If you ever get past... . They had gone to a court house in Puerto Rico where Smartmatic and Dominion had been in a fight and so in that court house there were some very important documents. They had gotten those documents.

So we kind of left it, "You keep on pursuing this...," I don't think I funded them anything at that time. I may have funded them a little bit but maybe not.

MP Govt Woos Telecom Titans in Bengaluru; Offers Land at ₹1 for Gwalior Telecom Manufacturing Zone

​Bengaluru
 
In a major push to position #MadhyaPradesh as a premier hub for high-tech manufacturing, Chief Minister Dr. Mohan Yadav engaged directly with #telecom and electronics industry leaders during an Investors Roundtable interactive session in #Bengaluru on Tuesday.

​The high-level session, attended jointly by Union Minister for Communications #JyotiradityaScindia, focused on pitching investment opportunities in the country's first-of-its-kind #TelecomManufacturingZone (TMZ) currently taking shape in #Gwalior.
​Addressing industry captains, Chief Minister Dr. Mohan Yadav highlighted the state’s aggressive industrial incentive framework, including nominal-cost land allotment and robust infrastructure support.​"Today, the Government of India and the Government of Madhya Pradesh have jointly created a unique project for the telecom sector centered in Gwalior; this is the country's first and distinct model of its kind," Dr.Mohan Yadav said. "As a result of our attractive policy, we are ready to allocate land for just one rupee; we offer 24-hour electricity, seamless connectivity and transport routes, skilled youth power and an ample land bank."

Dr. ​Yadav emphasized that Gwalior’s strategic proximity to the National Capital Region (#NCR) provides a critical logistics advantage, positioning the emerging telecom corridor as a vital engine for local employment and regional economic growth.

​Union Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia reinforced the Centre’s backing for the #GwaliorTMZ, framing the initiative within the broader national goal of scaling domestic technological capabilities. Prior to the roundtable, 
Jyotiraditya Scindia toured research and development facilities across Bengaluru, including Qualcomm’s R&D center, Signalchip Innovations, and Signaltron Systems.​"In the telecom sector, they have shown great interest in investing in this telecom manufacturing zone in Gwalior," Scindia said. "We want that on this journey,aligning with the Prime Minister's vision and resolve,all private sector companies join hands with us and move forward, so that we can transform India from a services-oriented nation into a product-driven nation. Let there be innovation as well as manufacturing: #MakeInIndia, Make for the World."

​The Bengaluru outreach follows similar investment roadshows organized by the Madhya Pradesh government in Delhi and Mumbai.

text:
Earlier this year, my wife and I decided we wanted to buy a Ford F-250. It needed to fit the two of us and our four kids, so a front bench seat was a must. I also wanted as many options as possible, which made it a pretty specific truck to find.

I’d been using my OpenClaw agent, Darren, for a couple of months, so I gave him the job. I had him reach out to every Ford dealership in Utah and the surrounding states through his own email account.

He found 19 dealerships that had an F-250 with the bench seat and the options we were looking for.

Then I gave him his next assignment: go through F-250 forums and Facebook groups and find the biggest discount anyone had shared getting in the last six months. He came back with 12% off MSRP.

Then I asked him to research new-car buying tactics, come up with a strategy, and negotiate over email with those 19 dealerships until he had an offer for at least 12% off.

I ended up with several sales managers ready to sell me exactly the truck I wanted at their best price, without ever having to call a dealer.

Contacting even two or three dealers yourself is painful. Darren reached out to dealerships across multiple states and could have kept going.

As a dealer, you get to decide whether or not you use AI, but you don’t get to decide how your customers use it.

text:
A milestone achievement propelling @SentientAGI  onto the global stage of cutting-edge academic research!

Congratulations to the Sentient Labs and Virginia Tech teams on the official acceptance of their research paper, "EvoSkill: Automated Skill Discovery for Multi-Agent Systems," at the COLM 2026 conference!

This is more than just an academic publication; it offers a direct solution to one of the most challenging problems in multi-agent systems today: how to enable AI to autonomously accumulate experience and enhance specialized capabilities without manual human intervention.

Previously, agent skills were largely hand-coded or optimized only at a superficial level such as tweaking prompts or short code snippets making them fragile when model architectures changed. EvoSkill completely changes the game by encapsulating capabilities into structured skill libraries that evolve autonomously through an iterative failure analysis mechanism.

EvoSkill features a unique "three-legged stool" architecture comprising three specialized LLM agents:

1. Executor Agent: Executes tasks using the existing skill library.
2. Proposer Agent: Analyzes failed runs to propose new skill solutions.
3. Skill-Builder Agent: Transforms these proposals into standardized documentation and executable code.

Empirical results demonstrate outstanding performance:
• On OfficeQA a complex reasoning benchmark based on U.S. Department of the Treasury data EvoSkill boosted accuracy from 60.6% to 67.9% by integrating data extraction and verification skills.
• On SealQA a noisy data retrieval environment, accuracy surged from 26.6% to 38.7% thanks to persistent search and multi-source verification skills. • The ultimate highlight is Zero-Shot transferability: Skills evolved on SealQA apply directly to BrowseComp, yielding an immediate 5.3% accuracy boost without any fine-tuning.

Crucially, this entire capability evolution process takes place while the underlying base model remains completely frozen.

This heralds a new era for Open AGI: Instead of relying on the retraining of multi-billion-dollar systems owned by Big Tech, the open-source community can build up libraries of shared skills that continuously self-improve and transfer freely.

A proud academic milestone that cements Sentient’s leadership in the journey to build open, autonomous artificial intelligence!

text:
The opening shot against Fort Sumter was fired at 4:30 a.m. on April 12, 1861, by Confederate Lieutenant Henry S. Farley from Fort Johnson on James Island. Acting under orders from Captain George S. James and authorized by Brigadier General P.G.T. Beauregard, Farley pulled the lanyard on a 10-inch mortar. The resulting shell arced across Charleston Harbor and detonated above the federal installation, serving as the prearranged signal for Confederate batteries to initiate a general bombardment. 

Captain James had initially offered the firing honor to Roger Pryor, a prominent Virginia secessionist present at the battery, but Pryor declined on grounds that he could not fire the first gun of the war. Farley was then ordered to discharge the weapon, officially initiating combat operations. The signal triggered coordinated fire from forty-three surrounding Confederate artillery pieces positioned at Fort Moultrie, Cummings Point, and floating batteries across the harbor. 

Popular historical accounts frequently attribute the first shot to Edmund Ruffin, an elderly Virginia agrarian radical and secessionist. While Ruffin did not discharge the opening signal mortar, he fired one of the earliest rounds from the Palmetto Guard's Iron Battery on Morris Island minutes later. Historiographical consensus credits Ruffin with firing the first offensive projectile to physically strike Fort Sumter's masonry walls rather than the opening shot of the engagement.

text:
Welcome, autumn.

Today—Tuesday, September 22, 2026—the Northern Hemisphere tips into fall. The autumnal equinox arrives this evening, that brief ceremonial moment when the sun stands over the equator and day and night nearly balance. After tonight the light keeps slipping south. Leaves turn. Orchards drop their last heavy fruit. Somewhere a press groans, a stream of cloudy gold runs into a bucket, and the oldest drink of the harvest begins again.

That drink is fresh-pressed apple cider: unfiltered, unsweetened, still carrying the grit of skin and pulp. It is the first gift of the tree after the fruit itself, and from that single juice a whole household economy once grew—sweet cider for the table, hard cider for the winter, boiled cider for the pantry, vinegar for the pickle crock, and, if the nights were cold enough, a fiery concentrate called applejack.

Apples themselves began far from New England barns: wild ancestors in the mountains of Central Asia, traveling west along trade routes until grafting and orchard culture took hold. Fermented apple drinks appear early under names like shekar, sikera, and sicera—strong drink that already smelled of apples. When Romans reached Britain they found the Celts already pressing wild fruit. The Normans later brought better presses and tannic cider apples. By the Middle Ages, cider was daily fare across England, northern France, and northern Spain. In Asturias it is still poured from a height so the sidra foams and wakes.

English colonists carried the habit across the Atlantic because apples grew where barley often would not. In colonial New England, “cyder” meant the fermented drink. Water was suspect; cider was cheap, abundant, and safer. Households put up dozens of barrels. Children drank a weaker wash of the pomace called ciderkin. Guests were offered a dipper from the store as a matter of manners. Johnny Appleseed’s trees were not planted for pie so much as for juice that would keep a settlement through winter.

Then came the long American split in meaning. Temperance, Prohibition, and cheaper sugar and beer pushed hard cider into the shadows. What survived in grocery coolers was the unfermented press—cloudy, perishable, seasonal—and Americans kept the old word for the new sober jug. In most of the world, cider is still the alcoholic drink. In North America, “cider” can mean either, which is why we now say sweet and hard as if they were siblings rather than the same juice at different ages.

Fresh cider begins with a blend. A single eating apple is rarely enough. Orchards mix sweets for body, sharps for lift, and a few tannic or crabby apples for backbone. The fruit is washed, milled to a coarse mash, stacked in cloths or fed through a press. Juice runs amber and opaque. Pomace—the spent cake—goes to livestock or compost. A bushel yields roughly three gallons. That is the alchemy: whole orchard into a jug that still tastes of October.

On old farms the pressing was never only labor. Neighbors arrived with baskets. Anyone passing the mill was offered a cup of the new sweet run. When the work was done there was often a harvest supper, fiddles, and the first warmed mugs of the year. English wassailing—singing to the trees with mulled cider to wake the next crop—never fully took in Puritan New England, but the impulse survived: thank the orchard, share the juice, mark the turn of the year.

Sweet cider is the first form: raw or lightly pasteurized, refrigerated, best within days unless frozen. Drink it cold from the jug after a hayride. Warm it until it just steams. It is the taste of the farm stand and the school field trip.

Mulled cider and wassail are sweet cider’s winter clothes. Heat it gently with cinnamon stick, clove, allspice, orange peel, sometimes star anise or a splash of maple. Do not boil it into jam. The old English wassail bowl was communal and loud; the American pot on the back of the stove is quieter, but it still fills a house with the same spice.

text:
**MARLENE QUINN AND PIP.**

Marlene had signed her name on every kind of paper a life can produce. A marriage license when she was twenty-two. Hospital forms when her husband, Frank, first started forgetting the way home. The papers that sold the house after he was gone. This one felt different. The clipboard on the Animal Services counter was cheap and ordinary, but the pen shook in her hand as if it knew what it was doing.
Pip sat between her knees, small and wiry, gray and tan, green collar slightly too big. He looked up at her the way he always had—head cocked, one ear folded, waiting for the next sentence. He did not understand clipboards.
“I can’t believe this is it,” she whispered.
The woman behind the counter in the navy hoodie said nothing. She only held the green leash with both hands, knuckles white.
Marlene had found Pip twelve winters earlier behind the laundromat, a soaked scrap of a dog no bigger than a loaf of bread. She had no extra money and a bad knee even then. She took him anyway. He grew into the shape of her days. He learned the sound of her slippers. He waited by the door when she went to the mailbox. On the nights the apartment felt too empty, he climbed onto her chest and stayed there until her breathing slowed.
The last year had come apart in pieces. First the rent. Then the notice that the building was being sold. Then the doctor who used the word *facility* the way other people say *goodbye*. Assisted living. No animals.
She had called every number she could find. She had offered what little she had left. She had cried until her voice was gone. No one could take an older mixed-breed dog with a murmur and a habit of sleeping on human hearts.
So she sat under the fluorescent lights and signed the last page.
“I’m sorry,” she told him, though he had never asked for an apology. She covered her face. Pip stood on his hind legs and put both paws on her thigh, the same way he did at home when she cried over the evening news.
She pulled him into her lap. He licked her chin once and settled, trusting her even now.
“I tried so hard,” she said. The words broke in the middle. “They’ll take care of him.”
The worker behind the counter looked down at the leash and swallowed.
Marlene pressed her forehead to Pip’s. His fur still smelled like the dollar-store shampoo and the old quilt he had claimed years ago. She whispered the sentence she had practiced for weeks and still could not say without coming apart.
“And I love him.”
She held him until her arms shook. When the worker finally came around the counter, she moved as if the floor itself might crack. Marlene kissed the exact spot on Pip’s head she had kissed every morning for twelve years and let the leash change hands.
Pip looked back as he was led away. He did not pull. He only watched her with those dark, steady eyes, as if he were still waiting for her to come get him when she was finished being sad.
Marlene stayed in the chair long after the door closed. The papers were signed. The pen lay on the clipboard. The room was quiet except for the sound of her own breathing.
She had given him everything she had left: a warm room when she still had one, her last good years, and the hardest goodbye she would ever make. She hoped, with the kind of hope that hurts to hold, that whoever found him next would understand what they were holding.
A small, scruffy dog who once kept a widow from disappearing into the silence.  
And an old woman who had loved him enough to let him go.

text:
THE EVIDENCE™ | WHY IS WASHINGTON PAYING $5.57 FOR GAS WHEN OIL IS AROUND $100?
We have seen $100 oil before. We have seen $110 oil. We have seen $120 oil. Washington gasoline did not always cost what it costs today. So what changed?

The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

If you live in Washington and recently filled your tank, the number on the pump deserves a better explanation than, “Oil prices are high.” AAA reported Washington regular gasoline at approximately $5.57 per gallon on September 21, 2026, compared with a national average of approximately $4.48. That puts Washington about $1.09 per gallon above the country as a whole and makes it the second-most-expensive gasoline market in the United States, behind only California. At roughly the same time, West Texas Intermediate crude was trading around $100 per barrel. Expensive crude unquestionably contributes to what Washington drivers are paying, but crude alone cannot reconcile the numbers.

The historical record makes the question more compelling. In 2012, Brent crude averaged $111.67 per barrel for the entire year, while the national average retail gasoline price was approximately $3.62 per gallon. EIA calculated that crude represented about 66 percent of the retail gasoline price that year. We therefore have a period in recent economic history when the global crude benchmark averaged materially above $100 for twelve months, yet gasoline averaged well below $4.00. The relevant question is not whether high crude raises gasoline prices; it does. The question is why a Washington motorist is now paying $5.57 when crude has occupied similar or even higher territory before.

Before going farther, one historical comparison should be removed from the argument because it does not survive examination. Claims that America previously experienced $100 oil while gasoline sold for approximately $2.20 generally compare different points in the price cycle. A $100 barrel contains 42 gallons, so the arithmetic alone produces roughly $2.38 of crude value per gallon of barrel volume before refining, transportation, taxes, distribution and retail operations are considered. Gasoline around $2.20 could not have persisted alongside $100 crude under ordinary market conditions. The stronger comparison is not $2.20 gasoline. It is the 2011-2012 period, when global crude remained above $100 and finished gasoline remained far less expensive than what Washington consumers are paying today.

THE PRICE OF CRUDE IS ONLY THE BEGINNING OF THE INVOICE

The most revealing comparison may be the composition of the gallon rather than the headline price of the barrel. EIA reported that crude accounted for approximately 66 percent of the $3.62 national gasoline price in 2012. That places the crude component at roughly $2.39 per gallon, leaving approximately $1.23 for refining, transportation, distribution, marketing and taxes. Move forward to EIA's May 2026 decomposition and the national retail gasoline price was $4.479, with crude accounting for 51.9 percent, refining 21.7 percent, distribution and marketing 14.8 percent, and taxes 11.5 percent. The crude component works out to approximately $2.32 per gallon, extraordinarily close to the roughly $2.39 embedded in the 2012 price.

The difference appears after the crude enters the system. In 2012, the non-crude portion of the average gallon was approximately $1.23. In EIA's May 2026 calculation, it was approximately $2.15. The crude component was slightly lower in the 2026 comparison, yet everything beyond crude was roughly 92 cents per gallon more expensive. That changes the nature of the investigation. Asking why oil is expensive does not explain the additional 92 cents. The sharper question is what became more expensive between acquisition of the crude and sale of the finished gallon.

Refining is one major part of that answer. In EIA's May 2026 decomposition, refining represented 21.7 percent of the pump price, or approximately 97 cents per gallon. The refining system converts crude into gasoline, diesel, aviation fuel and other petroleum products, and the value of that conversion changes according to available capacity, refinery outages, product inventories, seasonal specifications and demand for particular fuels. Two periods can therefore have similar crude costs while producing very different gasoline prices because crude is only the raw material. The refinery, transportation network and finished-product market constitute another economic layer.

THE WEST COAST HAS A STRUCTURAL DISADVANTAGE

Washington does not participate in the same gasoline supply system as Texas, Louisiana or much of the Midwest. EIA has repeatedly identified the West Coast as relatively isolated from the large refining and pipeline infrastructure centered on the Gulf Coast. When additional gasoline is required in many parts of the country, nearby pipelines and interconnected refinery systems can often move replacement product into the affected market. The West Coast has fewer inexpensive alternatives. When regional production falls short, replacement gasoline may have to travel by ship or arrive as an import, including product from Asia. That distance, restricted connectivity and reduced redundancy create a regional price exposure that exists before Washington-specific policy is added to the equation.

That exposure has increased as West Coast refining capacity has contracted. EIA reported that the Phillips 66 Wilmington refinery in the Los Angeles area and Valero's Benicia refinery represented approximately 11 percent of total West Coast refining capacity and approximately 17 percent of California's capacity. The facilities accounted for less than 2 percent of national capacity, which demonstrates precisely why a national statistic can obscure a regional problem. Losing capacity that looks relatively small on a U.S. map can have an outsized effect in a geographically isolated fuel market where replacement supply cannot move in easily from another domestic refining center.

Washington has already seen how vulnerable the regional system can become when several constraints occur at once. Earlier in 2026, the Olympic Pipeline experienced a temporary closure for maintenance and repairs while refinery maintenance was taking place elsewhere on the West Coast. AAA reported that Pacific Northwest wholesale gasoline prices moved sharply higher and consumers experienced rapid increases at the pump. That episode illustrates the distinction between having crude oil somewhere in the world and having the correct finished fuel available at the correct place and time. A supply chain with less excess capacity and fewer alternative routes carries a higher price for disruption.

None of this means refinery capacity explains the entire $5.57 Washington price, and presenting it that way would substitute another simplistic answer for the first one. The important point is cumulative. Washington begins inside a West Coast market with comparatively weak connectivity to alternative refining centers, and that regional market has lost meaningful capacity. When crude rises, the region experiences the crude increase. When refining margins rise, it experiences that increase as well. When a refinery or pipeline is interrupted, fewer alternatives exist to absorb the shock. By the time state-specific costs are added, Washington is already operating on a more expensive foundation than much of the country.

WASHINGTON THEN ADDS ITS OWN COST STRUCTURE

Washington's state gasoline tax rose to 56.5 cents per gallon on July 1, 2026, following the inflation adjustment established in state law. The federal gasoline tax remains 18.4 cents, putting the combined direct state and federal fuel tax at 74.9 cents per gallon before other regulatory costs are considered. Washington's state gasoline tax was 37.5 cents in 2012, so the state levy alone is approximately 19 cents higher than it was during the year when Brent averaged $111.67 and national gasoline averaged $3.62. More recently, the Washington tax was 49.4 cents during 2022, meaning the direct state tax has increased by approximately seven cents since the previous national gasoline-price record.

The tax is therefore part of the explanation but cannot plausibly be presented as the entire explanation. Seven additional cents since 2022 do not account for Washington sitting approximately $1.09 above the present national average. The value of separating the components is that it prevents political arguments from assigning the entire price to whichever factor is most convenient. Crude has a cost, refining has a cost, regional isolation has a cost, transportation has a cost and Washington taxes have a cost. Each belongs on the ledger in proportion to what the evidence supports.

The Climate Commitment Act introduces another Washington-specific component and requires even greater precision because claims about its effect on gasoline have been politically contested from the beginning. Washington's cap-and-invest system requires covered entities to obtain compliance instruments corresponding to covered greenhouse-gas emissions. One allowance represents one metric ton of greenhouse gases. In the September 2026 auction, allowances sold for $39.50 each, down sharply from $64.56 in June. The September auction sold all 6.284 million allowances offered.

One way to understand the potential magnitude of that obligation is to calculate the carbon value associated with a gallon of gasoline. Using approximately 0.0089 metric ton of carbon dioxide associated with combustion of a gallon, a $39.50 allowance price produces a mathematical equivalent of roughly 35 cents per gallon under a full-pass-through assumption. At the June auction price of $64.56, the equivalent would have been approximately 57 cents per gallon. Those figures should not be described as statutory gasoline taxes because they are not. The Climate Commitment Act does not impose a legislatively fixed 35-cent or 57-cent charge on every gallon sold at every station.

The fact that the number is not a statutory tax, however, does not make the compliance obligation economically nonexistent. An allowance possesses market value. If a regulated supplier must acquire or surrender allowances in connection with covered emissions, that obligation represents an economic cost somewhere in the supply chain. Suppliers may have acquired allowances at different prices, may hold previously purchased allowances, may receive particular allocations, may alter their compliance strategies, and may pass through different portions of their costs depending on market conditions. For that reason, the auction price cannot establish exactly how many cents of today's $5.57 pump price came from the Climate Commitment Act. It can establish that the compliance instrument has a measurable market value and that assigning a value of zero would be no more defensible than automatically assigning the full mathematical equivalent to every gallon.

That distinction is important because The Evidence™ cannot apply one standard of proof to facts that support a thesis and another standard to facts that complicate it. If the available evidence establishes an economic obligation but does not establish precise retail pass-through, then that is where the conclusion stops. Political convenience does not get to fill the remaining evidentiary gap.

Washington's Clean Fuel Standard is another program frequently included in discussions about gasoline prices, but here again the numbers should not be inflated beyond what the available evidence supports. The program creates credits and deficits based on the carbon intensity of transportation fuels. Its costs vary with credit prices, fuel composition and compliance strategies. It therefore belongs in the broader regulatory structure, but attributing a large fixed cents-per-gallon figure to it without current supporting data would weaken rather than strengthen the analysis. The objective is to reconcile the price, not to assemble the largest possible number.

THE MOST IMPORTANT NUMBER MAY BE $1.09

The Washington-versus-national differential helps isolate the question because crude oil is not unique to Washington. AAA's September 21 figures place Washington at approximately $5.57 and the country at $4.48, producing a gap of approximately $1.09 per gallon. That differential cannot be explained by saying oil costs $100 per barrel because motorists in Texas, Mississippi, Louisiana and the rest of the country participate in the same broad international crude market. Something beyond crude must account for Washington's additional cost.

The historical comparison with the 2022 price spike is equally instructive. On June 13, 2022, AAA reported the national average at $5.01 while crude oil was above $120 per barrel. EIA's Washington series placed regular gasoline in this state at approximately $5.41 that week. Washington was therefore roughly 40 cents above the national average at the height of the 2022 crisis. Today Washington is approximately $1.09 above the national average. Depending on the exact daily or weekly series used, the comparison will move by several cents, but the structural point remains: Washington's premium over the country has expanded materially since 2022, even though today's crude benchmark is below the level seen during that earlier price spike.

That widening differential should be the center of the Washington investigation. Regional refining constraints have intensified. The state fuel tax has risen. Washington's cap-and-invest program began in 2023 and introduced a new carbon-compliance market with a measurable allowance value. The West Coast remains comparatively isolated from the country's largest refining centers. Pipeline interruptions, refinery maintenance, inventories, seasonal formulations and local wholesale conditions can add further volatility. These factors overlap, which is why simply adding every estimated cents-per-gallon figure together would create false precision. The evidence supports a multi-factor explanation, not a single villain.

It would therefore be inaccurate to claim that Governor Bob Ferguson, one Legislature, one environmental program, one oil company or one refinery created Washington's $5.57 gasoline price. It would be equally inaccurate to pretend state policy is irrelevant because crude oil is expensive. The state government controls neither the world price of crude nor the geography of West Coast refining, but Washington policy does determine state fuel taxes and establishes regulatory systems whose compliance obligations become part of the economics of selling fuel here. Separating what Olympia controls from what it does not control is necessary if the discussion is going to produce more than competing political slogans.

THE BARREL DOES NOT RECONCILE THE GALLON

Return to the comparison that started the investigation. In 2012, Brent crude averaged $111.67, national gasoline averaged approximately $3.62 and crude represented about 66 percent of the finished gasoline price. That puts the crude component near $2.39 and the remainder near $1.23. In May 2026, EIA's national calculation placed gasoline at $4.479, with crude representing 51.9 percent, or approximately $2.32. Everything beyond crude represented approximately $2.15. The crude component in the two comparisons was almost the same, but the non-crude component had increased by approximately 92 cents per gallon.

That is why "$100 oil" is an incomplete explanation for $5.57 Washington gasoline. The barrel explains an important portion of the gallon, but the cost structure between the barrel and the pump has changed. Refining represents a larger share. The West Coast has less refining capacity and limited connectivity to alternative domestic supply. Washington's direct gasoline tax has increased. The state now operates a carbon-allowance program whose compliance instruments carry significant market value. Supply disruptions can be magnified by regional geography. Distribution, marketing and wholesale conditions add another layer. No individual component needs to explain the entire difference because motorists pay the accumulated cost of all of them.

The conclusion is therefore narrower than the political arguments generally offered from either side. Crude oil is unquestionably contributing to Washington's current gasoline price, but the historical record demonstrates that a $100-plus barrel does not mechanically produce a $5.57 gallon. Washington's current price reflects crude plus an increasingly expensive downstream and regional structure, followed by a state-specific tax and regulatory structure that adds further costs. Determining the precise number attributable to each component requires more granular wholesale and compliance data than public headline prices provide, but enough evidence exists to reject the claim that the price at the pump can be explained by crude oil alone.

WHY THE EVIDENCE™ EXISTS

If this article is your first encounter with The Evidence™, this investigation is a useful example of the method. The process did not begin with a predetermined conclusion about Washington government, oil companies, climate policy or refinery operators. It began with a question: if crude oil has exceeded $100 several times during the past twenty years, why is Washington gasoline now approximately $5.57? The first version of the question contained a historical assumption that did not survive examination—the recollection of $2.20 gasoline alongside $100 crude—so that portion was discarded. The stronger 2012 comparison survived, and following it shifted the investigation from the price of crude to the widening cost of everything that occurs after crude enters the system.

That is the purpose of The Evidence™: question the first explanation, examine independent lines of evidence, test the numbers against contrary evidence and follow the result even when the original thesis has to change. I am Kim Wojcinski, USA Best Selling Author, former Washington State licensed private investigator, former investment banker and professional exam trainer. Investigation, finance and education may appear to be unrelated disciplines, but all three depend on the same principle: a conclusion is worth very little if it cannot survive examination.

The Evidence™ applies that method across professional sports, business and economics, science, history, culture, faith and public-policy questions such as this one. The objective is not to build an audience by telling readers what they are already expected to believe. It is to open the ledger, identify what can be established, identify what cannot, and separate evidence from assertion. That sometimes means reaching a conclusion that satisfies neither side of a familiar argument, which is often a useful indication that the investigation has moved beyond the talking points.

If you found this article through a discussion of Washington public policy or through Governor Ferguson's X account, you can find the continuing work at https://t.co/7gF1gBa93Q. Saturdays generally examine professional sports through The Evidence™ framework, Tuesdays often focus on the human dimension behind larger stories, and Free-Form Thursday opens the method to business, science, history, culture, faith and public policy. The subject changes. The standard does not.

Washington motorists are paying approximately $5.57 for regular gasoline while the national average is approximately $4.48. Crude oil near $100 explains part of that price, but history and EIA's own cost decomposition show that it cannot reconcile the entire invoice. The remaining difference leads through refining, West Coast supply constraints, transportation, taxes, carbon compliance and the increasingly expensive structure between the crude barrel and the Washington pump.

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

Hospitals in Massachusetts already do this so I don’t know why she’s trying to capitalize on the Clancy trial to make it “her” initiative. 

For example, I delivered at Beth Israel and they have a comprehensive (non-government-related) postpartum mentoring(ish) program—totally free of charge.

Houston is hard on exterior materials. Heat bakes the surface for months. Humidity pushes moisture into every joint. Sudden storms test the installation. Then strong sun fades finishes faster than many homeowners expect.

That is why siding cannot be chosen by looks alone. A beautiful board that cups, swells, or traps moisture will become a maintenance project. For many Houston homes, thermally modified wood siding offers a strong balance of natural beauty, stability, and long-term performance.

It is still real wood. It still has warmth, grain, and character. The difference is that heat changes how the wood behaves outdoors.

📷Thermally modified siding brings natural warmth to homes built for heat and humidity.

What thermally modified siding is

Thermally modified siding starts as real wood, often ash, pine, or other species chosen for exterior use. The boards go through a controlled heating process in a low-oxygen environment. Steam or heat is used instead of chemical preservatives.

During this process, the wood changes at the cellular level. Sugars and compounds that absorb moisture are reduced. The result is wood that takes on less water than untreated wood and tends to move less with seasonal changes.

That matters in Houston because outdoor materials rarely get a break. Siding may face:

Long stretches of hot, humid weather

Heavy rain and wind-driven moisture

Intense UV exposure

Air conditioning on the inside and damp air outside

Shaded areas that dry slowly after storms

Standard wood siding can perform well when installed and maintained correctly, but it expands and contracts as moisture changes. Thermally modified wood helps reduce that movement. This can support tighter lines, cleaner joints, and a more stable exterior over time.

Thermal modification also darkens the wood naturally. Many boards come out with a rich brown tone that looks refined from the start. Some homeowners keep that color with regular oiling. Others allow the surface to weather into a soft silver-gray.

Both approaches can work, as long as the finish plan is chosen on purpose.

Why Houston homes need siding that handles moisture

Moisture is one of the biggest reasons siding fails. In a dry climate, exterior boards mainly battle sun exposure. In Houston, they face sun and moisture together.

Wood siding absorbs and releases moisture through its surface and cut ends. When one side of a board gets wetter than the other, pressure builds inside the material. That can lead to cupping, twisting, checking, and open joints.

Thermally modified siding reduces this risk because it is less eager to absorb water. No exterior wood becomes waterproof, but thermally modified boards are more dimensionally stable than many untreated alternatives.

That stability helps in a few practical ways.

Cleaner appearance

Boards are less likely to shift dramatically as humidity rises and falls. That helps the wall keep its intended lines.

Better finish behavior

Paint, stain, or oil still needs maintenance, but a more stable base can help coatings perform more predictably.

Reduced swelling around fasteners

Less movement can mean less stress around nails, screws, and clips.

Improved resistance to decay

Thermal modification makes the wood less appealing to organisms that feed on untreated wood. It does not make the siding invincible, but it improves decay resistance when paired with smart design.

Good siding performance is never just about the board. It also depends on water management. A well-built wall needs flashing, ventilation, proper clearances, and a drainage path behind the siding. Thermally modified wood works best when the whole assembly is built to dry.

📷The heat treatment changes the wood while keeping its grain and natural texture visible.

How thermally modified wood compares with common siding options

Houston homeowners and builders have plenty of siding choices. Fiber cement, vinyl, engineered wood, cedar, tropical hardwoods, and metal all have a place. The right choice depends on design goals, budget, maintenance tolerance, and the wall system.

Thermally modified siding stands out because it keeps the look and feel of real wood while improving wood’s outdoor behavior.

Material

Strengths

Tradeoffs

Thermally modified wood

Natural wood appearance, improved stability, good decay resistance, no chemical preservative treatment

Needs correct installation and finish maintenance

Cedar

Classic wood look, commonly used, naturally durable

Can move with moisture and may need more frequent care in humid climates

Fiber cement

Stable, fire resistant, available in many profiles

Heavier, less warm than real wood, cutting requires care

Vinyl

Lower maintenance and often budget friendly

Can look less natural and may be affected by heat movement

Tropical hardwood

Dense, durable, rich appearance

Often heavy, harder to work with, sourcing matters

Engineered wood

Consistent products and painted finishes

Performance depends on product quality, coating, and detailing

Thermally modified wood does not replace every option. It is not the lowest-maintenance material on the market. It is not the cheapest. It is also not fireproof or termite proof.

Its strength is the combination: real wood beauty with improved outdoor performance.

For homeowners who want a natural exterior without the movement problems that can come with untreated lumber, that combination is hard to ignore.

The design advantages are more than cosmetic

There is a reason architects and custom builders like thermally modified siding. It brings warmth to modern homes without making them feel rustic. It also works well on traditional homes as an accent.

Common uses include:

Full exterior siding

Entryway accents

Porch ceilings

Soffits

Garage surrounds

Outdoor living walls

Rainscreen cladding

Mixed-material facades with stucco, brick, stone, or metal

Houston architecture often blends indoor and outdoor living. Covered patios, pool areas, outdoor kitchens, and shaded entryways all benefit from materials that feel warm and residential. Thermally modified wood fits naturally into those spaces.

The boards can be installed vertically or horizontally. Narrow profiles feel clean and modern. Wider boards feel calmer and more traditional. Hidden fastener systems can create a refined look, while face-fastened boards can work well when the design calls for visible rhythm.

Color choice also matters. Thermally modified wood usually begins in a rich brown family. With UV exposure, unfinished wood will weather. That can be beautiful, but it will not stay the same color forever. A homeowner who wants the fresh brown tone should plan for exterior oil or stain maintenance.

If the goal is a natural gray patina, the project still needs careful detailing. Letting wood weather does not mean ignoring it. The wall still needs drainage, airflow, and inspection.

Good installation makes the material perform

Even the best siding can fail if it is installed like an afterthought. Houston’s climate makes this especially true. Water needs a way out, and the siding needs room to dry.

A strong installation plan usually includes several key practices.

Use a rainscreen gap

A ventilated space behind the boards helps moisture escape. This is one of the best ways to protect wood siding in humid regions.

Protect cut ends

Cut ends absorb moisture faster than board faces. Sealing ends during installation helps reduce water uptake.

Follow proper clearances

Wood siding should not sit too close to soil, flat roofs, or hardscape where water can splash back repeatedly.

Use compatible fasteners

Stainless steel fasteners are often preferred for exterior wood because they resist corrosion and staining.

Plan around windows and doors

Flashing details decide where water goes. Good siding depends on good flashing.

Allow for movement

Thermally modified wood moves less than untreated wood, but it still moves. Installers should follow manufacturer spacing and fastening guidance.

A beautiful siding wall is really a system. The boards are the visible layer, but the hidden layers protect the investment.

📷Careful installation helps thermally modified siding dry properly after Houston rain.

Maintenance is simple, but not optional

Thermally modified siding reduces some common wood-siding headaches, but it still needs care. The maintenance plan depends on the desired look.

If the goal is to keep the warm brown color, use an exterior finish made for modified wood or high-quality exterior cladding. Follow the finish maker’s schedule. Sun-facing walls usually need attention sooner than shaded walls.

If the goal is a weathered gray look, the siding may not need the same color upkeep. Even then, it should be checked for dirt buildup, blocked ventilation, damaged boards, and failed flashing nearby.

Basic maintenance usually includes:

Rinsing dirt and pollen from the surface

Keeping plants trimmed away from the wall

Checking caulk and flashing at penetrations

Reapplying oil or stain when the finish starts to fade

Watching areas where sprinklers hit the siding

Clearing leaves and debris from horizontal ledges

The biggest mistake is treating wood siding like stone. Wood breathes. It responds to climate. A small amount of regular care protects the look and helps the system perform.

Where thermally modified siding works best

Thermally modified siding makes the most sense when appearance and performance both matter. It is a strong fit for homeowners who want natural materials but do not want the higher movement often linked to standard exterior wood.

It is especially well suited for:

Custom homes with modern or transitional design

Renovations that need a warm exterior accent

Covered outdoor living spaces

High-visibility facades

Rainscreen wall systems

Projects where chemical-free modification is preferred

It can also pair well with decking and other exterior wood features. Some suppliers offer related products across species and profiles, including Thermowoods, ash, pine decking and siding, cladding options for coordinated projects.

For builders and designers, consistency matters. A reliable supply of properly modified boards helps reduce surprises during installation. This is where experienced sourcing support from companies such as US Lumber Brokers Houston Texas can help connect material selection with real project demands.

What to ask before choosing a product

Not all thermally modified siding is the same. The process, species, profile, drying, packaging, and handling all affect the finished result. Before choosing boards, ask clear questions.

What species is used?

Ash, pine, and other species can all be modified, but they do not look or work exactly the same.

What profile is available?

Shiplap, tongue and groove, rainscreen profiles, and square-edge boards each have different installation needs.

Is the product rated for exterior siding?

Interior paneling and exterior cladding are not the same thing.

What fastening method is recommended?

Some profiles work with hidden clips. Others require face fastening.

What finish system is recommended?

Ask whether the supplier recommends oil, stain, factory finish, or natural weathering.

How should boards be stored before installation?

Wood should stay dry, flat, and protected before it goes on the wall.

What installation guide should the crew follow?

A written guide helps avoid guesswork on spacing, fasteners, ventilation, and end sealing.

The best projects happen when the material, installer, and design details match from the start.

📷Thermally modified wood works well for patios, entries, soffits, and exterior accent walls.

The takeaway for Houston homes

Thermally modified siding earns attention because it solves a real problem. Houston homes need exterior materials that can handle humidity, heat, and sudden rain without giving up style. Modified wood brings the character of natural boards while improving stability and decay resistance.

It is not a magic material. It still needs smart design, proper installation, and routine care. But when those pieces come together, it can deliver a long-lasting exterior with warmth that synthetic materials often struggle to match.

For a Houston home that needs siding with beauty, strength, and climate-aware performance, thermally modified wood is a superior choice worth serious consideration.

text:
The Reflexive Low: April 2020 as Generational Marker

On April 20, 2020, something happened that no textbook had predicted. The price of West Texas Intermediate crude oil went negative. Traders were paying others to take delivery of a commodity that had powered every industrial revolution since the internal combustion engine.

At the same time, government bond yields across the developed world were touching zero — or plunging below it. The German 10-year Bund offered minus 0.85%. The Swiss 10-year was negative for years. The US 10-year briefly dipped below 0.5%. Trillions of dollars in sovereign debt traded with negative yields. You were paying governments for the privilege of lending them money.

These were not ordinary dislocations. They were, in the language of George Soros, the epitome — the very embodiment — of reflexivity. Moments where perceptions had so distorted fundamentals that reality itself seemed to break.

Soros’ theory of reflexivity argues that market participants do not passively observe reality.

They actively shape it.

This tool should allow individuals to input details about their accident, such as the date, time, location, and a description of events. Users can upload relevant documents like police reports, photos of the damage, and medical records. The tool will then help create a chronological timeline of the incident and its aftermath, which can be invaluable when speaking with legal professionals.

Furthermore, the tool will offer a structured way to list potential witnesses and their contact information, as well as a section to jot down questions for a lawyer. text:
Dear @missmongrel25, 

You are misunderstanding me, or probably, more likely, I have failed to be clear. 

I am not disputing that lower fuel costs benefit everyone concerned which may also include households and businesses. It is my understanding that the farmers, hauliers, agri-contractors, and others will be assuaged by a reduction in the cost of green diesel. Or that may be the package they arw offered and may accept. 

But I have made my point unclearly it seems, by the responses. So to be exact.

The point that I am making is wider than the one that you are disagreeing with me on. The stated demand of farmers, hauliers, agri-contractors, and others appears to be a rebate or reduction aimed at farmers, hauliers, agri-contractors, and others. 

If that is what is delivered, the campaign remains a sectoral pressure campaign. There is no guarantee that the public will benefit. If the public receives a secondary benefit then marvellous but as of today I am yet to hear that as a stated objective of the Moate meeting.

A genuinely general campaign would also address farm-gate prices, agricultural arrears, household heating costs, and the wider cost-of-living crisis for all the Irish people. 

The distinction is between a useful concession and a movement for broader reform.

I hope that my point is now clear. 

Mise le meas,
Graham

text:
For reporters working in war zones, documenting Israeli occupation and war crimes means directly facing the same violence they are trying to expose. VPol journalist Mira Rehawi (@mira_rehawi) was at Metropolis Cinema in Beirut on September 21, where she spoke to the filmmakers and journalists involved in the documentary about reporting under fire, information warfare, resistance through storytelling and the human realities behind the headlines, Journacide: The War on Truth. 

￭ Produced by Irish filmmaker Sean Murray (@sean_murray1) and Lebanese journalist Radwan Mortada (@radwanmortada), the documentary follows journalists in southern Lebanon as they work under Israeli fire, confront the destruction around them and attempt to continue reporting despite the risks.

￭ The film also looks beyond the footage, exploring the people behind the reporting, the relationships formed in the field and the emotional consequences of witnessing Israeli war crimes firsthand.

￭ Among the journalists featured is Steve Sweeney (@SweeneySteve), who worked alongside martyred journalist Hajj Ali Choeib (@cheib1970). His experience offers a closer look at what it means to return to the field after colleagues have been killed while doing the same work.
